children.title: Lineality-Space Cases
children.top_down_role: Lift geometry containing nontrivial bidirectional recession directions.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is a nonempty closed convex set in a finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C+L=C\), and \(q(C)\subseteq X/L\) contains no nonzero line.

notation.meaning: Canonical quotient map onto X modulo L.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional lineality decomposition for nonempty closed convex sets.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The lineality space satisfies
\[
L=\{d\in X:x+td\in C\text{ for every }x\in C\text{ and }t\in\mathbb R\}.
\]
Consequently, \(C+L=C\). The quotient recession cone obeys \(\operatorname{rec}(q(C))=q(\operatorname{rec}C)\), and its lineality space is trivial. Thus all two-sided unbounded directions of \(C\) are isolated in \(L\), while the quotient geometry is line-free.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lineality space consists of directions along which the set is invariant; quotienting by it removes every two-sided unbounded direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Lineality-Space Cases

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53

children.title: Translated-Cone Cases
children.top_down_role: Affine shifts of cone-based feasible regions.

assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq X\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}C=Q\), \(\operatorname{lin}C=Q\cap(-Q)\), and \(C-a=Q\).

notation.meaning: Closed convex cone determining the translated set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes affine translates of closed convex cones through recession geometry.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the translated cone \(C=a+Q\), translation does not alter asymptotic directions:
\[
\operatorname{rec}C=Q,
\qquad
\operatorname{lin}C=Q\cap(-Q).
\]
Conversely, a nonempty closed convex set \(C\) is a translate of its recession cone precisely when there exists \(a\in C\) such that \(C-a=\operatorname{rec}C\); in that case \(C=a+\operatorname{rec}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A translated closed cone has that cone as its recession cone, and this equality after recentering characterizes the translated-cone case.
knowledge_statements.title: Translated-Cone Cases

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

children.title: Pointed Quotient Reduction
children.top_down_role: Removal of lineality to expose pointed quotient geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq X\) is a closed convex cone.
\(L=Q\cap(-Q)\) and \(q:X\to X/L\) is the quotient map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q(Q)\) is a closed pointed convex cone and \(Q=q^{-1}(q(Q))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of a nonpointed closed cone by its full lineality space.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The quotient cone
\[
\bar Q=q(Q)\subseteq X/L
\]
is closed, convex, and pointed: \(\bar Q\cap(-\bar Q)=\{0\}\). Moreover, \(Q\) is saturated along \(L\), so
\[
Q=q^{-1}(\bar Q).
\]
Hence membership in \(Q\) is equivalent to membership of the quotient class in \(\bar Q\), while the discarded component records only unrestricted lineality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotienting a closed cone by its lineality produces a closed pointed cone, and the original cone is the quotient cone's full inverse image.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointed Quotient Reduction

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

children.title: Translation Recovery
children.top_down_role: Transfer between shifted representations and origin-centered cone descriptions.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=a+Q\) if and only if \(C-a\) is a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact criterion for recovering a translating apex from a convex set.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(a\in C\) recovers \(C\) as a translated cone exactly when
\[
C-a=\operatorname{rec}C.
\]
Equivalently, \(C-a\) must be closed under multiplication by every scalar \(t\geq0\). Under this condition the translation is \(C=a+Q\). The set of all valid translations is
\[
\{a\in C:C=a+Q\},
\]
and any two valid translations differ by an element of \(\operatorname{lin}Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is a valid translating apex exactly when recentering the set there yields its recession cone; valid apices differ only by lineality.
knowledge_statements.title: Translation Recovery

children.title: Polar Set Representations
children.top_down_role: Representation structure for polar convex sets.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is a nonempty closed convex set containing \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^\circ=\{z\in X:\sigma_C(z)\leq1\}\) and \(C=(C^\circ)^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polar-set representation for closed convex sets containing the origin.

source_refs.locator: 1.11 The Dual Space p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The polar and support-function descriptions coincide:
\[
C^\circ=\{z\in X:\langle z,x\rangle\leq1\ \text{for every }x\in C\}
       =\{z\in X:\sigma_C(z)\leq1\},
\qquad
\sigma_C(z)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle z,x\rangle.
\]
Because \(C\) is closed, convex, and contains the origin, the bipolar identity gives \((C^\circ)^\circ=C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar is the unit sublevel set of the support function, and polarizing twice recovers a closed convex set containing the origin.
knowledge_statements.title: Polar Set Representations

children.title: Dual Lift Constructions
children.top_down_role: Lifted descriptions transferred through dual geometric data.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Lift Constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-cone construction of a polar lift under explicit support-problem duality and attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in X:\exists y\in Y,\ b-Ax-By\in K\}\). If every support problem with finite value has zero duality gap and an attained dual optimum, then \[\sigma_C(z)=\min\{\langle b,w\rangle:w\in K^*,\ A^*w=z,\ B^*w=0\}\] whenever \(\sigma_C(z)<+\infty\). Consequently, \[C^\circ=\{z\in X:\exists w\in K^*,\ A^*w=z,\ B^*w=0,\ \langle b,w\rangle\leq1\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the lifted support problems have zero duality gap and attained dual optima, the polar has an exact existential representation over the dual cone.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone, \(A:X\to E\) and \(B:Y\to E\) are linear, and \(b\in E\).
\(C=\{x\in X:\exists y\in Y,\ b-Ax-By\in K\}\) is nonempty.
For every \(z\in X\) with \(\sigma_C(z)<+\infty\), the support conic program has zero duality gap and its dual minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^\circ=\{z\in X:\exists w\in K^*,\ A^*w=z,\ B^*w=0,\ \langle b,w\rangle\leq1\}\).

children.title: Polar-Lift Transfer
children.top_down_role: Correspondence between primal lift structure and polar representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Polar-Lift Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cone-duality transfer principle for exact finite-dimensional lifts under explicit support duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(C=\{x\in X:\exists y\in Y,\ b-Ax-By\in K\}\). If every support problem with finite value has zero duality gap and an attained dual optimum, then polarity transfers this lift from \(K\) to \(K^*\): \[C^\circ=\{z\in X:\exists w\in K^*,\ A^*w=z,\ B^*w=0,\ \langle b,w\rangle\leq1\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under attained, gap-free support duality, polarizing a conic lift replaces the primal cone by its dual and the lift variables by dual feasibility multipliers.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone, \(A:X\to E\) and \(B:Y\to E\) are linear, and \(b\in E\).
\(C=\{x\in X:\exists y\in Y,\ b-Ax-By\in K\}\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
For every \(z\in X\) with \(\sigma_C(z)<+\infty\), the support conic program has zero duality gap and its dual minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed \(K\)-lift of \(C\) yields the displayed \(K^*\)-lift of \(C^\circ\).

notation.meaning: The primal lift cone and its dual cone.

children.title: Nonclosed Polar Transfer
children.top_down_role: Closure-sensitive cases affecting polarity-based lift transfer.

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq X\) is nonempty and may be nonclosed or nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S^\circ=(\operatorname{cl}S)^\circ=(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S\cup\{0\}))^\circ\) and \((S^\circ)^\circ=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S\cup\{0\})\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the closure information necessarily lost when polarity is applied to a nonclosed lifted image.

source_refs.locator: 1.11 The Dual Space p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Polarity cannot distinguish a set from its closed convex hull after adjoining the origin:
\[
S^\circ=(\operatorname{cl}S)^\circ
=(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S\cup\{0\}))^\circ.
\]
Consequently,
\[
(S^\circ)^\circ=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S\cup\{0\}).
\]
Hence a polar lift transferred from a nonclosed projected image represents the same polar as its closure, and bipolar recovery returns the closed convex completion rather than the original nonclosed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity erases nonclosedness: a set and its closure have the same polar, while the bipolar returns the closed convex hull containing the origin.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Polar Transfer

children.title: Dual Cone Geometry
children.top_down_role: Faces, interiors, and structural features of dual cones.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^{**}=K\), \(\operatorname{lin}K=(\operatorname{span}K^*)^\perp\), and \(K\) is pointed iff \(\operatorname{int}K^*\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic finite-dimensional geometry of a closed convex cone and its dual.

source_refs.locator: 4.4 Symmetries, Dual Cones, and Facial Structure p. 167
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The dual cone
\[
K^*=\{z\in E:\langle z,x\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }x\in K\}
\]
is closed and convex, and the bipolar identity gives \(K^{**}=K\). Its span detects primal lineality:
\[
\operatorname{lin}K=(\operatorname{span}K^*)^\perp.
\]
Moreover, \(K\) is pointed if and only if \(K^*\) has nonempty interior in \(E\), while \(K\) has nonempty interior if and only if \(K^*\) is pointed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual cones are closed, recover closed primal cones by biduality, encode primal lineality through their span, and exchange pointedness with full dimensionality.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Cone Geometry

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional dual family associated with a linear inverse-image cone representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the inverse-image cone \(C=A^{-1}K\), \[C^*=\operatorname{cl}(A^*K^*)=\operatorname{cl}\{A^*w:w\in K^*\}.\] If \(A^*K^*\) is closed, this reduces to the exact representation \(C^*=A^*K^*\).

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone and \(A:X\to E\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^*=\operatorname{cl}(A^*K^*)\).

children.title: Primal-Dual Representation Transfer

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Representation Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional transfer from primal lifted feasibility to dual-cone support and valid-inequality representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(z\in X\) with finite support value, attained strong conic duality gives \[\sigma_C(z)=\sup\{\langle z,x\rangle:\exists y\in Y,\ b-Ax-By\in K\}=\min\{\langle b,w\rangle:w\in K^*,\ A^*w=z,\ B^*w=0\}.\] Consequently, for every \(z\in X\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), the inequality \(\langle z,x\rangle\leq\alpha\) is valid for all \(x\in C\) if and only if there exists \(w\in K^*\) satisfying \(A^*w=z\), \(B^*w=0\), and \(\langle b,w\rangle\leq\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under attained strong conic duality for every finite support problem, optimization over the primal lift equals an adjoint feasibility problem over the dual cone, and every valid linear inequality has a dual-multiplier certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone, \(A:X\to E\) and \(B:Y\to E\) are linear, and \(b\in E\).
\(C=\{x\in X:\exists y\in Y,\ b-Ax-By\in K\}\) is nonempty.
For every \(z\in X\) with \(\sigma_C(z)<+\infty\), the associated support conic program has zero duality gap and an attained dual minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(z\in X\) with \(\sigma_C(z)<+\infty\), \(\sigma_C(z)=\min\{\langle b,w\rangle:w\in K^*,\ A^*w=z,\ B^*w=0\}\).

children.title: Dualization Gap Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regularity-sensitive cases where expected representation transfer breaks down.

knowledge_statements.title: Dualization Gap Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic duality at the loss of strict primal feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(F\) be finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone, let \(A:E\to F\) be linear, and let \(c\in E\) and \(b\in F\). Define \(p^*=\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:x\in K,\ Ax=b\}\) and \(d^*=\sup\{\langle b,y\rangle:y\in F,\ c-A^*y\in K^*\}\). Weak duality gives \(d^*\le p^*\). If \(p^*\in\mathbb R\) and there exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{int}K\) with \(A\bar x=b\), then \(d^*=p^*\) and the dual optimum is attained. If instead every primal feasible point lies in \(\partial K\), zero gap and dual attainment are no longer guaranteed; nonclosed conic images can produce dual nonattainment or a positive duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite-dimensional conic primal-dual pair, strict primal feasibility and a finite primal value ensure zero duality gap and dual attainment. If all feasible points lie on the cone boundary, nonclosed conic images can instead cause nonattainment or a positive gap.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone, \(A:E\to F\) is linear, \(c\in E\), and \(b\in F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(A\bar x=b\) for some \(\bar x\in\operatorname{int}K\), then \(d^*=p^*\) and the dual optimum is attained; boundary-only feasibility supplies no such guarantee.

notation.meaning: Dual cone under the chosen inner product on E.
Adjoint of A under the chosen inner products.

children.top_down_role: Cone classes invariant under the relevant duality pairing.

knowledge_statements.title: Self-Dual Cone Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical finite-dimensional cone families under their standard Euclidean or trace pairings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A closed convex cone \(K\subseteq E\) is self-dual for an inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\) when \(K=K^*\), where \(K^*:=\{y\in E:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\ \text{for every }x\in K\}\). For every integer \(n\ge1\), canonical self-dual families under their standard pairings include the nonnegative orthant \(\mathbb R_+^n\), the Lorentz cone \(\mathcal L_n:=\{(t,u)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{n-1}:t\ge\|u\|_2\}\), and the positive-semidefinite cone \(\mathbb S_+^n\) with trace pairing \(\langle X,Y\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(XY)\). Finite Cartesian products of self-dual cones are self-dual under the product pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone is self-dual when it equals its dual under a specified inner product. The nonnegative orthants, Lorentz cones, positive-semidefinite cones, and finite products of such cones are self-dual under their standard pairings.
assumptions_latex: Each cone carries the stated standard pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathbb R_+^n)^*=\mathbb R_+^n\), \(\mathcal L_n^*=\mathcal L_n\), and \((\mathbb S_+^n)^*=\mathbb S_+^n\) under their standard pairings.

notation.meaning: Dual cone for the specified pairing.
Cone of real symmetric positive-semidefinite n-by-n matrices.

children.title: Self-Dual Lift Architectures
children.top_down_role: Lift structures preserving self-dual organization.

knowledge_statements.title: Self-Dual Lift Architectures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic lifts whose auxiliary cone is self-dual under a fixed pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A self-dual-cone lift of a convex set \(C\subseteq V\) is a representation \[C=\pi(K\cap L),\] where \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone satisfying \(K=K^*\) under a specified inner product, \(L\subseteq E\) is affine, and \(\pi:E\to V\) is linear. Equivalently, an affine conic formulation may be written \[C=\{x\in V:\exists z,\ Bx+Dz-e\in K\}.\] The architecture is proper when the affine image \(\{Bx+Dz-e:x,z\}\) meets \(\operatorname{int}K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A self-dual lift represents a convex set as a linear image of an affine slice of a cone equal to its dual under a specified pairing.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is closed and self-dual under the declared pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\pi(K\cap L)=\{x:\exists z,\ Bx+Dz-e\in K\}\) for compatible lift data.

notation.meaning: Affine slicing subspace in the lifted space.
Linear projection from the lifted space.

children.title: Self-Duality Transfer
children.top_down_role: Conditions governing passage from cone self-duality to lift self-duality.

knowledge_statements.title: Self-Duality Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer of a homogeneous conic lift to its dual cone under a constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\), \(V\), and \(W\) be finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed self-dual cone, and let \(A:E\to V\) and \(B:E\to W\) be linear. Define \(C:=A(K\cap\ker B)\). If \(\ker B\cap\operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing\), then \((K\cap\ker B)^*=K+\operatorname{range}B^*\), and consequently \[C^*=\{y\in V:A^*y\in K+\operatorname{range}B^*\}=\{y\in V:\exists z\in W,\ A^*y-B^*z\in K\}.\] Thus the dual cone has a lift over the same self-dual cone family, with changed linear maps and an auxiliary equality multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under strict feasibility, the dual of a cone represented by a self-dual conic lift has another lift over the same cone, with an auxiliary multiplier in the equality-constraint space.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed self-dual cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^*=\{y\in V:\exists z\in W,\ A^*y-B^*z\in K\}\).

notation.meaning: Dual cone of C under the pairing on V.
Adjoints under the selected inner products.

children.title: Pairing Dependence
children.top_down_role: Dependence of self-duality claims on the selected inner product or pairing.

knowledge_statements.title: Pairing Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of cone duality and self-duality on the chosen inner product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a reference Euclidean inner product on a finite-dimensional space \(E\), let \(K\subseteq E\) be a convex cone, and let \(G:E\to E\) be self-adjoint and positive definite. For the modified inner product \(\langle x,y\rangle_G:=\langle Gx,y\rangle\), the dual cone is \[K^{*G}:=\{y\in E:\langle x,y\rangle_G\ge0\ \text{for every }x\in K\}=G^{-1}K^*.\] Consequently, self-duality under the reference pairing does not imply self-duality under every pairing: \(K=K^{*G}\) holds exactly when \(GK=K^*\). Adjoints used in transferred lift formulas must likewise be computed with respect to the selected pairings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing the inner product transforms a cone's dual by the inverse metric. Hence self-duality and adjoint-based lift formulas depend on the selected pairing.
assumptions_latex: \(G:E\to E\) is self-adjoint and positive definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^{*G}=G^{-1}K^*\), and \(K\) is self-dual under the G-weighted inner product exactly when \(GK=K^*\).

notation.meaning: Dual cone under the G-weighted inner product.

children.title: Proper Lift Regime
children.top_down_role: Lift configurations satisfying the relevant interior regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Proper Lift Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Slater-type properness for an affine slice of a closed convex cone with nonempty ambient interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(V\) be finite-dimensional spaces, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone with \(\operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing\), let \(L\subseteq E\) be affine, and let \(\pi:E\to V\) be linear. The representation \(C=\pi(K\cap L)\) is a proper conic lift precisely when \[L\cap\operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing.\] Equivalently, the affine slice contains a point satisfying the cone constraint strictly. This is the standard Slater constraint qualification used in conic duality and exact dual-lift transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic representation is a proper lift when its affine slice contains a point in the ambient interior of the lifting cone, thereby satisfying the usual Slater condition.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone with \(\operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing\).
\(L\subseteq E\) is affine and \(\pi:E\to V\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The representation \(C=\pi(K\cap L)\) is a proper lift if and only if \(L\cap\operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Linear projection to the represented space.

children.title: Improper Lift Regime
children.top_down_role: Lift configurations confined to boundary faces of the cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Improper Lift Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible affine conic lifts that fail ambient strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(V\) be finite-dimensional spaces, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone with \(\operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing\), let \(L\subseteq E\) be affine, and let \(\pi:E\to V\) be linear. The representation \(C=\pi(K\cap L)\) is feasible but improper when \[K\cap L\ne\varnothing\quad\text{and}\quad L\cap\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing.\] Every lifted feasible point then lies in \(\partial K\), and the feasible slice is contained in a proper face of \(K\). Ambient Slater conclusions, including automatic closedness of relevant dual sums and dual attainment, cannot be invoked without facial reduction or another regularity condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic representation is feasible but improper when its lifted feasible slice is nonempty yet contains no point in the cone interior. All lifted feasible points then lie on the boundary, so ordinary Slater conclusions need not apply.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone with \(\operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing\).
\(L\subseteq E\) is affine and \(\pi:E\to V\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lift is feasible but improper exactly when \(K\cap L\ne\varnothing\) and \(L\cap\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Boundary of K in its ambient space.
Linear projection defining the represented set.

children.title: Properness Restoration
children.top_down_role: Facial restriction or reformulation used to recover regular lift geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Properness Restoration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facial reduction of an improper lift to its minimal cone face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a feasible lift \(C=\pi(K\cap L)\). Initialize \(F_0=K\). While \(L\cap\operatorname{ri}F_i=\varnothing\), find a nonzero exposing vector \(s_i\in F_i^*\) satisfying \(\langle s_i,x\rangle=0\) for every \(x\in L\cap F_i\), and set \(F_{i+1}=F_i\cap s_i^\perp\). Stop at the first \(F_r\) with \(L\cap\operatorname{ri}F_r\ne\varnothing\). Then \[K\cap L=F_r\cap L,\qquad C=\pi(F_r\cap L),\] so the reduced lift is proper relative to \(\operatorname{span}F_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facial reduction repeatedly replaces the cone by an exposed face containing the feasible slice until relative-interior feasibility—and hence relative properness—is obtained.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone admitting the required exposing certificates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The terminal face \(F_r\) satisfies \(K\cap L=F_r\cap L\) and \(L\cap\operatorname{ri}F_r\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Current face in the facial-reduction sequence.
Hyperplane orthogonal to the exposing vector.

children.title: Boundary-Only Feasibility
children.top_down_role: Feasible lifts whose conic variables cannot enter the required relative interior.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Only Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible slices contained entirely in the ambient boundary of the lifting cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone with nonempty interior and let \(L\subseteq E\) be affine. Boundary-only feasibility means \[\varnothing\ne K\cap L\subseteq\partial K.\] This is equivalent to \(K\cap L\ne\varnothing\) together with \(L\cap\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing\). Every such slice lies in a proper face of \(K\); replacing \(K\) by the minimal face containing \(K\cap L\) converts ambient boundary feasibility into relative-interior feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boundary-only feasibility occurs when a conic slice is nonempty but every feasible lifted point lies on the cone boundary; facial reduction can restore relative strict feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone with nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\cap L\subseteq\partial K\iff L\cap\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing\).

children.title: Closed Conic Images
children.top_down_role: Linear or affine cone images possessing closed visible geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Conic Images
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization and a standard sufficient regime for closed linear cone images.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(V\) be finite-dimensional spaces, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone, and let \(A:E\to V\) be linear. The conic image \(A(K)\) is closed exactly when, for every sequence \((x_j)_{j\ge1}\subseteq K\) such that \(Ax_j\to y\in V\), one has \(y\in A(K)\). Equivalently, every limit of image points has a preimage in \(K\). If \(K\) is polyhedral, then \(A(K)\) is polyhedral and hence closed for every linear map \(A\). Closedness need not hold for nonpolyhedral cones, including positive-semidefinite cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic image is closed exactly when every limit of image points remains attainable. Images of polyhedral cones are always closed, whereas images of nonpolyhedral cones such as positive-semidefinite cones need not be.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A(K)\) is closed if and only if \(A(K)=\overline{A(K)}\); this equality holds automatically when \(K\) is polyhedral.

notation.meaning: Linear image of the cone K.

children.title: Nonclosed Conic Images
children.top_down_role: Cone images missing visible limit points.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Conic Images
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A two-dimensional semidefinite image with an unattained boundary ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\mathbb S_+^2\) and define \(A:\mathbb S^2\to\mathbb R^2\) by \[A\!\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{smallmatrix}\right)=(a,b).\] Positive semidefiniteness implies either \(a>0\), in which case every \(b\in\mathbb R\) is possible by choosing \(c\ge b^2/a\), or \(a=0\) and \(b=0\). Hence \[A(K)=\{(a,b):a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\},\qquad \overline{A(K)}=\{(a,b):a\ge0\}.\] Thus \((0,1)\) lies in the closure but not in the image.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting a two-by-two positive-semidefinite matrix onto its first diagonal and off-diagonal entries gives a convex cone whose nonzero boundary points are unattained.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb S^2\) carries its usual Euclidean topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A(\mathbb S_+^2)\) is not closed because \((0,1)\in\overline{A(K)}\setminus A(K)\).

notation.meaning: Cone of two-by-two real positive-semidefinite matrices.

children.title: Image-Closure Completion
children.top_down_role: Closure-based comparison between an image and its completed visible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Image-Closure Completion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical completion of a conic image by bipolar closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone and \(A:E\to V\) linear. Although \(A(K)\) may be nonclosed, its canonical closed completion is \[\overline{A(K)}=A(K)^{**}=\{y\in V:\langle z,y\rangle\ge0\ \forall z\in V\text{ with }A^*z\in K^*\}.\] Here \(A(K)^*=\{z:A^*z\in K^*\}\), and the bipolar theorem supplies the second equality. The completion preserves all continuous linear inequalities valid on \(A(K)\), but it may add boundary points having no preimage in \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closure of any conic image is its bipolar, describable by all dual vectors whose adjoint images lie in the original dual cone.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone and \(A\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{A(K)}=A(K)^{**}=\{y:\langle z,y\rangle\ge0\ \forall z\text{ satisfying }A^*z\in K^*\}\).

notation.meaning: Adjoint of A under the chosen inner products.

children.title: Nonattained Image Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limit points lacking finite lifted witnesses.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\in\operatorname{cl}L(K)\setminus L(K)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional characterization of boundary points approached by, but not attained in, a conic image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(z\in Z\) lies on a nonattained image boundary when \(z\in\operatorname{cl}L(K)\setminus L(K)\). Equivalently, there exists a sequence \((u_k)_{k\geq1}\subseteq K\) such that \(L(u_k)\to z\), while the feasibility system \(u\in K\), \(L(u)=z\) has no solution. Thus every neighborhood of \(z\) meets \(L(K)\), but \(z\) itself has no conic preimage. This phenomenon is possible even though \(K\) is closed, because a linear image of a closed convex cone need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonattained boundary point is the limit of images of cone points but has no cone point mapping to it.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonattained Image Boundary

children.title: Minimal Face Identification
children.top_down_role: Smallest cone face containing the lifted feasible region.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Face Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identification of the smallest cone face supporting all feasible lifted slacks in finite dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(S:=K\cap H\), define
\[
F_{\min}:=\bigcap\{F:F\text{ is a face of }K\text{ and }S\subseteq F\}.
\]
Then \(F_{\min}\) is the unique face of \(K\) such that \(S\subseteq F_{\min}\), \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_{\min}\neq\varnothing\), and \(F_{\min}\subseteq F\) for every face \(F\) of \(K\) containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite-dimensional space, the minimal face is the unique smallest face containing the nonempty feasible slack set, and that set meets its relative interior.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone, \(H\subseteq E\) is affine, and \(S:=K\cap H\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\min}\) is the unique smallest face containing \(S\), and \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_{\min}\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Minimal face of the cone containing the feasible slacks

children.title: Reduced Lift Construction
children.top_down_role: Lift reformulation over the identified face or a lower-dimensional cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduced Lift Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reduction of a nonempty conic lift to its minimal feasible face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
S:=\{Ax+By+b:(x,y)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^q,\ Ax+By+b\in K\},
\]
and let \(F_{\min}\) be the minimal face of \(K\) containing \(S\). The reduced representation is
\[
C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^q,\ Ax+By+b\in F_{\min}\}.
\]
Its feasible slack set meets \(\operatorname{ri}F_{\min}\). If \(J:E_F\to E\) is injective and \(J(K_F)=F_{\min}\), the equivalent parameterized representation is
\[
C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^q,\exists u\in K_F,\ Ax+By+b=Ju\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty conic lift can be restricted exactly to the minimal face containing all feasible slacks, where relative-interior feasibility holds.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone, \(A:\mathbb R^n\to E\) and \(B:\mathbb R^q\to E\) are linear, and \(b\in E\).
\(F_{\min}\) is the minimal face of \(K\) containing the feasible slack set \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^q,\ Ax+By+b\in F_{\min}\}\) and \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_{\min}\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Relative interior of the minimal face

knowledge_statements.title: Facial Reduction Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One facial-reduction step exposed by a certificate of failed relative strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exists
\[
y\in K^*\cap L^\perp\setminus K^\perp
\quad\text{with}\quad
\langle y,h_0\rangle=0.
\]
Every point of \(K\cap H\) belongs to the proper exposed face \(K\cap y^\perp\). Replacing \(K\) by this face preserves \(K\cap H\) and constitutes one facial-reduction step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure of relative strict feasibility yields a dual certificate exposing a proper face that contains every feasible slack.

\(H=h_0+L\subseteq E\) is affine, where \(L\) is a linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(y\in K^*\cap L^\perp\setminus K^\perp\) with \(\langle y,h_0\rangle=0\) such that \(K\cap H\subseteq K\cap y^\perp\lhd K\).

children.title: Irreducible Face Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits on further cone or dimension reduction.

knowledge_statements.title: Irreducible Face Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stopping boundary for facial reduction after passage to the minimal feasible face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The minimal feasible face satisfies
\[
H\cap\operatorname{ri}F_{\min}\neq\varnothing.
\]
Consequently, there is no nonzero \(y\in F_{\min}^{*,\mathrm{int}}\cap L^\perp\) satisfying \(\langle y,h_0\rangle=0\), where
\[
F_{\min}^{*,\mathrm{int}}:=\{y\in\operatorname{span}F_{\min}:\langle y,f\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }f\in F_{\min}\}.
\]
Thus no intrinsic certificate exposes a proper face of \(F_{\min}\) containing all feasible slacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facial reduction stops at the minimal feasible face because the affine slack set meets that face's relative interior and no further intrinsic reducing certificate exists.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional Euclidean space and \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone.
\(F_{\min}\) is the minimal face of \(K\) containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\cap\operatorname{ri}F_{\min}\neq\varnothing\), and no nonzero intrinsic reducing certificate exposes a proper feasible subface of \(F_{\min}\).

children.title: Intersection Constructions

knowledge_statements.title: Intersection Constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite intersections formed by stacking independent conic lift constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The finite intersection has the product-cone representation
\[
\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i
=
\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y_i\in\mathbb R^{q_i}\ \text{for every }i,\ 
\bigl(A_i x+B_i y_i+b_i\bigr)_{i=1}^m
\in\prod_{i=1}^m K_i\right\}.
\]
The construction uses independent auxiliary witnesses and the Cartesian product of the lifting cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite intersection is represented by stacking the individual lift constraints, with independent auxiliary witnesses in the product cone.
assumptions_latex: For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), \(E_i\) is a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, \(K_i\subseteq E_i\) is a convex cone, \(A_i:\mathbb R^n\to E_i\) and \(B_i:\mathbb R^{q_i}\to E_i\) are linear, and \(b_i\in E_i\).
\(C_i:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y_i\in\mathbb R^{q_i},\ A_i x+B_i y_i+b_i\in K_i\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\) has the displayed lift over \(\prod_{i=1}^m K_i\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Cartesian product admits the block-separable representation
\[
\prod_{i=1}^m C_i
=
\left\{(x_1,\ldots,x_m):\exists(y_1,\ldots,y_m),\ 
\bigl(A_i x_i+B_i y_i+b_i\bigr)_{i=1}^m
\in\prod_{i=1}^m K_i\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, the defining affine map is block diagonal in the pairs \((x_i,y_i)\). Each product coordinate has its own conic witness, so feasibility of the combined lift is equivalent to coordinatewise membership \(x_i\in C_i\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Cartesian product of conically represented sets has a block-diagonal lift over the Cartesian product of their cones.
knowledge_statements.title: Cartesian-Product Constructions

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:\exists u,\ \Phi_i(x,u)\in K_i\ \forall i\}=\{x:\bigcap_i U_i(x)\neq\varnothing\}\subseteq\bigcap_i C_i\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition required when several lift constraints reuse one auxiliary variable.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.3 Tractable representation of (2.17): general case p. 44

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(x\), the shared-auxiliary system is feasible exactly when
\[
\bigcap_{i=1}^m U_i(x)\neq\varnothing.
\]
Therefore
\[
\{x:\exists u,\ \Phi_i(x,u)\in K_i\text{ for all }i\}
\subseteq\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i.
\]
Equality holds precisely when every \(x\in\bigcap_i C_i\) has mutually compatible witnesses, meaning \(\bigcap_i U_i(x)\neq\varnothing\). Separate existence of some witness in each \(U_i(x)\) does not imply existence of one common witness; absent the compatibility condition, sharing auxiliaries can strictly shrink the represented intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shared auxiliary represents the full intersection exactly when every common point has one witness satisfying all lifted systems simultaneously.

children.title: Dimension Growth Boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension Growth Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive size bound for the canonical product-cone construction, without a minimality claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the canonical independent-block construction, the combined auxiliary vector belongs to \(\mathbb R^{q_1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb R^{q_m}\), and the product cone has ambient dimension \(d_1+\cdots+d_m\). Hence
\[
q_{\mathrm{prod}}=\sum_{i=1}^m q_i,
\qquad
d_{\mathrm{prod}}=\sum_{i=1}^m d_i.
\]
The construction uses \(m\) affine-conic blocks. These equalities describe the canonical construction and do not assert lower bounds on extension complexity; shared auxiliaries or a different representation may have smaller dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The canonical product construction adds the auxiliary and cone dimensions across factors, while alternative coordinated representations may be smaller.
assumptions_latex: For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), the ith lift uses an auxiliary space of dimension \(q_i\) and a cone whose ambient space has dimension \(d_i\).
The canonical product construction keeps all auxiliary and cone blocks independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_{\mathrm{prod}}=\sum_{i=1}^m q_i\) and \(d_{\mathrm{prod}}=\sum_{i=1}^m d_i\).

notation.meaning: Auxiliary dimension of the ith lift

children.title: Affine-Image Constructions
children.top_down_role: Forward transport of represented sets through affine maps.

assumptions_latex: \(T(x)=Mx+t\) is an affine map into \(\mathbb R^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(C)=\{z:\exists x,y,\ z=Mx+t,\ Ax+By+b\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended conic representation of an affine image, retaining the original point as an auxiliary variable.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.3 Tractable representation of (2.17): general case p. 44

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The affine image has the extended representation
\[
T(C)=\{z\in\mathbb R^p:\exists x,y,\ z=Mx+t,\ Ax+By+b\in K\}.
\]
The equality constraint \(z=Mx+t\) is an affine constraint in the lift and may equivalently be encoded using a zero-cone factor. The construction is exact: a feasible pair \((x,y)\) establishes both \(x\in C\) and \(z=T(x)\), while every \(z\in T(C)\) has such an \(x\) and inherits a conic witness \(y\). No injectivity or full-rank assumption on \(M\) is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine image is represented by retaining the original point as an auxiliary variable and imposing the affine image equation.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Image Constructions

children.title: Affine-Preimage Constructions
children.top_down_role: Pullback of represented sets through affine maps.

assumptions_latex: \(T(x)=Mx+t\) is an affine map from \(\mathbb R^n\) to \(\mathbb R^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^{-1}(C)=\{x:\exists y,\ AMx+By+(At+b)\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine preimages obtained by direct substitution into a conic lift.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Tractable representation of (2.17): simple cases p. 43

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Substitution of the affine map into the lift gives
\[
T^{-1}(C)
=
\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y,\ A(Mx+t)+By+b\in K\}
=
\{x:\exists y,\ AMx+By+(At+b)\in K\}.
\]
Thus affine preimages preserve conic representability without introducing an auxiliary copy of the image variable. The lifting cone and original auxiliary dimension remain unchanged. The construction is exact for every affine map \(T\); neither injectivity, surjectivity, nor a rank condition on \(M\) is needed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine preimage is represented by substituting the affine map into the original conic constraint, with no new auxiliary variable.

children.title: Map Composition Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Representation transport across composed affine mappings.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((T\circ S)^{-1}(C)=S^{-1}(T^{-1}(C))\), with substitution matrix \(MN\) and offset \(Ms+t\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functorial compatibility of affine substitution with conic preimage representations.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Tractable representation of (2.17): simple cases p. 43

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The composition is
\[
(T\circ S)(w)=M(Nw+s)+t=MNw+(Ms+t),
\]
and affine preimages obey
\[
(T\circ S)^{-1}(C)=S^{-1}\bigl(T^{-1}(C)\bigr).
\]
If \(C=\{z:\exists y,\ Az+By+b\in K\}\), either direct substitution of \(T\circ S\) or successive substitution first by \(T\) and then by \(S\) yields
\[
\{w:\exists y,\ AMNw+By+A(Ms+t)+b\in K\}.
\]
Hence the conic representation calculus is compatible with affine-map composition, including rank-deficient maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Direct substitution of a composed affine map gives exactly the same conic preimage lift as two successive substitutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Map Composition Compatibility

children.title: Rank-Deficient Map Boundary
children.top_down_role: Dimension loss, redundant fibers, or degeneracy caused by deficient maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Deficient Map Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A semidefinite image showing that a rank-deficient linear map need not preserve closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K=\mathbb S_+^2\) and define \(L:\mathbb S^2\to\mathbb R^3\) by \(L(X)=(X_{11},X_{12},0)\). The map has rank \(2<3\), and
\[
L(K)=\{(a,b,0):a>0\}\cup\{(0,0,0)\}.
\]
Indeed, \((a,b,0)\in L(K)\) exactly when there exists \(c\in\mathbb R\) such that \(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\). Consequently, \((1/k,1,0)\in L(K)\) for every positive integer \(k\), whereas \((1/k,1,0)\to(0,1,0)\notin L(K)\). Thus a closed convex cone can have a nonclosed image under a rank-deficient linear map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A genuinely rank-deficient linear image of the closed two-by-two positive-semidefinite cone can fail to be closed.
assumptions_latex: \(K=\mathbb S_+^2\) is the cone of two-by-two real positive-semidefinite matrices.

notation.meaning: cone of two-by-two real positive-semidefinite matrices

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Admissible aggregation certificate for a scalar consequence of a conic inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier characterization of scalar affine consequences of a cone-ordered linear vector inequality; strict feasibility is required for the general conic converse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
(V):\ Ax-b\in K,
\qquad
(S):\ c^Tx\ge d.
\]
If there exists \(\lambda\in K_*\) such that
\[
A^T\lambda=c,\qquad \lambda^Tb\ge d,
\]
then \((S)\) is a consequence of \((V)\). Conversely, if \((V)\) is strictly feasible and \((S)\) is a consequence of \((V)\), then such a vector \(\lambda\in K_*\) exists. For the coordinatewise order \(K=\mathbb{R}_+^m\), strict feasibility may be omitted from the converse; for a general cone order it cannot in general be omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual-cone multiplier whose aggregation reproduces the scalar inequality certifies that the inequality follows from the conic vector system. Under strict feasibility, every such scalar consequence has this multiplier representation. For coordinatewise linear inequalities the converse does not require strict feasibility, unlike the general conic case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\exists\lambda\in K_*:\ A^T\lambda=c,\ \lambda^Tb\ge d\bigr]\Rightarrow\bigl[(V)\Rightarrow(S)\bigr],\quad \operatorname{strict\ feasibility}(V)\Rightarrow\left(\bigl[(V)\Rightarrow(S)\bigr]\Rightarrow\exists\lambda\in K_*:\ A^T\lambda=c,\ \lambda^Tb\ge d\right),\quad K=\mathbb R_+^m\text{ permits omission of strict feasibility in the converse}.

children.title: Minkowski-Sum Constructions
children.top_down_role: Representations of sums formed from independently selected set elements.

knowledge_statements.title: Minkowski-Sum Constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-cone lift for a finite Minkowski sum of conically represented sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\in\mathbb N\). For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), let \(U_i\) and \(E_i\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(K_i\subseteq E_i\) be a convex cone, let \(A_i:\mathbb R^n\to E_i\) and \(B_i:U_i\to E_i\) be linear, let \(c_i\in E_i\), and suppose
\[
S_i=\{x_i\in\mathbb R^n:\exists u_i\in U_i,\ A_i x_i+B_i u_i+c_i\in K_i\}.
\]
Then
\[
S_1+\cdots+S_m=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists(x_i,u_i)\in\mathbb R^n\times U_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ x=\sum_{i=1}^m x_i,\ (A_i x_i+B_i u_i+c_i)_{i=1}^m\in\prod_{i=1}^mK_i\right\}.
\]
Thus the component conic constraints remain separate, while one linear equation couples their visible variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite Minkowski sum is represented by independent component lifts and one equation setting the output equal to the sum of the component points.
assumptions_latex: For each \(i\), \(S_i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) has the displayed conic lift over a convex cone \(K_i\subseteq E_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed product-cone lift projects exactly onto \(S_1+\cdots+S_m\).

notation.meaning: set of sums containing one point from each component set

children.title: Linear-Aggregation Constructions
children.top_down_role: Representations formed by linear aggregation of multiple represented components.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Aggregation Constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lift for sums of linear images of independently represented component sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\in\mathbb N\). For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), let \(X_i,U_i,E_i\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(K_i\subseteq E_i\) be a convex cone, let \(A_i:X_i\to E_i\), \(B_i:U_i\to E_i\), and \(L_i:X_i\to\mathbb R^p\) be linear maps, let \(c_i\in E_i\), and define
\[
S_i=\{x_i\in X_i:\exists u_i\in U_i,\ A_i x_i+B_i u_i+c_i\in K_i\}.
\]
Then the linear aggregate
\[
T=\sum_{i=1}^mL_iS_i:=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^mL_i x_i:x_i\in S_i\right\}
\]
has the conic lift
\[
T=\left\{y\in\mathbb R^p:\exists(x_i,u_i)\in X_i\times U_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ y=\sum_{i=1}^mL_i x_i,\ (A_i x_i+B_i u_i+c_i)_{i=1}^m\in\prod_{i=1}^mK_i\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sum of linear images is represented by imposing each component lift independently and coupling the components through the output aggregation equation.
assumptions_latex: Each \(S_i\subseteq X_i\) has the displayed conic representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed lifted set projects exactly onto \(\sum_{i=1}^mL_iS_i\).

linear aggregate of the component sets

children.title: Component Coupling Structure
children.top_down_role: Shared variables or constraints linking aggregated components.

knowledge_statements.title: Component Coupling Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of local cone constraints from the global linear aggregation constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\in\mathbb N\). For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), let \(X_i,U_i,E_i\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(K_i\subseteq E_i\) be a convex cone, let \(A_i:X_i\to E_i\), \(B_i:U_i\to E_i\), and \(L_i:X_i\to\mathbb R^p\) be linear, and let \(c_i\in E_i\). For variables \(x_i\in X_i\), \(u_i\in U_i\), and \(y\in\mathbb R^p\), define \(w_i=A_i x_i+B_i u_i+c_i\). Feasibility of the aggregate lift is equivalent to
\[
w_i\in K_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad y-\sum_{i=1}^mL_i x_i=0.
\]
Hence the conic constraints are block-separable over \(K_1\times\cdots\times K_m\), and distinct component blocks interact only through the linear output equation. Removing that equation leaves the Cartesian product of the component lifts; imposing it selects the tuples producing the specified aggregate \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The component cone constraints are block-separable, and all cross-component interaction is concentrated in the linear equation defining the aggregate output.
assumptions_latex: Each component has variables \((x_i,u_i)\in X_i\times U_i\) and cone constraint \(A_i x_i+B_i u_i+c_i\in K_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lift is product-cone separable except for the linear coupling equation \(y-\sum_{i=1}^mL_i x_i=0\).

notation.meaning: component slack expression belonging to the cone K_i

children.title: Aggregation Closure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Closedness or attainment issues in aggregated images.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation Closure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed component sets can have a nonclosed Minkowski sum or linear aggregate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ xy\ge 1\},\qquad D=\{0\}\times\mathbb R.
\]
Both \(C\) and \(D\) are closed convex sets, but
\[
C+D=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0\},
\]
which is not closed. Equivalently, aggregation with the closed linear subspace \(D\) acts as a projection whose image loses closedness. Therefore finite-dimensional closedness and convexity of all component sets do not suffice to make a Minkowski sum, or the associated lifted linear image, closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even two closed convex sets can have a nonclosed Minkowski sum; additional boundedness, compactness, or recession regularity is needed for closedness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C+D=\{(x,t):x>0\}\) is convex but not closed.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of the two sets

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lifted Conic Representation of a Finite-Union Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disjunctive homogenization of finitely many nonempty convex conic-quadratic-representable sets, including the closure gap and two exactness regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(i=1,\ldots,k\), let \(X_i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, with \(X_i=\{x\mid \exists u_i:\ A_ix+B_iu_i+b_i\geq_{\mathbf K_i}0\}\), where each \(\mathbf K_i\) is a direct product of second-order cones. Define \(Y\) by the existence of \(\xi^i,\eta^i,t_i\) satisfying \[A_i\xi^i+B_i\eta^i+t_ib_i\geq_{\mathbf K_i}0\quad(i=1,\ldots,k),\qquad t_i\geq0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^kt_i=1,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^k\xi^i=x.\] Then \[\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^kX_i\right)\subseteq Y\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^kX_i\right).\] If either every \(X_i\) is closed and bounded, or \(X_i=Z_i+W\) for closed bounded sets \(Z_i\) and a common closed convex set \(W\), then all three sets are equal. Consequently, the convex hull of the union is conic-quadratic representable in either exactness regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard homogenized disjunctive formulation lies between the convex hull of finitely many nonempty convex second-order-cone-representable sets and its closure. It is exact when all disjuncts are closed and bounded, or when they have closed bounded parts plus a common closed convex summand.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf K_i\text{ is a direct product of second-order cones}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iX_i)\subseteq Y\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\bigcup_iX_i);\quad [\forall i,\ X_i\text{ closed and bounded}]\ \lor\ [X_i=Z_i+W,\ Z_i\text{ closed and bounded},\ W\text{ common, closed, and convex}]\Rightarrow Y=\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iX_i)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\bigcup_iX_i).

children.title: Convex-Hull Constructions
children.top_down_role: Lifted representations of convex hulls generated from constituent sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Hull Constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogenized lift of the convex hull of finitely many compact convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S_1,\ldots,S_m\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty compact convex sets and define
\[
H_i=\{(z,\lambda):\lambda\ge0,\ z\in\lambda S_i\},
\]
with \(0S_i=\{0\}\). Then
\[
\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^mS_i\right)=\left\{x:\exists(z_i,\lambda_i)_{i=1}^m,\ x=\sum_i z_i,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1,\ (z_i,\lambda_i)\in H_i\right\}.
\]
If each homogenized cone \(H_i\) has a conic lift, their product together with the two displayed linear equations is a conic lift of the convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of finitely many compact convex sets is obtained by homogenizing each set, weighting its block, and summing the blocks.
assumptions_latex: Each \(S_i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed homogenized formulation equals \(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iS_i)\).

notation.meaning: homogenized cone over the component set
scaled point contributed by component i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compact-set homogenized convex-hull formulation is mathematically precise and the representation content kind fits the leaf, but no source or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Disjunctive Constructions
children.top_down_role: Representations organized around alternatives or set unions.

knowledge_statements.title: Disjunctive Constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixed-integer homogenized representation of a finite union of compact convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\in\mathbb N\), let \(S_1,\ldots,S_m\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty compact convex sets, and define
\[
H_i=\{(z,\lambda)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:\lambda\ge0,\ z\in\lambda S_i\},
\]
using the convention \(0S_i=\{0\}\). Then
\[
\bigcup_{i=1}^mS_i=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists(z_i,\lambda_i)\in H_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ x=\sum_{i=1}^m z_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1,\ \lambda_i\in\{0,1\}\ (i=1,\ldots,m)\right\}.
\]
The binary simplex constraint selects exactly one component. Its block satisfies \(z_i\in S_i\), while every inactive block vanishes. If every \(H_i\) has a conic lift, the system gives a mixed-integer conic representation of the union.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary simplex selectors and homogenized component blocks give an exact mixed-integer conic representation of a finite union of compact convex sets.
assumptions_latex: Each \(S_i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
Each homogenized set \(H_i\) is conically representable when the final mixed-integer conic conclusion is invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed binary formulation projects exactly onto \(\bigcup_{i=1}^mS_i\).

children.title: Disjunctive Hull Interface
children.top_down_role: Passage from alternative-set descriptions to convexified representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Disjunctive Hull Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous relaxation of the selector formulation recovers the convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the homogenized disjunctive formulation for nonempty compact convex sets \(S_i\). Replacing
\[
\lambda_i\in\{0,1\},\qquad \sum_i\lambda_i=1
\]
by
\[
\lambda_i\ge0,\qquad \sum_i\lambda_i=1
\]
changes its projection from \(\bigcup_iS_i\) to \(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iS_i)\). Consequently the convex-hull construction is precisely the continuous relaxation of the binary disjunctive construction in the same extended variables. When every \(H_i\) is represented exactly, this relaxation is ideal at the level of the visible variable \(x\): its projected feasible region is the disjunctive hull, not a larger convex relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxing binary selectors to simplex weights converts the union formulation exactly into the convex-hull formulation in the visible variables.
assumptions_latex: The component sets are nonempty, compact, and convex.
The same exact homogenized blocks \(H_i\) are used in both formulations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The continuous selector relaxation projects onto \(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iS_i)\).

notation.meaning: binary selector or relaxed simplex weight

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Under the stated compactness assumptions and exact homogenized blocks, the relaxation claim is correct and the property content kind fits the interface leaf. No source or inspectable locator is supplied for the ideal-formulation assertion.

children.title: Recession Compatibility Boundary
children.top_down_role: Unbounded constituent behavior affecting hull exactness or closedness.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Compatibility Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-weight homogenized blocks expose recession directions and possible hull nonclosedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty closed convex set \(S_i\), let
\[
\widehat H_i=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}\{(x,1):x\in S_i\}.
\]
Its zero-weight slice is
\[
\{d:(d,0)\in\widehat H_i\}=\operatorname{rec}(S_i).
\]
Thus a homogenized hull formulation may admit nonzero recession contributions from blocks with \(\lambda_i=0\), and in general its projection represents \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iS_i)\), not necessarily the unclosed hull. If the finitely many sets share a common recession cone, then their convex hull is closed and has that recession cone; this compatibility removes the closure gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For unbounded sets, zero-weight blocks can carry recession directions. A common recession cone prevents the resulting homogenized formulation from adding closure points.
assumptions_latex: Each \(S_i\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
Only finitely many component sets are present.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Zero-weight slices equal \(\operatorname{rec}(S_i)\); a common recession cone ensures the finite disjunctive hull is closed.

children.title: Epigraph Calculus
children.top_down_role: Representation-preserving operations for convex upper-value sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic epigraph construction for positive weighted sums of convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\in\mathbb N\). For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), let \(f_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and convex, let \(U_i,E_i\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(K_i\subseteq E_i\) be a convex cone, let \(A_i:\mathbb R^n\to E_i\) and \(B_i:U_i\to E_i\) be linear, and let \(a_i,c_i\in E_i\). Suppose
\[
\operatorname{epi}f_i=\{(x,t_i)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:\exists u_i\in U_i,\ A_i x+a_i t_i+B_i u_i+c_i\in K_i\}.
\]
For \(\alpha_i>0\), define \(f=\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i f_i\). Then
\[
\operatorname{epi}f=\left\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:\exists(t_i,u_i)\in\mathbb R\times U_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ t\ge\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i t_i,\ A_i x+a_i t_i+B_i u_i+c_i\in K_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m)\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of a positive finite weighted sum is represented using one epigraph block per summand and an inequality aggregating their upper bounds.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is proper and convex and has the displayed epigraph lift.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed product-cone system represents \(\operatorname{epi}(\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i f_i)\).

children.title: Hypograph Calculus
children.top_down_role: Representation-preserving operations for concave lower-value sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Hypograph Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic hypograph construction for positive weighted sums of concave functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\in\mathbb N\). For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), let \(g_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\) be proper and concave, let \(U_i,E_i\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(K_i\subseteq E_i\) be a convex cone, let \(A_i:\mathbb R^n\to E_i\) and \(B_i:U_i\to E_i\) be linear, and let \(a_i,c_i\in E_i\). Suppose
\[
\operatorname{hypo}g_i=\{(x,s_i)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:\exists u_i\in U_i,\ A_i x+a_i s_i+B_i u_i+c_i\in K_i\}.
\]
For \(\alpha_i>0\), define \(g=\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i g_i\). Then
\[
\operatorname{hypo}g=\left\{(x,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:\exists(s_i,u_i)\in\mathbb R\times U_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ s\le\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i s_i,\ A_i x+a_i s_i+B_i u_i+c_i\in K_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m)\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hypograph of a positive finite weighted sum is represented using one hypograph block per summand and an inequality aggregating their lower bounds.
assumptions_latex: Each \(g_i\) is proper and concave and has the displayed hypograph lift.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed product-cone system represents \(\operatorname{hypo}(\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i g_i)\).

children.title: Graph-Level Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Shared boundary structure linking epi- and hypographic representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Level Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition for obtaining a function graph from convex epigraph and hypograph lifts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\). Then
\[
\operatorname{graph}f=\operatorname{epi}f\cap\operatorname{hypo}f.
\]
The graph is convex if and only if
\[
f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)=\theta f(x)+(1-\theta)f(y)
\]
for all \(x,y\in D\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\), meaning that \(f\) is affine on \(D\). Consequently, simultaneous convex-conic epigraph and hypograph representations can be combined into a convex-conic graph representation only when their domains and level coordinates agree and the represented function is affine on the convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compatible epigraph and hypograph lifts describe a convex function graph only when they share a domain and level coordinate and the function is affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{graph}f\) is convex if and only if \(f\) is affine on \(D\).

children.title: Curvature Mismatch Boundary
children.top_down_role: Operations whose curvature orientation prevents the intended representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature Mismatch Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Wrong epigraph/hypograph orientation can destroy convexity before any conic lifting is attempted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a concave function \(g\), the convex graph-oriented set is its hypograph, not generally its epigraph. Concretely, let \(g(x)=-x^2\) on \(\mathbb R\). Its epigraph \(E=\{(x,t):t\ge -x^2\}\) is nonconvex: \((-1,-1),(1,-1)\in E\), while their midpoint \((0,-1)\notin E\). Hence replacing the hypograph constraint \(u\le g(x)\) by the epigraph constraint \(u\ge g(x)\) in a convex lifted formulation crosses the curvature-compatibility boundary unless \(g\) has additional structure, such as affinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A concave inner function generally requires a hypograph lift. Using its epigraph instead can produce a nonconvex lifted set, as demonstrated by the function minus the square.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi} g\) is nonconvex, whereas \(\operatorname{hypo} g\) is convex.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample and failure-boundary classification are mathematically correct, but the record supplies no inspectable citation or explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Composition Calculus
children.top_down_role: Representability of composed functions through compatible lifted descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Composition Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex composition rule with coordinate-dependent monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:D\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex. For each \(i\), suppose that throughout \(D\), \(h\) is nondecreasing in coordinate \(i\) and \(g_i:C\to\mathbb R\) is convex, or \(h\) is nonincreasing in coordinate \(i\) and \(g_i\) is concave; an affine \(g_i\) is admissible in either regime. If \(C\) is convex and \(g(x)=(g_1(x),\ldots,g_m(x))\in D\) for every \(x\in C\), then \(x\mapsto h(g(x))\) is convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex outer function composed with convex or concave inner functions remains convex when each inner curvature matches the outer function’s coordinate monotonicity.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is convex and has the stated coordinatewise monotonicity on \(D\).
\(g(C)\subseteq D\), with each \(g_i\) having compatible curvature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\circ g\) is convex on \(C\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional monotone composition theorem is precise and appropriately classified, but no authoritative source and locator are supplied.

children.title: Monotonicity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Coordinatewise monotonicity patterns relevant to valid compositions.

knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Signed coordinate order used to state sufficient curvature compatibility conditions for convex composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\sigma\in\{-1,+1\}^m\). A function \(h:D\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) has monotonicity regime \(\sigma\) on \(D\) if, for all \(u,v\in D\), the inequalities \(\sigma_i u_i\le \sigma_i v_i\) for every \(i\) imply \(h(u)\le h(v)\). Thus \(\sigma_i=+1\) encodes nondecreasing dependence on coordinate \(i\), whereas \(\sigma_i=-1\) encodes nonincreasing dependence. In the standard sufficient rule for convex composition, a convex inner function \(g_i\) is compatible with \(\sigma_i=+1\), a concave inner function \(g_i\) is compatible with \(\sigma_i=-1\), and an affine \(g_i\) is compatible with either sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sign vector records whether the outer function increases or decreases in each coordinate. For the standard sufficient convex-composition rule, increasing coordinates accept convex inner functions, decreasing coordinates accept concave inner functions, and affine inner functions work in either regime.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is the domain on which the signed-order comparisons are made.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For the standard sufficient convex-composition rule, \(\sigma_i=+1\) is compatible with convex \(g_i\), \(\sigma_i=-1\) is compatible with concave \(g_i\), and affine \(g_i\) is compatible with either sign.

notation.meaning: Outer-function domain on which monotonicity is asserted.

children.title: Inner-Outer Representation Interface
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between inner function outputs and outer function domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Inner-Outer Representation Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oriented auxiliary variables connect inner graph-set lifts to an outer epigraph lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h\) be convex with monotonicity signs \(\sigma_i\), and set \(f(x)=h(g_1(x),\ldots,g_m(x))\). Assume the epigraph of \(h\) and each compatible oriented graph set of \(g_i\) have conic lifts. Then
\[\operatorname{epi}f=\left\{(x,r):\exists u,\ (u,r)\in\operatorname{epi}h,\ u_i\ge g_i(x)\ \text{if }\sigma_i=+1,\ u_i\le g_i(x)\ \text{if }\sigma_i=-1\right\}.\]
Consequently, substituting the conic lifts of these epigraph or hypograph constraints yields a conic lift of \(\operatorname{epi}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Auxiliary variables enter above increasing-coordinate inner functions and below decreasing-coordinate inner functions; combining these oriented lifts with the outer epigraph represents the composition.
assumptions_latex: All displayed outer and oriented inner sets possess conic lifts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}(h\circ g)\) has the displayed lifted-conic representation.

notation.meaning: Interface variables connecting inner and outer representations.

children.title: Composition Validity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Curvature, domain, or monotonicity mismatches blocking conic representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Composition Validity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the curvature–monotonicity pairing can make a scalar composition nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Convexity of the outer function and one-sided curvature of the inner function do not alone ensure convexity of their composition. Let \(h(u)=e^u\), which is convex and strictly increasing, and let \(g(x)=-x^2\), which is concave. Then \(f(x)=h(g(x))=e^{-x^2}\) satisfies \(f''(x)=(4x^2-2)e^{-x^2}\), which is negative for \(|x|<1/\sqrt 2\). Thus \(f\) is not convex, showing failure when an increasing convex outer function is paired with a nonaffine concave inner function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A curvature mismatch invalidates the composition rule: the exponential of minus the square is not convex despite having a convex increasing outer function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\circ g=e^{-x^2}\) is not convex on \(\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: Second derivative of the scalar composition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The derivative-based counterexample correctly identifies a composition-validity failure and fits the failure-boundary container, but it has no cited source or explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Perspective Calculus
children.top_down_role: Representation transport under perspective scaling.

knowledge_statements.title: Perspective Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed perspective of a proper closed convex function, including its recession boundary at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper closed convex function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), define its closed perspective by
\[f^{\pi}(x,t)=\begin{cases}t f(x/t),&t>0,\\ f^{\infty}(x),&t=0,\\ +\infty,&t<0.\end{cases}\]
Then \(f^{\pi}\) is proper, closed, convex, and positively homogeneous. Its epigraph satisfies
\[\operatorname{epi}f^{\pi}=\operatorname{cl}\left\{(t z,t r,t):t>0,\ (z,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f\right\}.\]
Thus homogenizing an epigraph lift of \(f\), followed by closure when necessary, produces a conic representation of the closed perspective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed perspective homogenizes a convex function’s epigraph; at zero scale its value is the recession function, and closure supplies the boundary points.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{\pi}\) is closed convex and has the stated homogenized epigraph.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closed-perspective definition, recession slice, and homogenized epigraph formula are standard and internally consistent, but no authoritative source with a locator is supplied.

children.title: Partial-Minimization Calculus
children.top_down_role: Representation transport through elimination by minimization over auxiliary variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Minimization Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity and epigraph projection under elimination of auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex and define \(g(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb R^p}F(x,y)\), assuming \(g(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\). Then \(g\) is convex. Moreover,
\[\{(x,r):g(x)<r\}=\{(x,r):\exists y,\ F(x,y)<r\}.\]
If the infimum is attained whenever \(g(x)<+\infty\), then
\[\operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,r):\exists y,\ F(x,y)\le r\}=\operatorname{proj}_{x,r}(\operatorname{epi}F).\]
Hence an attained partial minimization is represented by eliminating the lifted variable \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial minimization preserves convexity. Its strict epigraph is always a projection, while the closed epigraph projection formula requires boundary attainment or an appropriate closure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is convex, with the displayed projection formula when the infimum is attained.

notation.meaning: Value function obtained by minimizing over \(y\).

children.title: Perspective-Elimination Interface
children.top_down_role: Interactions between scaling variables and minimized coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Perspective-Elimination Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perspective epigraphs arise by homogenization followed by elimination of the original epigraph variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be proper, closed, and convex, and suppose
\[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(z,r):\exists w,\ A z+a r+B w+b\in K\}\]
for a closed convex cone \(K\). For \(t>0\), the perspective inequality \(t f(x/t)\le s\) is equivalent to
\[\exists \widehat w,\ A x+a s+B\widehat w+t b\in K,\]
where \(\widehat w=t w\). Eliminating \(\widehat w\) gives the positive-scale perspective epigraph. The closed perspective epigraph is the closure of this lifted set as \(t\downarrow0\), with its zero-scale slice governed by \(f^{\infty}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homogenize every affine term in an epigraph lift, rescale auxiliary variables, and eliminate them; closure then adds the recession slice at zero scale.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone and the displayed lift represents \(\operatorname{epi}f\).
The direct equivalence is asserted for \(t>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The homogenized conic system represents \(\operatorname{epi}f^{\pi}\) after elimination and, when needed, closure at \(t=0\).

notation.meaning: Cone used by the epigraph lift.
Recession function determining the zero-scale slice.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-scale homogenization and rescaling are algebraically consistent, and closure correctly addresses the zero-scale recession slice, but the nontrivial lifted-representation claim has no source.

children.title: Infimum Attainment Boundary
children.top_down_role: Nonattainment or nonclosedness arising during partial minimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Infimum Attainment Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonattainment can remove boundary points from a projected lifted epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be defined by \(F(x,y)=e^y\). Then \(g(x)=\inf_y F(x,y)=0\) for every \(x\), but no finite \(y\) attains this infimum. Consequently,
\[\operatorname{proj}_{x,r}(\operatorname{epi}F)=\mathbb R^n\times(0,+\infty),\qquad \operatorname{epi}g=\mathbb R^n\times[0,+\infty).\]
Thus exact epigraph projection fails at the value-function boundary without attainment; taking the closure restores the missing points in this example.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an eliminated infimum is not attained, projection can omit the value function’s boundary. The exponential example loses every point having epigraph height zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_{x,r}(\operatorname{epi}F)\ne\operatorname{epi}g\), although its closure equals \(\operatorname{epi}g\).
