children.title: Conjugacy Calculus
children.top_down_role: Representation transport under convex conjugation.

knowledge_statements.title: Conjugacy Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel conjugacy and biconjugacy for proper closed convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), its Fenchel conjugate is
\[f^*(y)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{\langle y,x\rangle-f(x)\}.\]
The conjugate \(f^*\) is closed and convex. If \(f\) is also closed and convex, then
\[f(x)=f^{**}(x)=\sup_{y\in\mathbb R^n}\{\langle x,y\rangle-f^*(y)\}.\]
Accordingly, conjugation converts a primal epigraph description into a family of affine upper bounds on \(\langle y,x\rangle-f(x)\), while biconjugation recovers the closed convex primal function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel conjugation forms a closed convex dual function by taking affine suprema, and biconjugation exactly recovers every proper closed convex function.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is additionally closed and convex for \(f=f^{**}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*\) is closed convex and, under the additional assumptions, \(f=f^{**}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conjugacy and biconjugacy statements are mathematically standard, properly qualified, and correctly classified as duality, but no source with a locator is provided.

children.title: Dual Epigraph Representations
children.top_down_role: Lifted descriptions of epigraphs in dual-variable space.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Epigraph Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic-duality representation of a conjugate epigraph under strong duality and dual attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[f(x)=\inf_z\{d^{\mathsf T}x+c^{\mathsf T}z:A z+B x-b\in K\},\]
where \(K\) is a closed convex cone, and assume that \(f\) is proper. Suppose the lifted feasible set has a Slater point and, for every \(y\) with \(f^*(y)<+\infty\), the conic dual of the maximization defining \(f^*(y)\) attains its optimum. Then
\[(y,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f^*\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists\lambda\in K^*:\ A^{\mathsf T}\lambda=c,\ B^{\mathsf T}\lambda=d-y,\ -b^{\mathsf T}\lambda\le t.\]
Thus conic dualization converts the lifted primal value function into a lifted representation of its conjugate epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under conic strong duality and dual attainment, the conjugate epigraph is represented by a nonnegative dual-cone multiplier satisfying two linear equations and an epigraph inequality with value minus the multiplier pairing with b.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone and \(f\) is proper.
There exist \(x\) and \(z\) such that \(A z+B x-b\in\operatorname{int}K\).
For every \(y\) satisfying \(f^*(y)<+\infty\), the associated conic dual attains its optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}f^*\) has the displayed lifted representation over \(K^*\).

children.title: Primal-Dual Epigraph Transfer
children.top_down_role: Correspondence between primal function representations and dual epigraphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Epigraph Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Biconjugate transfer between primal and conjugate epigraph descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex. Then
\[(x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \langle x,y\rangle-s\le r\quad\text{for every }(y,s)\in\operatorname{epi}f^*.\]
Equivalently,
\[\operatorname{epi}f=\bigcap_{(y,s)\in\operatorname{epi}f^*}\{(x,r):\langle x,y\rangle-s\le r\}.\]
Hence a representation of the dual epigraph determines the primal epigraph through biconjugacy. Conversely, applying the same construction to \(f^*\) recovers \(\operatorname{epi}f^*\) from \(\operatorname{epi}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate epigraph indexes affine halfspaces whose intersection is the primal epigraph; proper closed convexity makes this primal-dual transfer exact.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}f\) equals the displayed intersection of halfspaces indexed by \(\operatorname{epi}f^*\).

notation.meaning: Dual epigraph indexing the affine inequalities.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The halfspace intersection follows correctly from biconjugacy, and the duality classification fits the transfer leaf, but the record supplies no authoritative citation with a locator.

children.title: Closure Sensitivity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Domain or closedness effects limiting exact conjugacy-based representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Sensitivity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel biconjugacy and the failure caused by omitting lower-semicontinuous closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and admit an affine minorant. Its biconjugate \(f^{**}\) is the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function majorized by \(f\); equivalently, \(\operatorname{epi} f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi} f)\). Hence \(f=f^{**}\) holds exactly when \(f\) is convex and lower semicontinuous. Closure cannot generally be omitted: for \(f=\delta_{(-1,1)}\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), one has \(f^{**}=\delta_{[-1,1]}\), so \(\operatorname{epi} f^{**}\neq\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi} f)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Biconjugacy returns the closed convex envelope. An open-domain indicator becomes the indicator of its closure, demonstrating that closure cannot be discarded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi} f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi} f)\), and closure is essential in general.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional closure claim, Fenchel-Moreau equivalence, and open-domain indicator example are mathematically plausible and fit the failure-boundary container, but the record supplies no source or inspectable locator. Authoritative support is required before the precise hypotheses and epigraph identity can be accepted.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-over-Linear Epigraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed extended-value quadratic-over-linear function represented by a rotated second-order cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(q:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(q(x,s)=\|x\|_2^2/s\) when \(s>0\), \(q(0,0)=0\), and \(q(x,s)=+\infty\) otherwise. For the rotated cone \(\mathcal Q_r^{n+2}=\{(u,v,w):u\ge0,\ v\ge0,\ 2uv\ge\|w\|_2^2\}\), the closed epigraph satisfies \[\operatorname{epi}q=\{(x,s,t):(s,t,\sqrt2 x)\in\mathcal Q_r^{n+2}\}.\] Thus the cone constraint includes both the positive-denominator formula and its closed boundary value at \(s=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed quadratic-over-linear epigraph is exactly one rotated second-order-cone constraint, including its zero-denominator boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q(x,s)\le t\iff(s,t,\sqrt2x)\in\mathcal Q_r^{n+2}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Rotated-Cone Lifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rotated-cone lift of a positive-semidefinite quadratic perspective inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\), choose \(L\) with \(Q=L^\top L\), and let \(s,t\in\mathbb R\). Then \[x^\top Qx\le st,\quad s\ge0,\quad t\ge0\] holds if and only if \[(s,t,\sqrt2Lx)\in\mathcal Q_r^{m+2},\] where \(m\) is the number of rows of \(L\) and \(\mathcal Q_r^{m+2}=\{(u,v,w):u\ge0,\ v\ge0,\ 2uv\ge\|w\|_2^2\}\). The factor variable provides a conic lift independent of the chosen square-root factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-semidefinite quadratic bounded by a product of nonnegative scalars is equivalent to a rotated-cone membership constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\top Qx\le st,\ s,t\ge0\iff(s,t,\sqrt2Lx)\in\mathcal Q_r^{m+2}\).

children.title: Epigraph-to-Cone Interface
children.top_down_role: Correspondence between quadratic epigraph geometry and rotated-cone membership.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph-to-Cone Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine quadratic-over-linear epigraph translated into the standard rotated-cone interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and define the closed perspective function \(g(x,s)=\|Ax+b\|_2^2/s\) for \(s>0\), with value \(0\) when \(s=0\) and \(Ax+b=0\), and \(+\infty\) otherwise. Its epigraph has the conic interface \[g(x,s)\le t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(s,t,\sqrt2(Ax+b))\in\mathcal Q_r^{m+2}.\] Consequently, any optimization model using this epigraph can replace it by one affine map into a rotated second-order cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine quadratic-over-linear epigraph becomes a single affine rotated-cone constraint, with the closed boundary included automatically.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,s,t):(s,t,\sqrt2(Ax+b))\in\mathcal Q_r^{m+2}\}\).

children.title: Zero-Denominator Boundary
children.top_down_role: Domain and closure behavior at vanishing scale coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Denominator Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed perspective behavior at a vanishing denominator and the excluded nonzero-numerator case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the closed quadratic perspective \(q(x,s)\), the rotated-cone constraint \((s,t,\sqrt2x)\in\mathcal Q_r^{n+2}\) with \(s=0\) implies \(x=0\) and \(t\ge0\). Hence \(q(0,0)=0\), while \(q(x,0)=+\infty\) for every \(x\ne0\). Assigning any finite value at \((x,0)\) with \(x\ne0\) would violate lower semicontinuity, since \(\|x\|_2^2/s\to+\infty\) as \(s\downarrow0\). The zero-denominator boundary is therefore determined uniquely by closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At zero denominator, only a zero numerator has finite perspective value. Any nonzero numerator must receive positive infinity to preserve closedness.

knowledge_statements.title: Schur-Complement Lifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-definite Schur-complement representation of a matrix-fractional quadratic epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\), \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(t\in\mathbb R\). The Schur-complement equivalence gives \[t\ge x^\top Q^{-1}x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \begin{pmatrix}Q&x\\x^\top&t\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.\] Thus the epigraph of the matrix-fractional quadratic map \((x,Q)\mapsto x^\top Q^{-1}x\), on the domain \(Q\succ0\), is represented by an affine positive-semidefinite matrix constraint. Positive definiteness ensures that the ordinary inverse and Schur complement are well defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix-fractional quadratic upper bound is equivalent to positive semidefiniteness of one bordered matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\ge x^\top Q^{-1}x\iff\begin{pmatrix}Q&x\\x^\top&t\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Gram-Matrix Lifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factor and inner-product characterization of bounded-rank positive-semidefinite matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb S^n\) and an integer \(r\ge1\), the following are equivalent: \(X\succeq0\) and \(\operatorname{rank}X\le r\); there exists \(V\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\) such that \(X=VV^\top\); and there exist vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^r\) satisfying \(X_{ij}=v_i^\top v_j\) for all \(i,j\). Thus quadratic products of factor variables can be lifted to entries of a Gram matrix, while the factor dimension is recorded by the rank bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-semidefinite matrix of rank at most r is exactly the Gram matrix of vectors in r-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\succeq0,\ \operatorname{rank}X\le r\iff X=VV^\top\) for some \(V\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\).

notation.meaning: matrix whose rows are Gram vectors

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x,c\in\mathbb R^n\), \(X,Q\in\mathbb S^n\), and \(d\in\mathbb R\), and define \(M=\begin{pmatrix}1&x^\top\\x&X\end{pmatrix}\). Then \[X=xx^\top\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad M\succeq0\ \text{ and }\ \operatorname{rank}M=1.\] Under the exact relation \(X=xx^\top\), one has \[x^\top Qx+2c^\top x+d=\langle Q,X\rangle+2c^\top x+d.\] Thus quadratic products become affine in the lifted variables, while the rank-one condition retains the nonconvexity of the exact lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector and its quadratic products have an exact bordered positive-semidefinite lift when the bordered matrix is constrained to rank one; quadratic expressions then become affine in the lifted variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-One Matrix Lifts

children.title: Convex Matrix Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Convex feasible regions obtained after weakening rank restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Matrix Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite outer relaxation obtained by deleting the rank constraint from a quadratic matrix lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider quadratic functions \(q_i(x)=x^\top Q_i x+2c_i^\top x+d_i\). Introduce \(X\in\mathbb S^n\) and replace each \(q_i(x)\) by \(\widehat q_i(x,X)=\langle Q_i,X\rangle+2c_i^\top x+d_i\). The exact lifted relation is \(M(x,X)=\begin{pmatrix}1&x^\top\\x&X\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\) together with \(\operatorname{rank}M(x,X)=1\). Dropping the rank condition yields the convex constraint \(M(x,X)\succeq0\), equivalently \(X\succeq xx^\top\), and therefore an outer relaxation of every feasible set described using the \(q_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dropping rank one from the lifted quadratic model produces a semidefinite outer relaxation in which every quadratic becomes affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X=xx^\top\) is relaxed to \(M(x,X)\succeq0\), equivalently \(X\succeq xx^\top\).

notation.meaning: affine lift of the quadratic function

children.title: Relaxation Exactness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem structures where relaxed solutions retain rank-one representatives.

assumptions_latex: \(X,S\in\mathbb S_+^n\) are complementary optimal primal and dual-slack matrices, so \(SX=0\).
Rank-one feasible matrices of the relaxation correspond to feasible points of the original lifted model with the same objective value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}X=1\), so \(X=zz^\top\) for some nonzero \(z\in\mathbb R^n\), and the stated correspondence certifies exactness of the relaxation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-slack corank-one certificate for exactness of a homogeneous semidefinite rank relaxation.

source_refs.locator: 3.7.1 A: The faces of the semidefinite cone p. 63

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,S\in\mathbb S_+^n\) be optimal primal and dual-slack matrices for a semidefinite relaxation, and suppose complementarity gives \(SX=0\). Assume a primal normalization ensures \(X\ne0\), and assume \(\operatorname{rank}S=n-1\). Then \(\operatorname{range}X\subseteq\ker S\) and \(\dim\ker S=1\), so \(\operatorname{rank}X=1\). Hence \(X=zz^\top\) for some nonzero \(z\in\mathbb R^n\). If rank-one feasible matrices correspond to feasible points of the original lifted model with the same objective value, this rank-one optimum certifies exactness of the relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero complementary primal optimum must be rank one when the dual slack has a one-dimensional kernel. When rank-one relaxed solutions correspond to original feasible solutions with the same value, this certifies exactness.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Exactness Regimes

children.title: Rank-Recovery Boundary
children.top_down_role: Cases where convex relaxation yields only higher-rank solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Recovery Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of rank recovery when complementary slackness leaves a multidimensional kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(X,S\succeq0\) and \(SX=0\), then only \(\operatorname{range}X\subseteq\ker S\) and \(\operatorname{rank}X\le\dim\ker S\) follow. When \(\dim\ker S\ge2\), complementarity alone does not force rank one. Concretely, the spectrahedron in \(\mathbb S_+^2\) defined by \(X_{11}=X_{22}=1/2\) and \(X_{12}=0\) contains only \(X=I_2/2\), which has rank two; taking \(S=0\) satisfies complementarity. Thus no rank-one recovery is possible without additional structure or a sharper certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual slack with a multidimensional kernel permits higher-rank optima. A singleton spectrahedron containing only half the identity demonstrates complete failure of rank-one recovery.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim\ker S\ge2\) does not imply \(\operatorname{rank}X=1\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{diag}(X_1,\ldots,X_p)\succeq0\iff X_k\succeq0\) for every \(k=1,\ldots,p\), and the product cone is linearly isomorphic to the corresponding block-diagonal linear section of \(\mathbb S_+^{n_1+\cdots+n_p}\).

notation.meaning: block-diagonal matrix with the listed blocks

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product positive-semidefinite cones represented as one block-diagonal positive-semidefinite constraint.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\ge1\), let \(n_1,\ldots,n_p\) be positive integers, and let \(X_k\in\mathbb S^{n_k}\) for \(k=1,\ldots,p\). Form \(X=\operatorname{diag}(X_1,\ldots,X_p)\). Then \[X\succeq0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad X_k\succeq0\ \text{ for every }\ k=1,\ldots,p.\] Consequently, the product cone \(\mathbb S_+^{n_1}\times\cdots\times\mathbb S_+^{n_p}\) is linearly isomorphic to the intersection of \(\mathbb S_+^{n_1+\cdots+n_p}\) with the linear subspace of block-diagonal matrices having the prescribed partition. Separate semidefinite representations can therefore be aggregated without cross-block coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Several independent positive-semidefinite constraints are equivalent to one positive-semidefinite constraint on their block-diagonal aggregate. The aggregate cone is a block-diagonal linear section of the larger positive-semidefinite cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Block-Diagonal Positive-Semidefinite Representations

children.title: Spectral-Function Epigraphs
children.top_down_role: Epigraph representations for functions determined by eigenvalues or singular values.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, closed, convex, and invariant under coordinate permutations.
\(X\in\mathbb{S}^n\), and \(\lambda(X)\) lists its eigenvalues in nonincreasing order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}F=\{(X,t):f(\lambda(X))\le t\}\) is closed, convex, and orthogonally invariant.

notation.meaning: real symmetric matrices of order n
ordered eigenvalue vector of a symmetric matrix

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional symmetric-matrix spectral functions induced by symmetric closed convex functions.

source_refs.locator: 6 Semidefinite Representability p. 251

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the spectral function \(F:\mathbb{S}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) by \(F(X)=f(\lambda(X))\). Its epigraph has the representation
\[
\operatorname{epi}F=\{(X,t)\in\mathbb{S}^n\times\mathbb{R}:f(\lambda(X))\le t\}.
\]
For every orthogonal matrix \(Q\), \(F(QXQ^{\mathsf T})=F(X)\). Symmetry and convexity of \(f\) imply that this epigraph is convex; closedness of \(f\) implies that it is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric closed convex function of eigenvalues induces a closed convex, orthogonally invariant matrix epigraph.
knowledge_statements.title: Spectral-Function Epigraphs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity and semidefinite representability of Ky Fan singular-value sums
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Retains the representation-theoretic conclusion appropriate to the spectral-function epigraph node, while treating the general SVD facts as supporting spectral background.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times l}\) with \(k\le l\), and let \[\sigma_1(A)\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_k(A)\ge0\] be the eigenvalues of \((AA^T)^{1/2}\). For every \(r\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), the Ky Fan singular-value sum \[\Sigma_r(A)=\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i(A)\] is a convex and semidefinite-representable function of \(A\). In particular, \[\Sigma_1(A)=\sigma_1(A)=\|A\|_{2\to2}=\max_{\|x\|_2\le1}\|Ax\|_2\] is semidefinite representable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a rectangular matrix, every sum of a prescribed number of its largest singular values is convex and semidefinite representable. The one-term case is the Euclidean operator norm, so that norm is semidefinite representable as well.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Sigma_r(A)=\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i(A)\text{ is convex and SDr; in particular, }\|A\|_{2\to2}=\Sigma_1(A)\text{ is SDr.}

children.title: Matrix-Norm Epigraphs
children.top_down_role: Epigraph representations for operator, Schatten, or related matrix norms.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The spectral- and nuclear-norm epigraphs admit the displayed semidefinite lifts.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard semidefinite lifts for rectangular spectral and nuclear norms.

source_refs.locator: 2.2 Applications of Semidefinite Optimization p. 25
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The spectral-norm epigraph is
\[
\|X\|_2\le t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\begin{pmatrix}tI_m&X\\X^{\mathsf T}&tI_n\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.
\]
The nuclear-norm epigraph is
\[
\|X\|_*\le t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists U\in\mathbb{S}^m,\ V\in\mathbb{S}^n:\
\begin{pmatrix}U&X\\X^{\mathsf T}&V\end{pmatrix}\succeq0,
\quad \tfrac12(\operatorname{tr}U+\operatorname{tr}V)\le t.
\]
Thus both matrix-norm inequalities are projections of affine slices of positive-semidefinite cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Spectral- and nuclear-norm epigraphs are projections of explicit block positive-semidefinite constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Norm Epigraphs

children.title: Eigenvalue Epigraph Regimes
children.top_down_role: Representation structures driven by symmetric eigenvalue functions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both the largest-eigenvalue and top-\(k\)-eigenvalue-sum epigraphs are semidefinite representable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Largest and top-sum eigenvalue epigraph regimes for real symmetric matrices.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 From Linear to Semidefinite Optimization p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The largest-eigenvalue epigraph satisfies
\[
\lambda_1(X)\le t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad tI_n-X\succeq0.
\]
More generally, the sum of the \(k\) largest eigenvalues obeys
\[
\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i(X)\le t
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists s\in\mathbb{R},\ Z\in\mathbb{S}^n:
Z\succeq0,
\quad Z\succeq X-sI_n,
\quad ks+\operatorname{tr}Z\le t.
\]
These formulas distinguish a direct linear matrix inequality from a lifted semidefinite representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum eigenvalue has a direct LMI epigraph; the sum of the largest k eigenvalues has a lifted SDP epigraph.
knowledge_statements.title: Eigenvalue Epigraph Regimes

children.title: Singular-Value Epigraph Regimes
children.top_down_role: Representation structures driven by singular-value functions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximum singular value has a block-LMI epigraph, while Ky Fan sums reduce to a symmetric eigenvalue lift.

notation.meaning: i-th largest singular value of X

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum and Ky Fan singular-value epigraphs for real rectangular matrices.

source_refs.locator: 6.4 Constructing Semidefinite Representations p. 271
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The maximum-singular-value epigraph is
\[
\sigma_1(X)\le t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\begin{pmatrix}tI_m&X\\X^{\mathsf T}&tI_n\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.
\]
For Ky Fan sums, define the symmetric dilation
\[
\mathcal{D}(X)=\begin{pmatrix}0&X\\X^{\mathsf T}&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its positive eigenvalues are the singular values of \(X\); consequently,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^k\sigma_i(X)\le t
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i(\mathcal{D}(X))\le t,
\]
and the right-hand side has the lifted semidefinite representation for a top-eigenvalue sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Singular-value epigraphs arise from a block LMI or by applying eigenvalue-sum lifts to the symmetric dilation.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Value Epigraph Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symmetric and Monic Symmetric Determinantal Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines symmetric determinantal representations of real polynomials and records the stated existence of a possibly nonmonic symmetric linear-pencil representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), a symmetric determinantal representation is an identity \(p(x)=\det L(x)\), where \(L(x)=L_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iL_i\) and every \(L_i\) is symmetric. Such a representation is called monic when \(L_0\succ0\). Moreover, every real polynomial can be expressed as the determinant of a symmetric linear pencil, although the pencil need not be monic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric determinantal representation expresses a real polynomial as the determinant of an affine linear matrix pencil with symmetric coefficient matrices. It is called monic when the constant matrix is positive definite. Every real polynomial has such a linear-pencil representation, but it need not be monic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p(x)=\det\!\left(L_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iL_i\right),\quad L_i=L_i^{\mathsf T};\qquad L_0\succ0\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{the representation is monic}.

children.title: Determinant Representations
children.top_down_role: Lifted descriptions involving determinant level sets or related matrix regions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\det(X)\ge r^n\) is equivalent to a geometric-mean inequality on the positive eigenvalues of \(X\).

notation.meaning: positive-definite symmetric matrices of order n

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Determinant-root superlevel representation on the positive-definite cone.

source_refs.locator: 6 Semidefinite Representability p. 251
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a positive-definite matrix, spectral factorization gives
\[
\det(X)=\prod_{i=1}^n\lambda_i(X),
\qquad
\det(X)^{1/n}=\left(\prod_{i=1}^n\lambda_i(X)\right)^{1/n}.
\]
Hence the determinant-root superlevel set has the representation
\[
\{X\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^n:\det(X)^{1/n}\ge r\}
=
\left\{X\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^n:
\left(\prod_{i=1}^n\lambda_i(X)\right)^{1/n}\ge r\right\}.
\]
Because the determinant root is concave on the positive-semidefinite cone, this superlevel set is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A determinant-root constraint is a geometric-mean constraint on positive eigenvalues, and its superlevel set is convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Determinant Representations

children.title: Log-Determinant Representations
children.top_down_role: Lifted epi- or hypographic descriptions for log-determinant functions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The epigraph of \(-\log\det\) equals a determinant superlevel constraint and is convex.

notation.meaning: positive-definite symmetric matrices of order n

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex negative-log-determinant epigraph on its natural matrix domain.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.4 Positive definite matrices p. 20

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On the positive-definite cone,
\[
-\log\det(X)=-\sum_{i=1}^n\log\lambda_i(X).
\]
Therefore its epigraph admits the equivalent determinant representation
\[
\operatorname{epi}(-\log\det)
=
\{(X,t)\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^n\times\mathbb{R}:-\log\det(X)\le t\}
=
\{(X,t):X\succ0,\ \det(X)\ge e^{-t}\}.
\]
The function \(-\log\det(X)\) is closed and strictly convex on \(\mathbb{S}_{++}^n\), so this epigraph is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative-log-determinant epigraph is equivalently a positive-definite determinant superlevel constraint and is convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Log-Determinant Representations

children.title: Positive-Definite Domain Regime
children.top_down_role: Interior-domain structure relevant to logarithmic determinant expressions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\succ0\) exactly when every eigenvalue, or equivalently every leading principal minor, is positive.

notation.meaning: leading principal submatrix of order k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent finite-dimensional tests for the natural domain of determinant barriers.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.4 Positive definite matrices p. 20

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The positive-definite domain is
\[
\mathbb{S}_{++}^n=\{X\in\mathbb{S}^n:u^{\mathsf T}Xu>0\text{ for every }u\ne0\}.
\]
For a symmetric matrix, the following conditions are equivalent:
\[
X\succ0;
\qquad \lambda_{\min}(X)>0;
\qquad \det(X_{1:k,1:k})>0\text{ for }k=1,\ldots,n.
\]
In particular, \(\det(X)>0\) alone is not sufficient for positive definiteness when \(n\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive definiteness is characterized by positive quadratic forms, positive eigenvalues, or Sylvester's leading-principal-minor criterion.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Definite Domain Regime

children.title: Singular-Matrix Boundary
children.top_down_role: Boundary behavior as determinant values vanish or matrices lose definiteness.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-\log\det(X_j)\to+\infty\), so the finite log-determinant representation does not extend to singular matrices.

notation.meaning: positive-semidefinite symmetric matrices of order n

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barrier behavior at the singular boundary of the positive-semidefinite cone.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.4 Positive definite matrices p. 20

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If positive-definite matrices \(X_j\) converge to a singular positive-semidefinite matrix \(X\), then at least one eigenvalue tends to zero and
\[
\det(X_j)=\prod_{i=1}^n\lambda_i(X_j)\longrightarrow0,
\qquad
-\log\det(X_j)\longrightarrow+\infty.
\]
Thus the closed extended-value barrier is
\[
\phi(X)=
\begin{cases}
-\log\det(X),&X\succ0,\\
+\infty,&X\not\succ0.
\end{cases}
\]
Finite log-determinant formulas requiring \(X\succ0\) fail on the singular boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approaching a singular positive-semidefinite matrix drives the negative log determinant to infinity; finite barrier formulas require strict positivity.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Matrix Boundary

children.title: Sparse Matrix Lifts
children.top_down_role: Lift constructions that preserve or exploit matrix sparsity.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is an undirected graph with all diagonal positions included.
\(\mathbb{S}^n(E)\) denotes symmetric matrices supported on the diagonal and edges of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A sparse semidefinite lift is obtained by introducing an unspecified completion matrix and projecting its positive-semidefinite constraint onto the specified entries.

notation.meaning: coordinate projection onto specified diagonal and edge entries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection lift for partial symmetric matrices with a prescribed sparsity pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\pi_E:\mathbb{S}^n\to\mathbb{S}^n(E)\) retain precisely the specified diagonal and edge entries. The cone of sparse data admitting a positive-semidefinite completion is
\[
\mathcal{K}_E
=
\pi_E(\mathbb{S}_{+}^n)
=
\{x\in\mathbb{S}^n(E):\exists Z\in\mathbb{S}_{+}^n\text{ with }\pi_E(Z)=x\}.
\]
The full matrix \(Z\) and its unspecified entries are lift variables. Hence constraints of the form \(x\in\mathcal{K}_E\) are projections of one positive-semidefinite constraint, independently of whether the sparsity graph is chordal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse partial-matrix data are PSD-completable exactly when they are the projection of a full positive-semidefinite matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Matrix Lifts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection characterization is mathematically standard and representation fits the sparse-lift container, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Chordal Matrix Lifts
children.top_down_role: Lift constructions organized by chordal graph structure.

assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a partial symmetric matrix specified on the diagonal and edges of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The partial matrix \(x\) has a positive-semidefinite completion exactly when every maximal-clique principal submatrix is positive semidefinite.

notation.meaning: principal submatrix indexed by clique C
maximal cliques of the chordal graph

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-semidefinite completion theorem for chordal sparsity graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a chordal graph, a partial symmetric matrix \(x\) has a completion \(Z\in\mathbb{S}_{+}^n\) satisfying \(\pi_E(Z)=x\) if and only if
\[
x[C_j]\succeq0\qquad\text{for every }j=1,\ldots,q.
\]
Consequently, the PSD-completion cone has the clique lift
\[
\mathcal{K}_E
=
\{x\in\mathbb{S}^n(E):x[C_j]\succeq0\text{ for }j=1,\ldots,q\}.
\]
Entries shared by two clique submatrices agree automatically because both are restrictions of the same partial matrix \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For chordal sparsity, positive semidefiniteness of every maximal-clique submatrix is necessary and sufficient for a global PSD completion.
knowledge_statements.title: Chordal Matrix Lifts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The chordal PSD-completion theorem is stated correctly, and theorem is an appropriate role for the exact characterization, but it lacks a cited source and specific theorem or page locator.

children.title: Clique-Based Semidefinite Decompositions
children.top_down_role: Local positive-semidefinite blocks indexed by maximal cliques.

assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb{S}^n(E)\) is supported on the diagonal and edges of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\succeq0\) exactly when it is a sum of embedded positive-semidefinite matrices supported on maximal cliques.

notation.meaning: coordinate selector from V to clique C
symmetric matrices supported on graph G

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposition of chordally sparse positive-semidefinite matrices into clique-supported terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E_{C_j}\) select the coordinates indexed by \(C_j\). The chordally sparse positive-semidefinite cone satisfies
\[
\mathbb{S}_{+}^n\cap\mathbb{S}^n(E)
=
\left\{
\sum_{j=1}^q E_{C_j}^{\mathsf T}X_jE_{C_j}:
X_j\in\mathbb{S}_{+}^{|C_j|}
\right\}.
\]
Thus \(X\in\mathbb{S}^n(E)\) is positive semidefinite if and only if there exist clique matrices \(X_j\succeq0\) whose embedded sum equals \(X\). This decomposition concerns sparse PSD matrices, whereas clique-wise PSD tests characterize PSD-completable partial matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A chordally sparse PSD matrix is exactly a sum of PSD matrices embedded on the graph's maximal cliques.
knowledge_statements.title: Clique-Based Semidefinite Decompositions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The chordally sparse PSD-cone decomposition is correctly distinguished from PSD completion, and representation fits the container. A specific supporting source locator is required.

children.title: Nonchordal Sparsity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural limitations arising before chordal completion.

assumptions_latex: \(G\) is the chordless four-cycle on vertices \(1,2,3,4\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Clique-wise positive semidefiniteness is insufficient for PSD completion on a nonchordal graph.

notation.meaning: Gram vectors in a hypothetical PSD completion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete four-cycle failure of the chordal clique-completion criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Specify a partial matrix on the four-cycle by
\[
x_{ii}=1,
\quad x_{12}=x_{23}=x_{34}=1,
\quad x_{41}=-1.
\]
Every maximal clique is an edge, and each specified edge matrix is either \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\) or \(\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}\), hence is positive semidefinite. A PSD completion would be a Gram matrix of unit vectors. The first three edge equalities force \(v_1=v_2=v_3=v_4\), while \(x_{41}=-1\) forces \(v_4=-v_1\), a contradiction. Thus no PSD completion exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a chordless four-cycle, all edge-clique matrices can be PSD while the partial matrix has no global PSD completion.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonchordal Sparsity Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The four-cycle construction is a valid counterexample and counterexample is the correct content kind for this boundary leaf, but no inspectable citation or locator is provided.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax\le b\iff b-Ax\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\).

notation.meaning: The componentwise nonnegative orthant in dimension m.
The slack vector associated with the inequalities.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine inequalities represented by orthant membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the nonnegative orthant by \(\mathbb{R}_+^m=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^m:s_i\ge 0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m\}\). For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the componentwise affine inequality \(Ax\le b\) is equivalent to the existence of a slack vector \(s\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\) satisfying \(Ax+s=b\), and hence to \(b-Ax\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\). Thus any finite system of affine inequalities is an affine preimage, or equivalently a slack-variable lift, of a nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite system of affine inequalities is equivalent to requiring its slack vector to belong to a nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonnegative-Orthant Representations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically correct and fits the leaf, but no citation or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Free Variable Blocks
children.top_down_role: Conic-form treatment of unrestricted variable blocks.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\iff \exists x^+,x^-\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\text{ with }x=x^+-x^-\).

notation.meaning: The nonnegative and nonpositive parts used to encode a free vector.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthant encoding of finite-dimensional unrestricted variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A free variable block \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) imposes no sign restriction. It admits the nonnegative-orthant representation \(x=x^+-x^-\), where \(x^+,x^-\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\). Conversely, every difference of two vectors in \(\mathbb{R}_+^n\) is a free vector. One canonical choice is \(x_i^+=\max\{x_i,0\}\) and \(x_i^-=\max\{-x_i,0\}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\), although the lifted pair need not be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unrestricted vector equals the difference of two componentwise nonnegative vectors; this gives an orthant encoding of a free block.
knowledge_statements.title: Free Variable Blocks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The free-variable orthant representation is correct and appropriately classified, but it has no supporting source or locator.

children.title: Zero Cone Blocks
children.top_down_role: Blocks constrained to the zero cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero Cone Blocks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional zero cone used in product-cone models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The zero cone of dimension \(m\) is \(\mathcal{Z}^m:=\{0\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\). A conic block constraint \(z\in\mathcal{Z}^m\) therefore requires every component of \(z\) to vanish. The cone is closed, convex, and polyhedral, and its dual cone under the standard Euclidean pairing is the free space \((\mathcal{Z}^m)^*=\mathbb{R}^m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-cone block contains only the zero vector, so membership enforces componentwise equality to zero; its dual block is unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\in\mathcal{Z}^m\iff z=0\).

notation.meaning: The zero cone in dimension m.

children.title: Equality Constraint Blocks
children.top_down_role: Linear equality blocks within conic representations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax=b\iff Ax-b\in\mathcal{Z}^m\).

notation.meaning: The zero cone containing only the origin of the residual space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine equalities encoded as zero-cone membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), an affine equality block \(Ax=b\) is exactly the zero-cone constraint \(Ax-b\in\mathcal{Z}^m\), where \(\mathcal{Z}^m=\{0\}\). In a product-cone formulation, equality residuals may therefore be stacked into a zero-cone factor without introducing inequality slacks. Under conic duality, the multiplier associated with this block belongs to \((\mathcal{Z}^m)^*=\mathbb{R}^m\) and is consequently unrestricted in sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine equality is precisely membership of its residual in a zero cone, whose associated dual multiplier is free.
knowledge_statements.title: Equality Constraint Blocks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-cone encoding of affine equalities and the associated free dual multiplier are correct, but no supporting citation is supplied.

children.title: Block Conversion Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Structural conversions among free-variable, zero-cone, and equality encodings.

knowledge_statements.title: Block Conversion Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conversions among free, zero, equality, and orthant blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) be a free block and let \(r\in\mathbb{R}^m\) be an equality residual. The free block may be replaced by \(x=x^+-x^-\), where \(x^+,x^-\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\). The equality \(r=0\) is equivalent to \(r\in\mathcal{Z}^m\), and it is also equivalent to the paired constraints \(r\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\) and \(-r\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\). These substitutions preserve the projected feasible set after introduced variables are eliminated, although the free-variable split is generally nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Free variables split into two nonnegative blocks, while an equality or zero-cone block converts exactly into two opposing nonnegative inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=x^+-x^-\), and \(r=0\iff (r,-r)\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\times\mathbb{R}_+^m\).
\(K=G\mathbb{R}_+^p=\{Gu:u\in\mathbb{R}_+^p\}\) for some finite \(p\) and matrix \(G\).

notation.meaning: A polyhedral cone in the original variable space.
A matrix whose columns generate the cone.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional generator lift of a polyhedral cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every polyhedral cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), there exist a finite integer \(p\) and a matrix \(G\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}\) such that \(K=G\mathbb{R}_+^p\). Equivalently, membership \(x\in K\) holds exactly when there exists \(u\in\mathbb{R}_+^p\) satisfying \(x=Gu\). Hence every finite-dimensional polyhedral cone has a lifted representation using a nonnegative-orthant block and linear equalities; eliminating \(u\) recovers precisely the original cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite-dimensional polyhedral cone is the linear image of a finite nonnegative orthant and therefore has an orthant-plus-equalities lift.
knowledge_statements.title: General Polyhedral-Cone Lifts

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-order cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the standard second-order cone in arbitrary dimension and its three-dimensional horizontal sections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(n\ge 1\), the \((n+1)\)-dimensional second-order cone is
\[
\mathcal K_n=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:\|x\|_2\le t\}.
\]
For \(n=2\), its section at \(t=\alpha\ge0\) is the disk \(\{x\in\mathbb R^2:\|x\|_2\le\alpha\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second-order cone consists of pairs (x,t) satisfying ||x||₂ ≤ t. In three dimensions, its horizontal section at nonnegative height α is a disk of radius α.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal K_n=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:\|x\|_2\le t\}

knowledge_statements.title: Lorentz-Cone Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard finite-dimensional Lorentz-cone convention and its affine membership form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\ge 1\), the Lorentz cone in \(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^m\) is \(\mathcal{Q}^{m+1}:=\{(t,z)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^m:t\ge\|z\|_2\}\). Equivalently, \((t,z)\in\mathcal{Q}^{m+1}\) exactly when \(t\ge0\) and \(t^2\ge z^\mathsf{T}z\). It is a closed, convex, pointed, self-dual cone under the standard Euclidean inner product. If \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), then \((a^\mathsf{T}x+\beta,Ax+b)\in\mathcal{Q}^{m+1}\) represents \(\|Ax+b\|_2\le a^\mathsf{T}x+\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lorentz cone contains scalar-vector pairs whose scalar component dominates the vector's Euclidean norm; affine membership represents a norm inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((t,z)\in\mathcal{Q}^{m+1}\iff t\ge\|z\|_2\).

notation.meaning: The Lorentz cone of dimension m+1.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The rotated second-order cone is \(\mathcal{Q}_r^{m+2}:=\{(u,v,z):u\ge0,\ v\ge0,\ 2uv\ge\|z\|_2^2\}\). It is linearly isomorphic to the Lorentz cone because \((u,v,z)\in\mathcal{Q}_r^{m+2}\) if and only if \(T(u,v,z):=(u+v,u-v,\sqrt{2}z)\in\mathcal{Q}^{m+2}\). Consequently, rotated-cone and Lorentz-cone blocks can be interconverted by an invertible linear change of coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rotated second-order cone encodes a nonnegative product dominating a squared norm and is linearly isomorphic to a Lorentz cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Norm Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean norm epigraphs of affine mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), and define \(r(x)=Ax+b\). The Euclidean norm epigraph has the exact second-order-cone representation \(\{(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:\|r(x)\|_2\le t\}=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:(t,r(x))\in\mathcal{Q}^{m+1}\}\). In particular, minimizing \(\|Ax+b\|_2\) is equivalent to minimizing \(t\) subject to \((t,Ax+b)\in\mathcal{Q}^{m+1}\). Cone membership automatically enforces \(t\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of the Euclidean norm of an affine mapping is exactly one Lorentz-cone constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|Ax+b\|_2\le t\iff (t,Ax+b)\in\mathcal{Q}^{m+1}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Distance Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean distance to a fixed point under an affine map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b,c\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(t\in\mathbb{R}\). For the affine point \(y(x)=Ax+b\) and fixed target \(c\), the Euclidean distance bound \(\|y(x)-c\|_2=\|Ax+b-c\|_2\le t\) is equivalent to \((t,Ax+b-c)\in\mathcal{Q}^{m+1}\). Therefore its epigraph is second-order-cone representable without auxiliary variables beyond \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Euclidean distance bound from an affine image to a fixed point is represented by one Lorentz-cone membership constraint.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Epigraph Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface separating affine residual construction from norm epigraph membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(q\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(t\in\mathbb{R}\). Introduce an explicit residual variable \(r\in\mathbb{R}^m\) through \(r=Rx-q\). The residual epigraph constraint \(\|Rx-q\|_2\le t\) is equivalent to the existence of \(r\in\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying \(r=Rx-q\) and \((t,r)\in\mathcal{Q}^{m+1}\). Eliminating \(r\) recovers the original norm inequality exactly. This interface separates residual assembly from Lorentz-cone norm domination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit residual equality followed by Lorentz-cone membership gives an exact modular interface for affine residual norm epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|Rx-q\|_2\le t\iff \exists r\in\mathbb{R}^m:\ r=Rx-q\ \text{and}\ (t,r)\in\mathcal{Q}^{m+1}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\), and choose \(R\) satisfying \(R^{\mathsf T}R=Q\). Let \(q\in\mathbb R^n\), \(r\in\mathbb R\), \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(t\in\mathbb R\). Define \(\mathcal Q_r=\{(u,v,w):u\ge0,\ v\ge0,\ 2uv\ge\lVert w\rVert_2^2\}\). Then \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx+q^{\mathsf T}x+r\le t\) if and only if there exists \(s\in\mathbb R\) such that \((s/2,1,Rx)\in\mathcal Q_r\) and \(s+q^{\mathsf T}x+r\le t\). Thus every positive-semidefinite quadratic epigraph has an exact second-order-cone representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-semidefinite quadratic epigraph is represented exactly by factoring its quadratic matrix and bounding the resulting squared norm with a rotated second-order cone.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((u,v,w)\in\mathcal Q_r\iff \lVert(\sqrt2w,u-v)\rVert_2\le u+v\).

notation.meaning: Rotated second-order cone with normalization \(2uv\ge\lVert w\rVert_2^2\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear equivalence between rotated and ordinary second-order cones.

source_refs.locator: 3 Conic Quadratic Programming p. 79

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\in\mathbb N\) and define \(\mathcal Q_r=\{(u,v,w)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^m:u\ge0,\ v\ge0,\ 2uv\ge\lVert w\rVert_2^2\}\). Then \((u,v,w)\in\mathcal Q_r\) if and only if \(\lVert(\sqrt2w,u-v)\rVert_2\le u+v\). Conversely, an ordinary cone constraint \(\lVert(z,s)\rVert_2\le t\), with \(z\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(s,t\in\mathbb R\), is transformed into rotated-cone membership by setting \(u=(t+s)/2\), \(v=(t-s)/2\), and \(w=z/\sqrt2\). These invertible linear substitutions preserve exact feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rotated second-order cone is linearly equivalent to an ordinary second-order cone, allowing product and squared-norm constraints to be interchanged exactly.
knowledge_statements.title: Rotated-Cone Reformulations

source_witnesses.locator: 3 Conic Quadratic Programming p. 79

children.title: Indefinite Quadratic Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Representability limits caused by loss of convex quadratic structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in\mathbb R^2:x^{\mathsf T}Hx\le0\}=\{x:|x_1|\le|x_2|\}\) is nonconvex and is not the projection of an affine slice of a product of convex cones.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity failure for an unrestricted indefinite quadratic sublevel set.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 What can be expressed via conic quadratic constraints? p. 85

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\in\mathbb S^2\) and \(x=(x_1,x_2)\in\mathbb R^2\). The indefinite quadratic sublevel set \(\{x\in\mathbb R^2:x^{\mathsf T}Hx\le0\}=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:|x_1|\le|x_2|\}\) is nonconvex and has no exact representation as the projection of an affine slice of a product of convex cones. It is the union of the two second-order-cone-representable branches \(\{x:x_2\ge|x_1|\}\) and \(\{x:-x_2\ge|x_1|\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indefinite quadratic inequality can join two convex branches into a nonconvex set; the full union has no exact convex-conic lift without branch selection.
knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite Quadratic Boundaries

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\le\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{\alpha_i}\iff \exists s_2,\ldots,s_n\) satisfying the stated power-cone recursion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive power-cone lift of a weighted geometric-mean hypograph.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 More examples of conic quadratic-representable functions and sets p. 104

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_k=\sum_{i=1}^k\alpha_i\), set \(s_1=x_1\), and define \(K_\beta=\{(u,v,w):u,v\ge0,\ u^\beta v^{1-\beta}\ge|w|\}\). The hypograph constraint \(t\le\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{\alpha_i}\) is represented by \((s_{k-1},x_k,s_k)\in K_{A_{k-1}/A_k}\) for \(k=2,\ldots,n\), together with \(t\le s_n\). The auxiliary variables may be chosen nonnegative, and eliminating them recovers exactly the weighted geometric-mean inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted geometric-mean hypograph has an exact recursive lift using one three-dimensional power cone for each additional factor.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Geometric-Mean Forms

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\ge|x|^p\iff(t,1,x)\in K_{1/p}\), and \(0\le t\le x^p\iff(x,1,t)\in K_p\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical scalar epigraph and hypograph power-cone forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\alpha<1\), let \(K_\alpha=\{(u,v,w):u,v\ge0,\ u^\alpha v^{1-\alpha}\ge|w|\}\). If \(p>1\), then \(t\ge|x|^p\) is equivalent to \((t,1,x)\in K_{1/p}\). If \(0<p<1\) and \(x,t\ge0\), then \(t\le x^p\) is equivalent to \((x,1,t)\in K_p\). Thus convex positive powers use epigraphs, whereas concave fractional powers use hypographs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive powers above one have power-cone epigraphs, while fractional powers between zero and one have power-cone hypographs.
knowledge_statements.title: Power-Function Forms

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{p/q}y^{1-p/q}\ge|z|\) has a finite lifted representation by rotated second-order cones.

notation.meaning: A power of two satisfying \(M\ge q\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite SOC lift for rational three-dimensional power cones.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 More examples of conic quadratic-representable functions and sets p. 104

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\alpha=p/q\) with integers \(0<p<q\), and choose \(M=2^m\ge q\). Introduce \(r\ge|z|\). Then \(x^p y^{q-p}\ge r^q\) is equivalent to requiring the geometric mean of \(p\) copies of \(x\), \(q-p\) copies of \(y\), and \(M-q\) copies of \(r\) to be at least \(r\). A balanced binary tree represents this dyadic geometric mean using constraints \(s^2\le uv\), each equivalent to a rotated second-order-cone constraint. Hence the rational power-cone inequality has a finite exact SOC lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational power-cone inequality becomes a dyadic geometric-mean tree after padding, and every binary geometric mean is rotated-SOC representable.
knowledge_statements.title: Rational-Power Decompositions

children.title: Primal Power-Cone Forms
children.top_down_role: Representations expressed through the primal power cone.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_\alpha=\{(x,y,z):x,y\ge0,\ x^\alpha y^{1-\alpha}\ge|z|\}\).

notation.meaning: Primal three-dimensional power cone with parameter \(\alpha\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed three-dimensional primal power cone under the standard absolute-value convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\alpha<1\), the primal power cone is \(K_\alpha=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ x^\alpha y^{1-\alpha}\ge|z|\}\). Powers at zero coordinates are interpreted by continuous extension from the nonnegative orthant. This set is a closed convex cone; its defining inequality is positively homogeneous because the exponents sum to one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal power cone contains nonnegative first coordinates whose weighted geometric mean dominates the absolute third coordinate.

children.title: Dual Power-Cone Forms
children.top_down_role: Representations expressed through the dual power cone.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_\alpha^*=\{(u,v,w):u,v\ge0,\ (u/\alpha)^\alpha(v/(1-\alpha))^{1-\alpha}\ge|w|\}\).

notation.meaning: Dual cone under the Euclidean inner product.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean dual of the standard three-dimensional primal power cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_\alpha=\{(x,y,z):x,y\ge0,\ x^\alpha y^{1-\alpha}\ge|z|\}\) for \(0<\alpha<1\). Its Euclidean dual is \(K_\alpha^*=\{(u,v,w):u\ge0,\ v\ge0,\ (u/\alpha)^\alpha(v/(1-\alpha))^{1-\alpha}\ge|w|\}\). Equivalently, \((u/\alpha,v/(1-\alpha),w)\in K_\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual power cone is a diagonally scaled copy of the primal cone, with scaling determined by the exponent and its complement.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Power-Cone Forms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Euclidean-dual formula is consistent with the stated primal normalization, and duality is the correct content kind. An authoritative source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Primal–Dual Parameter Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Parameter conventions linking primal and dual power-cone representations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_\alpha^*=D_\alpha K_\alpha\), where \(D_\alpha=\operatorname{diag}(\alpha,1-\alpha,1)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal correspondence between primal and dual power-cone coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\alpha<1\), define \(D_\alpha=\operatorname{diag}(\alpha,1-\alpha,1)\). Under the standard power-cone normalization, \(K_\alpha^*=D_\alpha K_\alpha\). Consequently, \(s\in K_\alpha^*\) if and only if \(D_\alpha^{-1}s\in K_\alpha\). Exchanging the first two coordinates changes the parameter from \(\alpha\) to \(1-\alpha\), so \((x,y,z)\in K_\alpha\) if and only if \((y,x,z)\in K_{1-\alpha}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal and dual power cones correspond by exponent-dependent diagonal scaling, while swapping the first coordinates complements the exponent.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Parameter Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diagonal primal-dual scaling and complementary-parameter coordinate swap are mathematically consistent and match the correspondence leaf. No inspectable authoritative citation is supplied.

children.title: Endpoint Parameter Regimes
children.top_down_role: Limiting representation regimes at power-parameter endpoints.

notation.meaning: Closed endpoint cones obtained by continuous extension.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous endpoint closures and degeneration of primal–dual scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Extending the primal family continuously to the endpoints gives \(K_0=\{(x,y,z):x\ge0,\ y\ge|z|\}\) and \(K_1=\{(x,y,z):y\ge0,\ x\ge|z|\}\). Thus one nonnegative coordinate decouples and the other two form a two-dimensional second-order cone. The scaling \(D_\alpha=\operatorname{diag}(\alpha,1-\alpha,1)\) becomes singular at \(\alpha=0\) or \(\alpha=1\); hence the interior-parameter formula using \(D_\alpha^{-1}\) must be replaced by direct endpoint dualization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At either endpoint the power cone degenerates to a nonnegative ray times a two-dimensional SOC, and the usual invertible primal-dual scaling fails.
knowledge_statements.title: Endpoint Parameter Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated endpoint cones agree with continuous extension of the chosen primal normalization, and the singularity of the interior scaling is a suitable failure-boundary statement for this leaf. Because endpoint conventions vary and no source is supplied, authoritative support is required before acceptance.

children.title: Exponential Forms
children.top_down_role: Exponential-cone representations of exponential expressions and epigraphs.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}(\exp)=\{(x,t):(x,1,t)\in K_{\exp}\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed exponential-cone representation of exponential and perspective epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The closed exponential cone is \(K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:y>0,\ y\exp(x/y)\le z\}\). Equivalently, it consists of points with \(y>0\) satisfying the displayed perspective inequality, together with boundary points satisfying \(y=0\), \(x\le0\), and \(z\ge0\). Therefore \(t\ge\exp(x)\) is equivalent to \((x,1,t)\in K_{\exp}\), and \(z\ge y\exp(x/y)\) for \(y>0\) is represented directly by cone membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential cone is the closed epigraph cone of the perspective of the exponential; fixing its scale coordinate to one represents an exponential epigraph.
knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Forms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closure description and exponential-epigraph representation are mathematically correct under the stated coordinate convention, and representation fits the leaf. No authoritative citation or specific locator is provided.

children.title: Logarithmic Forms

assumptions_latex: The exponential cone uses the stated closed-cone convention.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar logarithm hypograph represented by the closed exponential cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(u,v,w)\in\mathbb{R}^{3}:v>0,\ v\exp(u/v)\leq w\}\). For \(t,x\in\mathbb{R}\), the logarithmic hypograph has the exact conic representation
\[t\leq\log x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (t,1,x)\in K_{\exp}.\]
Membership with second coordinate \(1\) forces \(x>0\), so no separate positivity constraint is required. Consequently, an affine constraint \(t\leq\log(a^{\mathsf T}z+b)\) is represented by \((t,1,a^{\mathsf T}z+b)\in K_{\exp}\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[e^{x-t}\leq y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-t\leq\log y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (x-t,1,y)\in K_{\exp}.\]
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar inverse relation between exponential epigraphs and logarithmic hypographs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x,t,y\in\mathbb{R}\), with \(K_{\exp}\) denoting the closed exponential cone,
\[e^{x-t}\leq y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-t\leq\log y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (x-t,1,y)\in K_{\exp}.\]
Each condition necessarily implies \(y>0\). Thus the exponential epigraph and logarithmic hypograph descriptions are interchangeable after exchanging the dependent and independent scalar roles, and either description yields the same affine exponential-cone lift.

children.title: Domain-Boundary Closures
children.top_down_role: Closure behavior at logarithmic and exponential domain boundaries.

assumptions_latex: The exponential cone is defined as the Euclidean closure of its positive-perspective branch.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The closed exponential cone admits the explicit decomposition
\[K_{\exp}=\{(u,v,w)\in\mathbb{R}^{3}:v>0,\ v\exp(u/v)\leq w\}\cup\{(u,0,w)\in\mathbb{R}^{3}:u\leq0,\ w\geq0\}.\]

children.title: Zero-Argument Boundary Regimes
children.top_down_role: Closure conventions for entropy forms at zero-valued arguments.

assumptions_latex: The function is the lower-semicontinuous closure of \(x\log(x/y)\) from the positive orthant.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp zero-argument conventions for closed scalar relative entropy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The lower-semicontinuous extension of \(D(x,y)=x\log(x/y)\) from \(x>0\), \(y>0\) to \(x,y\geq0\) satisfies
\[D(0,y)=0\quad(y\geq0),\qquad D(x,0)=+\infty\quad(x>0).\]

children.title: Log-Partition Forms
children.top_down_role: Conic representations of log-partition expressions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[t\geq\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}e^{a_i^{\mathsf T}y+b_i}\right)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists z\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}:\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}z_i\leq1,\ (a_i^{\mathsf T}y+b_i-t,1,z_i)\in K_{\exp}\ \text{for all }i.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete affine log-partition epigraph represented by exponential-cone blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n,d\geq1\), let \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\) and \(b_i\in\mathbb{R}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\), and define \(A:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(A(y)=\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\exp(a_i^{\mathsf T}y+b_i)\right)\). For \(y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\) and \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), its epigraph satisfies
\[t\geq A(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists z\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}:\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}z_i\leq1,\quad (a_i^{\mathsf T}y+b_i-t,1,z_i)\in K_{\exp}\ \text{for all }i.\]
Thus every finite discrete log-partition function of this affine form has an affine exponential-cone lift.

notation.meaning: Normalized exponential weights at the minimal bound.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface between log-partition bounds and normalized exponential weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(n\geq1\), define \(\operatorname{lse}(x)=\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\exp(x_i)\right)\) for \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\). A scalar \(t\in\mathbb{R}\) bounds the log normalizer exactly when
\[t\geq\operatorname{lse}(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists p\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}:\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i\leq1,\quad (x_i-t,1,p_i)\in K_{\exp}\ \text{for all }i.\]
At the minimal value \(t=\operatorname{lse}(x)\), choosing \(p_i=\exp(x_i-t)\) gives \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i=1\). These \(p_i\) are the normalized exponential, or softmax, weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A log normalizer bound produces subnormalized exponential weights; at the exact normalizer, those weights sum to one and equal softmax probabilities.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n,d\geq1\), let \(x\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^{d}\), and set \(y_j=\log x_j\) for \(j=1,\ldots,d\). For \(i=1,\ldots,n\), let \(c_i>0\) and \(a_i=(a_{i1},\ldots,a_{id})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\). Then the posynomial constraint
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_i\prod_{j=1}^{d}x_j^{a_{ij}}\leq1\]
is equivalent to the existence of \(z\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}\) satisfying

Thus logarithmic variable substitution converts a positive-coefficient posynomial inequality into an affine exponential-cone lift.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semidefinite Programs as Negative-Semidefinite Cone Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records the semidefinite-cone representation and linear specialization without asserting that an arbitrary nonlinear semidefinite program is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a closed convex cone, \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), and \(G:\mathbb R^n\to\mathcal S^m\). The problem \[\min_{x\in C}f(x)\quad\text{subject to }G(x)\preccurlyeq0\] is a nonlinear semidefinite program and is equivalently constrained by \(G(x)\in\mathcal S_-^m\). If \(C=\mathbb R^n\), \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i x_i\), and \(G(x)=A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i\), the problem is a linear semidefinite program. More generally, \(G(x)\in K\) with a closed convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathcal Y\) is a cone constraint, and \(K=\mathbb R_-^p\) gives componentwise nonlinear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative-semidefinite matrix inequality is membership in the negative-semidefinite cone. Linear objectives and affine matrix mappings produce linear SDPs. General closed-cone constraints include ordinary componentwise inequalities through the negative orthant.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is a closed convex cone}
K\subseteq\mathcal Y\text{ is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional vector space}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G(x)\preccurlyeq0\iff G(x)\in\mathcal S_-^m;\qquad K=\mathbb R_-^p\text{ yields componentwise inequalities}.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectrahedral Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the affine-pencil definition of a real spectrahedron and qualifies the affine-slice interpretation when the pencil has redundant directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a spectrahedron if there exist an integer \(m\ge1\) and real symmetric matrices \(A_0,A_1,\ldots,A_n\in\mathbb S^m\) such that \[S=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i\succeq0\right\}.\] Thus \(S\) is the inverse image of \(\mathbb S_+^m\) under an affine symmetric-matrix pencil. If the linear part of the pencil is injective, its image identifies \(S\) with an affine slice of \(\mathbb S_+^m\); otherwise redundant kernel directions may be removed before making this identification. Empty and lower-dimensional feasible sets are allowed, and every spectrahedron is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spectrahedron is the inverse image of the positive-semidefinite cone under an affine symmetric-matrix pencil. An injective pencil identifies it with an affine slice; redundant kernel directions must otherwise be removed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i\succeq0\}\) is a spectrahedron and is closed and convex.

notation.meaning: The spectrahedron defined by the pencil.
Cone of real positive-semidefinite symmetric matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Slice Degeneracies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies degeneracy through failure of ambient-cone strict feasibility and reduction to the minimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:L(x)\succeq0\}\) be nonempty for an affine pencil \(L:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb S^m\). The slice is strictly feasible when there exists \(x\in S\) such that \(L(x)\succ0\). Let \(F_{\min}\) be the smallest face of \(\mathbb S_+^m\) containing \(\{L(x):x\in S\}\). Strict feasibility fails exactly when \(F_{\min}\subsetneq\mathbb S_+^m\), equivalently when every feasible matrix \(L(x)\) is singular. Replacing the ambient cone by \(F_{\min}\) is the associated facial reduction of the representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty LMI slice lacks strict feasibility exactly when all feasible matrices lie in a proper minimal face of the semidefinite cone, equivalently when every feasible matrix is singular.
assumptions_latex: \(L:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb S^m\) is affine and \(S=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:L(x)\succeq0\}\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict feasibility fails if and only if the feasible matrices lie in a proper face of \(\mathbb S_+^m\).

notation.meaning: Smallest face of the semidefinite cone containing all feasible matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection–Shadow Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equates coordinate projections and arbitrary linear images after a finite-dimensional lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-dimensional set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), the following are equivalent: \(S\) is a coordinate projection of a spectrahedron, and \(S\) is a linear image of a spectrahedron. More explicitly, if \(T\subseteq\mathbb R^q\) is a spectrahedron and \(M:\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^n\) is linear, then \[M(T)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists z\in\mathbb R^q,\ z\in T\text{ and }x=Mz\right\},\] which is a coordinate projection of a spectrahedron in the variables \((x,z)\). Hence projected spectrahedra and spectrahedral shadows are the same representation class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, coordinate projections of spectrahedra and arbitrary linear images of spectrahedra define the same class of sets.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(T\subseteq\mathbb R^q\) is a spectrahedron, and \(M:\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^n\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is a projected spectrahedron if and only if \(S\) is a spectrahedral shadow.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the closed-cone convention and roots of \(p(te-x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\) have degree \(d\) and be hyperbolic with respect to \(e\). Define real numbers \(\lambda_1(x),\ldots,\lambda_d(x)\) by \[p(te-x)=p(e)\prod_{k=1}^d\bigl(t-\lambda_k(x)\bigr).\] The associated closed hyperbolicity cone is \[\Lambda_+(p,e)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\lambda_k(x)\ge0\text{ for every }k\}.\] Equivalently, it is the closure of the connected component containing \(e\) of \(\{x:p(x)\ne0\}\). This set is a closed convex cone, and its interior is obtained by replacing every nonstrict root inequality by \(\lambda_k(x)>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hyperbolicity cone consists of points whose hyperbolic eigenvalues are nonnegative; equivalently, it closes the nonvanishing component containing the hyperbolicity direction.

children.title: Copositive Cones
children.top_down_role: Copositive-cone representations within lifted conic models.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\in\mathcal{COP}^n\iff x^{\mathsf T}Ax\ge0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R_+^n\).

notation.meaning: Trace inner product on symmetric matrices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the real copositive cone and records its basic cone-theoretic properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The copositive cone of order \(n\) is \[\mathcal{COP}^n=\left\{A\in\mathbb S^n:x^{\mathsf T}Ax\ge0\text{ for every }x\in\mathbb R_+^n\right\}.\] Because the quadratic form is homogeneous, it is equivalent to test all \(x\in\mathbb R_+^n\) satisfying \(\lVert x\rVert_2=1\). The set \(\mathcal{COP}^n\) is a closed convex cone: each fixed \(x\ge0\) imposes the closed linear inequality \(\langle A,xx^{\mathsf T}\rangle\ge0\), and the cone is their intersection. It contains both \(\mathbb S_+^n\) and the cone of entrywise nonnegative symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric matrix is copositive when its quadratic form is nonnegative throughout the nonnegative orthant; such matrices form a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Copositive Cones

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The copositive-cone definition and stated elementary properties are mathematically standard and fit the container, but the record has no inspectable authoritative citation or locator.

children.title: Completely Positive Cones
children.top_down_role: Completely-positive-cone representations within lifted conic models.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{CP}_n\) is a convex cone contained in \(\mathbb{S}_+^n\cap\mathbb{R}_+^{n\times n}\).

notation.meaning: space of real symmetric n-by-n matrices
completely positive cone of order n

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-dimensional completely positive cone definition is standard and unambiguous
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real symmetric-matrix convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The completely positive cone of order \(n\) is
\[
\mathcal{CP}_n:=\left\{\sum_{k=1}^{r}v_kv_k^{\mathsf T}: r\in\mathbb{N},\ v_k\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\right\}=\operatorname{cone}\{vv^{\mathsf T}:v\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\}.
\]
Thus \(X\in\mathcal{CP}_n\) exactly when \(X=BB^{\mathsf T}\) for some entrywise nonnegative matrix \(B\) having finitely many columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric matrix is completely positive exactly when it is a finite sum of outer products of nonnegative vectors, equivalently when it has an entrywise nonnegative Gram factor.
knowledge_statements.title: Completely Positive Cones

children.title: Cone Duality Interface
children.top_down_role: Dual pairing between copositive and completely positive cones.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb{S}^n\) carries the trace inner product \(\langle X,Y\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(XY)\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{CP}_n^*=\mathcal{COP}_n\) and \(\mathcal{COP}_n^*=\mathcal{CP}_n\).

notation.meaning: dual cone under the trace inner product

review_flags: pair-specific duality should be checked against a copositive-optimization source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Duality is taken in the finite-dimensional trace pairing.

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Conic duality p. 50

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
\mathcal{COP}_n:=\{Y\in\mathbb{S}^n:v^{\mathsf T}Yv\geq0\ \text{for every }v\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\}.
\]
For \(Y\in\mathbb{S}^n\), nonnegativity of \(\langle Y,vv^{\mathsf T}\rangle=v^{\mathsf T}Yv\) for every \(v\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\) is equivalent to nonnegativity on all of \(\mathcal{CP}_n\). Consequently,
\[
\mathcal{CP}_n^*=\mathcal{COP}_n,
\qquad
\mathcal{COP}_n^*=\mathcal{CP}_n.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the trace pairing, completely positive and copositive matrix cones are dual to one another.
knowledge_statements.title: Cone Duality Interface
