children.title: Tractable Inner Approximation Families
children.top_down_role: Structured inner approximations used in place of exact cone membership.

knowledge_statements.title: Tractable Inner Approximation Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral finite-generator approximations; no convergence rate is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite set \(V=\{v^1,\ldots,v^m\}\subset\mathbb{R}_+^n\), define
\[
\mathcal{CP}(V):=\operatorname{cone}\{v^j(v^j)^{\mathsf T}:1\leq j\leq m\}.
\]
Then \(\mathcal{CP}(V)\subseteq\mathcal{CP}_n\), and
\[
X\in\mathcal{CP}(V)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists\alpha\in\mathbb{R}_+^m:\ X=\sum_{j=1}^m\alpha_jv^j(v^j)^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Hence membership is a linear feasibility problem in \(\alpha\). Enlarging the generator set preserves nesting: if \(V\subseteq W\), then \(\mathcal{CP}(V)\subseteq\mathcal{CP}(W)\subseteq\mathcal{CP}_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite collections of nonnegative rank-one generators produce nested polyhedral inner approximations of the completely positive cone, with membership tested by linear feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{CP}(V)\subseteq\mathcal{CP}_n\), and membership in \(\mathcal{CP}(V)\) is representable by linear constraints.

notation.meaning: finite-generator inner approximation of the completely positive cone
completely positive cone of order n

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finitely generated subcones give an elementary tractable inner-approximation family

children.title: Matrix Cones
children.top_down_role: Specialized cones whose elements are matrices.

assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real matrix subspace
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is a matrix cone precisely when it is closed under nonnegative linear combinations.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: convex-cone definition specialized to a finite-dimensional matrix space
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General convex matrix cones; closedness and pointedness are optional additional properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A matrix cone in \(E\) is a set \(K\subseteq E\) satisfying
\[
X,Y\in K,\quad \alpha,\beta\geq0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\alpha X+\beta Y\in K.
\]
Equivalently, \(K\) is a convex cone whose elements are matrices. It is called closed when it is topologically closed, pointed when \(K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\), and full-dimensional when \(\operatorname{span}K=E\). These qualifications are not part of the basic matrix-cone definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix cone is a set of matrices closed under nonnegative linear combinations; closedness, pointedness, and full dimensionality are separate properties.
knowledge_statements.title: Matrix Cones

children.title: Spectral Cones
children.top_down_role: Cones characterized through eigenvalue or singular-value data.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real symmetric matrices with eigenvalues listed in nonincreasing order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The spectral cone induced by \(C\) is
\[
\mathcal{K}_C:=\{X\in\mathbb{S}^n:\lambda(X)\in C\}.
\]
Permutation invariance makes the construction independent of the enumeration chosen for the eigenvalues. The set \(\mathcal{K}_C\) is a convex cone and is orthogonally invariant:
\[
X\in\mathcal{K}_C,\quad Q\in\mathbb{O}(n)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
QXQ^{\mathsf T}\in\mathcal{K}_C.
\]
Thus membership depends only on the spectrum of the matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spectral cone consists of symmetric matrices whose eigenvalue vectors belong to a permutation-invariant convex cone; membership is unchanged by orthogonal conjugation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{K}_C=\{X\in\mathbb{S}^n:\lambda(X)\in C\}\) is an orthogonally invariant convex cone.

notation.meaning: ordered eigenvalue vector of a symmetric matrix

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: spectral sets are standard inverse images of symmetric vector sets under the eigenvalue map

children.title: Spectral-Lifting Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Lift structures connecting spectral constraints to matrix-cone representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral-Lifting Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact orbit interface, not a claim of convex conic representability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the spectral set \(\mathcal{K}_C:=\{X\in\mathbb{S}^n:\lambda(X)\in C\}\), the spectral decomposition gives the exact interface
\[
X\in\mathcal{K}_C
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists z\in C,\ \exists Q\in\mathbb{O}(n):
X=Q\operatorname{Diag}(z)Q^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\mathcal{K}_C=\{Q\operatorname{Diag}(z)Q^{\mathsf T}:z\in C,\ Q\in\mathbb{O}(n)\}.
\]
The orthogonal variable records eigenvectors, while \(z\) carries the constraint on eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spectral set is exactly the union of orthogonal conjugacy orbits of diagonal matrices whose diagonal vectors lie in the defining symmetric set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{K}_C\) is exactly the union of orthogonal orbits of diagonal matrices with diagonals in \(C\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact orthogonal-orbit representation follows from the real spectral decomposition

children.title: Eigenvalue-Multiplicity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Representation behavior at repeated spectral values.

knowledge_statements.title: Eigenvalue-Multiplicity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional perturbation boundary between simple and repeated symmetric eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(\mu\) occupies an index block of length \(r\) in the ordered spectrum of \(X\). For any \(H\in\mathbb{S}^n\), the directional derivatives of the eigenvalues in that block are the ordered eigenvalues of
\[
U^{\mathsf T}HU\in\mathbb{S}^r.
\]
When \(r=1\), the corresponding eigenvalue is differentiable with derivative \(u^{\mathsf T}Hu\). When \(r>1\), the ordered eigenvalue branches are generally not Fréchet differentiable because eigenvalue selection from \(U^{\mathsf T}HU\) is nonlinear in \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simple eigenvalues vary differentiably, while a repeated eigenvalue splits according to the compressed perturbation on its eigenspace, generally destroying differentiability of ordered eigenvalue branches.
assumptions_latex: \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\) has orthonormal columns spanning the \(\mu\)-eigenspace
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The first-order splitting of the repeated eigenvalue is governed by the eigenvalues of \(U^{\mathsf T}HU\).

notation.meaning: orthonormal basis matrix for the repeated eigenspace

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: first-order perturbation formula for a repeated symmetric eigenvalue is standard

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of a nonempty feasible region of an affine symmetric matrix pencil.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.4 The geometry of the feasible sets expressed with different variables p. 51

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The feasible region of the pencil is the closed convex set
\[
S=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:A_0+\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i\succeq0\}.
\]
Its recession cone and lineality space are
\[
\operatorname{rec}(S)=\left\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:\sum_{i=1}^n d_iA_i\succeq0\right\},
\qquad
\operatorname{lin}(S)=\left\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:\sum_{i=1}^n d_iA_i=0\right\}.
\]
Thus unbounded and two-sided invariant directions are determined entirely by the homogeneous part of the pencil.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine matrix pencil defines a closed convex feasible set; its recession and lineality directions are determined by the positive-semidefinite and zero directions of the homogeneous pencil.
knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Pencil Geometry

children.title: Spectrahedral Sets
children.top_down_role: Directly LMI-representable affine feasible regions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\{x:A_0+\sum_i x_iA_i\succeq0\}\) is a closed convex set.

notation.meaning: space of real symmetric m-by-m matrices

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct finite-dimensional LMI representation, without projection variables.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A spectrahedral set is a subset \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) admitting a direct linear matrix inequality representation
\[
S=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i\succeq0\right\}
\]
for some integer \(m\geq1\) and matrices \(A_0,A_1,\ldots,A_n\in\mathbb{S}^m\). It is the affine inverse image of \(\mathbb{S}_+^m\), and therefore it is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spectrahedral set is the feasible region of one affine linear matrix inequality, hence an affine inverse image of a positive-semidefinite cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Spectrahedral Sets

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

children.title: Spectrahedral Cones
children.top_down_role: Directly LMI-representable homogeneous cones.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=\{x:\sum_i x_iA_i\succeq0\}\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous direct LMI representation in finite dimensions.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A spectrahedral cone is a cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) representable by a homogeneous linear matrix inequality:
\[
K=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\mathcal{A}(x):=\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i\succeq0\right\}
\]
for some \(A_1,\ldots,A_n\in\mathbb{S}^m\). Equivalently, \(K=\mathcal{A}^{-1}(\mathbb{S}_+^m)\) for a linear map \(\mathcal{A}:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{S}^m\). Hence \(K\) is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spectrahedral cone is the inverse image of a positive-semidefinite cone under a linear matrix map, equivalently the feasible set of a homogeneous LMI.
knowledge_statements.title: Spectrahedral Cones

children.title: Conic Homogenization
children.top_down_role: Homogeneous embedding of affine spectrahedral geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Homogenization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed conic homogenization of a nonempty affine spectrahedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal{A}(x):=\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i\). The closed conic homogenization of \(S\) is
\[
H:=\{(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^n:t\geq0,\ tA_0+\mathcal{A}(x)\succeq0\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(H\) is defined by
\[
\operatorname{Diag}\bigl(t,tA_0+\mathcal{A}(x)\bigr)\succeq0,
\]
so it is spectrahedral. Moreover,
\[
H\cap\{t=1\}=\{1\}\times S,
\qquad
H=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}(\{(1,x):x\in S\}).
\]
Its zero-height slice consists of recession directions \(x\) satisfying \(\mathcal{A}(x)\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homogenizing an affine LMI produces a spectrahedral cone whose height-one slice is the original spectrahedron and whose height-zero slice records recession directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\) is spectrahedral, \(H\cap\{t=1\}=\{1\}\times S\), and \(H=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}(\{1\}\times S)\).

notation.meaning: homogeneous part of the affine pencil

children.title: Dehomogenization Slices
children.top_down_role: Affine slices recovering spectrahedral sets from homogeneous cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Dehomogenization Slices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recovery uses a functional strictly positive on every nonzero cone element; the formula explicitly covers the zero cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the dehomogenization slice
\[
S:=\{z\in K:\ell(z)=1\}.
\]
Every \(z\in K\setminus\{0\}\) has the unique normalization \(s=z/\ell(z)\in S\), and therefore
\[
K=\{0\}\cup\{ts:t>0,\ s\in S\}.
\]
If \(K\neq\{0\}\), this can equivalently be written as \(K=\{ts:t\geq0,\ s\in S\}\). If \(K\) is spectrahedral, then \(S\), viewed in the affine hyperplane \(\{z:\ell(z)=1\}\), is spectrahedral. If strict positivity of \(\ell\) is dropped, nonzero directions in \(K\cap\ker\ell\) are not represented by the height-one slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly positive linear functional cuts a cone at height one; every nonzero cone element is uniquely a positive scaling of a point in that slice, with the origin added separately when recovering the entire cone.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell:E\to\mathbb{R}\) is linear and \(\ell(z)>0\) for every \(z\in K\setminus\{0\}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(S=K\cap\{z:\ell(z)=1\}\), one has \(K=\{0\}\cup\{ts:t>0,\ s\in S\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The epigraph of \(f\) is directly LMI-representable if there exist symmetric matrices \(A_0,A_1,\ldots,A_n,B\in\mathbb{S}^r\) such that
\[
\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i+tB\succeq0\}.
\]
No auxiliary variables or projection are permitted in this representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LMI epigraph is described exactly by one affine positive-semidefinite matrix inequality in the original argument and epigraph variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Inequality Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard finite-dimensional definition of a spectrahedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A matrix-inequality set, or spectrahedron, is a set of the form
\[
S=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:A(x):=A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i\succeq0\right\}.
\]
Every such set \(S\) is a closed convex subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix-inequality set is the inverse image of the positive-semidefinite cone under an affine symmetric matrix pencil, and it is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is a closed convex subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The matrix inequality is equivalent to either scalar condition, with universal quantification over \(u\) in the quadratic-form version.

notation.meaning: Smallest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic-form and minimum-eigenvalue scalarizations of positive semidefiniteness.

source_refs.locator: 3 The Geometry of Semidefinite Programming p. 29

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), positive semidefiniteness admits the scalarizations
\[
A(x)\succeq0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
u^{\mathsf T}A(x)u\geq0\ \text{for every }u\in\mathbb{R}^r
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\lambda_{\min}(A(x))\geq0.
\]
Equivalently, the middle condition may be restricted to \(u\in\mathbb{S}^{r-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive semidefiniteness is equivalent to nonnegativity of every quadratic form, or to nonnegativity of the smallest eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.title: Scalarization Interfaces

children.title: Nonlinear Matrix-Pencil Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits of direct LMI representation beyond affine matrix pencils.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Matrix-Pencil Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonlinearity alone does not preserve the convexity guaranteed by affine LMIs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Replacing an affine pencil by a nonlinear symmetric matrix mapping can destroy convexity. For the scalar matrix mapping \(F:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{S}^1\) given by \(F(x)=[x^2-1]\),
\[
\{x\in\mathbb{R}:F(x)\succeq0\}=(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty).
\]
This feasible set is nonconvex and is neither a spectrahedron nor a spectrahedral shadow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonlinear positive-semidefinite constraint can be nonconvex; the inequality x squared minus one nonnegative gives two disjoint rays and has neither a spectrahedral nor a spectrahedral-shadow representation.
assumptions_latex: A matrix-valued mapping need not be affine or Loewner-concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonlinear positive-semidefinite inequality need not define a convex set and therefore need not be a spectrahedron or spectrahedral shadow.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Quasiconcavity Criterion for Projected Spectrahedrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient projected-LMI representability criterion for compact convex sets expressed as finite unions of basic closed polynomial sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S\subset\mathbb R^n be compact and convex, with S=\bigcup_{k=1}^mT_k and T_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_1^k(x)\geq0,\ldots,g_{m_k}^k(x)\geq0\}, where the g_i^k are polynomials. Suppose that for every u\in\partial S and every pair (k,i) satisfying g_i^k(u)=0, the set T_k has interior near u, meaning B(u,\delta)\cap\operatorname{int}(T_k)\neq\varnothing for every \delta>0, and g_i^k is strictly quasiconcave at u. Then S is a projected spectrahedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact convex finite union of basic closed polynomial sets is a projected spectrahedron if every polynomial vanishing at a boundary point is strictly quasiconcave there and its associated basic set has interior arbitrarily close to that point.
assumptions_latex: S\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is compact and convex}
\forall u\in\partial S\ \forall(k,i)\text{ with }g_i^k(u)=0:\ g_i^k\text{ is strictly quasiconcave at }u
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is a projected spectrahedron}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A spectrahedral shadow is a set
\[
S=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^m,\ A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i+\sum_{j=1}^m y_jB_j\succeq0\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spectrahedral shadow is a coordinate projection of a spectrahedron; it is convex and semialgebraic but may be nonclosed.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set \(S\) is semidefinite-representable if there exist integers \(m\geq0\) and \(r\geq1\), together with matrices \(A_0,A_i,B_j\in\mathbb{S}^r\), such that
\[
S=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^m,\ L(x,y):=A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i+\sum_{j=1}^m y_jB_j\succeq0\right\}.
\]
The variables \(y\) are auxiliary and are eliminated by projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semidefinite-representable set is the projection of a feasible region defined by one affine positive-semidefinite matrix inequality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Necessary Semialgebraic and Boundary-Curvature Properties of Projected Spectrahedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States necessary convexity, semialgebraic-representation, and boundary quasi-concavity properties; no converse is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $S\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a projected spectrahedron. Then $S$ is convex. Its interior is a finite union of basic open semialgebraic sets,
\[
\operatorname{int}(S)=\bigcup_{k=1}^m\{x:g_1^k(x)>0,\ldots,g_{m_k}^k(x)>0\},
\]
and its closure is a finite union of basic closed semialgebraic sets,
\[
\overline S=\bigcup_{k=1}^mT_k,\qquad T_k=\{x:g_1^k(x)\geq0,\ldots,g_{m_k}^k(x)\geq0\}.
\]
The polynomials in these two representations need not be the same. For the closed representation, if $u\in\partial\overline S$, $i\in I_k(u)$, and $g_i^k$ is irredundant and nonsingular at $u$, then $g_i^k$ is quasi-concave at $u$; equivalently,
\[
v^T\nabla^2g_i^k(u)v\leq0\qquad\text{for every }v\in\nabla g_i^k(u)^\perp.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every projected spectrahedron is convex. Its interior is a finite union of basic open semialgebraic sets, while its closure is a finite union of basic closed semialgebraic sets. Any active boundary polynomial in the closed representation that is irredundant and nonsingular must have nonpositive Hessian curvature along directions orthogonal to its gradient.
assumptions_latex: S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is a projected spectrahedron}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is convex};\quad \operatorname{int}(S)\text{ is a finite union of basic open semialgebraic sets};\quad \overline S\text{ is a finite union of basic closed semialgebraic sets};\quad (g_i^k\text{ irredundant and nonsingular at }u)\Rightarrow v^T\nabla^2g_i^k(u)v\leq0\ \forall v\in\nabla g_i^k(u)^\perp.

knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite-Representable Epigraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifted LMI representation of an extended-real-valued function epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The epigraph of \(f\) is semidefinite-representable if there exist integers \(m\geq0\) and \(r\geq1\), together with symmetric matrices \(A_0,A_1,\ldots,A_n,T,B_1,\ldots,B_m\in\mathbb{S}^r\), such that
\[
\operatorname{epi}f=\left\{(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^m,\ A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i+tT+\sum_{j=1}^m y_jB_j\succeq0\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(f(x)\leq t\) holds precisely when the displayed lifted LMI is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function has a semidefinite-representable epigraph when its epigraph is the projection of an affine LMI feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) has a semidefinite-representable epigraph exactly when \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is a spectrahedral shadow.

children.title: Set–Epigraph Conversion Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Structural passage between set representations and epigraph representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Set–Epigraph Conversion Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversions by affine slicing, Cartesian products, and extended-real indicators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is semidefinite-representable, then for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) the sublevel set
\[
L_\alpha(f):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(x)\leq\alpha\}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:(x,\alpha)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}
\]
is semidefinite-representable. For the extended-real indicator defined by \(\delta_S(x)=0\) when \(x\in S\) and \(\delta_S(x)=+\infty\) otherwise,
\[
\operatorname{epi}\delta_S=S\times[0,\infty).
\]
The set \(S\) is semidefinite-representable if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}\delta_S\) is semidefinite-representable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epigraph slices give semidefinite-representable sublevel sets, and a set is semidefinite-representable exactly when the epigraph of its extended-real indicator is semidefinite-representable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Epigraph representability yields representable sublevel sets, while set representability is equivalent to representability of the indicator epigraph.

children.title: Projection Closure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Closure issues affecting projected semidefinite representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Closure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness can fail under the projection used in semidefinite lifts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
Q=\left\{(a,b,c)\in\mathbb{R}^3:\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\right\}
\]
and let \(\pi:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^2\) be defined by \(\pi(a,b,c)=(a,b)\). The set \(Q\) is a closed spectrahedron, whereas
\[
\pi(Q)=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^2:a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}
\]
is not closed. Thus a spectrahedral shadow need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed spectrahedron may have a nonclosed projection; the two-by-two positive-semidefinite cone provides an explicit example.
assumptions_latex: Linear projection is applied to a closed spectrahedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Spectrahedral shadows are not necessarily closed.

notation.meaning: Cone of real positive semidefinite matrices of order two

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), define
\[
\operatorname{sdpsize}(S)=\min\left\{r:\exists m\geq0,\ S=\left\{x:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^m,\ A_0+\sum_i x_iA_i+\sum_j y_jB_j\succeq0\right\},\ A_i,B_j\in\mathbb{S}^r\right\}.
\]
If no such representation exists, set \(\operatorname{sdpsize}(S)=+\infty\). This measure records matrix order; auxiliary dimension \(m\) is a separate lift parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semidefinite lift size is the smallest PSD matrix order supporting a lifted LMI representation; auxiliary-variable count is a separate measure.

children.title: Semidefinite Block Structure
children.top_down_role: Organization of semidefinite lifts into matrix blocks.

assumptions_latex: A lifted LMI has symmetric diagonal blocks of orders \(r_1,\ldots,r_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Blockwise feasibility is equivalent to one block-diagonal PSD constraint, while retaining the product-cone decomposition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent product-cone and block-diagonal descriptions of structured lifts.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For affine symmetric pencils \(L_\ell(x,y)\in\mathbb{S}^{r_\ell}\), the structured constraint
\[
L_\ell(x,y)\succeq0\quad(\ell=1,\ldots,k)
\]
is equivalent to
\[
\operatorname{diag}(L_1(x,y),\ldots,L_k(x,y))\succeq0.
\]
Thus a block-structured lift uses the product cone \(\prod_{\ell=1}^k\mathbb{S}_+^{r_\ell}\), which embeds in \(\mathbb{S}_+^{r_1+\cdots+r_k}\) through block-diagonal matrices. The decomposition records structure lost by quoting only the aggregate order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Several PSD blocks equal one block-diagonal PSD constraint, but the product-cone description preserves the lift's exploitable structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Block Lift Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lift architecture using one unrestricted PSD block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an integer \(r\geq1\), the set \(S\) admits a single-block semidefinite lift of order \(r\) if there exist an integer \(m\geq0\), auxiliary variables \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and one affine pencil \(L:\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\to\mathbb{S}^r\) such that
\[
S=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^m,\ L(x,y)\succeq0\}.
\]
This formulation uses exactly one positive-semidefinite matrix block of order \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single-block lift projects the feasible region of exactly one affine PSD matrix constraint of a specified order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A single-block lift is precisely a projection of one affine slice of one PSD cone \(\mathbb{S}_+^r\).

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Diagonal Lift Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines semidefinite lifts assembled from independently sized positive-semidefinite blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) has a block-diagonal semidefinite lift with block sizes \(r_1,\ldots,r_k\) if there exist auxiliary variables \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) and affine symmetric pencils \(L_j(x,y)\in\mathbb S^{r_j}\) such that
\[
C=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^m,\ L_j(x,y)\succeq0\ \text{for every }j=1,\ldots,k\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, feasibility is expressed by the single block-diagonal constraint \(\operatorname{diag}(L_1(x,y),\ldots,L_k(x,y))\succeq0\). The regime restricts the admissible block sizes, not merely their total dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block-diagonal lift represents a convex set by projecting several simultaneous positive-semidefinite constraints with prescribed block sizes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\{x:\exists y,\operatorname{diag}(L_1(x,y),\ldots,L_k(x,y))\succeq0\}\).

children.title: Quadratic Representation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Positive semidefinite representations arising from quadratic structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Representation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Schur-complement representation of a scalar convex quadratic epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\), choose \(R\) with \(Q=R^{\mathsf T}R\), and define \(q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+2c^{\mathsf T}x+d\). Then
\[
q(x)\le t
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\begin{pmatrix}
t-d-2c^{\mathsf T}x&(Rx)^{\mathsf T}\\
Rx&I
\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.
\]
Consequently, the epigraph of every convex quadratic function is a spectrahedron. Intersections of finitely many such epigraph inequalities admit a block-diagonal semidefinite representation obtained by placing their Schur-complement pencils on the diagonal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex quadratic epigraph is represented exactly by a Schur-complement LMI, and multiple quadratic inequalities produce a block-diagonal lift.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}(q)=\{(x,t):\begin{psmallmatrix}t-d-2c^{\mathsf T}x&(Rx)^{\mathsf T}\\Rx&I\end{psmallmatrix}\succeq0\}\).

notation.meaning: identity matrix of the row dimension of R

children.title: Matrix-Convex Representation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Positive semidefinite representations arising from matrix-convex structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Convex Representation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the graded, free-variable meaning of matrix convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A graded family \(\mathcal C=(\mathcal C_s)_{s\ge1}\), with \(\mathcal C_s\subseteq(\mathbb S^s)^g\), is matrix convex if it is closed under direct sums and isometric compressions: whenever \(X\in\mathcal C_s\), \(Y\in\mathcal C_t\), and \(V:\mathbb R^r\to\mathbb R^s\) satisfies \(V^{\mathsf T}V=I_r\), one has
\[
X\oplus Y\in\mathcal C_{s+t},
\qquad
V^{\mathsf T}XV:=(V^{\mathsf T}X_1V,\ldots,V^{\mathsf T}X_gV)\in\mathcal C_r.
\]
A matrix-convex representation regime must enforce these conditions simultaneously at every matrix size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graded set is matrix convex when every level is compatible with direct sums and isometric compressions across matrix sizes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X,Y\in\mathcal C\) imply closure under \(X\oplus Y\) and under every isometric compression \(V^{\mathsf T}XV\).

notation.meaning: level s of the graded family

children.title: Free Spectrahedral Regimes
children.top_down_role: Matrix-level spectrahedral settings within matrix-convex geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Free Spectrahedral Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a monic free spectrahedron at all matrix levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For symmetric coefficient matrices \(A_1,\ldots,A_g\in\mathbb S^d\), the monic linear pencil evaluated at \(X=(X_1,\ldots,X_g)\in(\mathbb S^s)^g\) is
\[
L_A(X)=I_d\otimes I_s-\sum_{i=1}^g A_i\otimes X_i.
\]
The associated free spectrahedron is the graded family \(\mathcal D_A=(\mathcal D_A(s))_{s\ge1}\) defined by
\[
\mathcal D_A(s)=\{X\in(\mathbb S^s)^g:L_A(X)\succeq0\}.
\]
Every free spectrahedron is matrix convex because positivity of \(L_A\) is preserved by direct sums and isometric compressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A free spectrahedron is the positivity domain of one fixed linear matrix pencil evaluated uniformly at every matrix size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal D_A(s)=\{X:L_A(X)\succeq0\}\) defines a matrix-convex graded family.

notation.meaning: size-s level of the free spectrahedron

children.title: Scalarization Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits of transferring matrix-convex representability to scalar slices.

knowledge_statements.title: Scalarization Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates scalar convexity from matrix convexity across all levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Scalar convexity at level one does not imply matrix convexity. The polynomial \(p(t)=t^4\) is convex on \(\mathbb R\), but the functional calculus map \(X\mapsto X^4\) is not matrix convex on all real symmetric matrices: there exist an order \(s\), matrices \(X,Y\in\mathbb S^s\), and \(\lambda\in(0,1)\) for which
\[
p(\lambda X+(1-\lambda)Y)\npreceq \lambda p(X)+(1-\lambda)p(Y).
\]
Thus checking only commuting or scalar substitutions cannot certify a free matrix-convex representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scalar convexity is insufficient for free matrix convexity; the scalar-convex polynomial t⁴ fails the matrix Jensen inequality at some size.
assumptions_latex: Matrix powers are interpreted by polynomial functional calculus.
Matrix convexity is required at every size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(t)=t^4\) is scalar convex but not matrix convex on all symmetric matrices.

notation.meaning: polynomial functional calculus applied to X

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Hulls of Real Algebraic Curves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite representability theorem for compact semialgebraic subsets of real algebraic curves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a real affine algebraic curve and let \(K\subseteq C(\mathbb R)\) be compact and semialgebraic. For every regular map \(\phi:C\to\mathbb R^n\), the closed convex hull \(\operatorname{conv}(\phi(K))\) is a spectrahedral shadow. Equivalently, there exist integers \(m,r\) and symmetric matrices \(A_0,A_1,\ldots,A_n,B_1,\ldots,B_m\in\mathbb S^r\) such that
\[
\operatorname{conv}(\phi(K))=
\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^m,\ A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i+\sum_{j=1}^m y_jB_j\succeq0\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of a polynomial image of a compact semialgebraic subset of a real algebraic curve has a semidefinite lift.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a real affine algebraic curve.
\(K\subseteq C(\mathbb R)\) is compact and semialgebraic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(\phi(K))\) is a spectrahedral shadow.

notation.meaning: real points of the curve C

children.title: Moment Construction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Semidefinite representations built from moment data.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(K)\subseteq C_d\), and \(C_d\) is a spectrahedral shadow.

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Applications of Sum of Squares Programs p. 76
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\in\mathbb R[x]\), let \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_j(x)\ge0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\), set \(g_0=1\), and put \(d_j=\lceil\deg(g_j)/2\rceil\). For \(d\ge\max_{0\le j\le m}d_j\), define
\[
C_d=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\begin{array}{l}\exists y=(y_\alpha)_{|\alpha|\le2d},\ y_0=1,\ y_{e_i}=x_i\ \text{for }i=1,\ldots,n,\\ M_{d-d_j}(g_jy)\succeq0\ \text{for }j=0,\ldots,m\end{array}\right\}.
\]
Every probability measure supported on \(K\) supplies a feasible truncated moment sequence. Consequently, \(\operatorname{conv}(K)\subseteq C_d\). Each \(C_d\) is a spectrahedral shadow because the moment and localizing matrices depend affinely on the quantified truncated sequence \(y\).

knowledge_statements.title: Sum-of-Squares Construction Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degree-bounded quadratic-module certificates realized by positive-semidefinite Gram matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(K=\{x:g_j(x)\ge0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\), an affine polynomial \(\ell\) has a degree-\(2d\) sum-of-squares certificate of nonnegativity on \(K\) if
\[
\ell=\sigma_0+\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_jg_j,
\qquad
\sigma_j\in\Sigma[x],
\qquad
\deg(\sigma_jg_j)\le2d.
\]
This identity implies \(\ell(x)\ge0\) for every \(x\in K\). Writing each \(\sigma_j=v_j^{\mathsf T}Q_jv_j\) with \(Q_j\succeq0\) converts coefficient matching into affine equations and positive-semidefinite constraints, making the certificate semidefinite-representable and finitely verifiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-degree SOS identity certifies affine nonnegativity on K and becomes an SDP through positive-semidefinite Gram matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell=\sigma_0+\sum_j\sigma_jg_j\) certifies \(\ell\ge0\) on \(K\) through semidefinite Gram matrices.

notation.meaning: monomial vector of the required degree

knowledge_statements.title: Moment-Matrix Lift Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional pairing between moment positivity and sum-of-squares Gram representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L_y\) be the linear functional on polynomials of degree at most \(2d\) defined by \(L_y(x^\alpha)=y_\alpha\), and let \(v_d(x)\) contain all monomials of degree at most \(d\). The moment matrix is determined by
\[
L_y\!\left(v_dv_d^{\mathsf T}\right)=M_d(y).
\]
For every symmetric Gram matrix \(Q\),
\[
L_y(v_d^{\mathsf T}Qv_d)=\langle Q,M_d(y)\rangle.
\]
Therefore \(M_d(y)\succeq0\) if and only if \(L_y(p^2)\ge0\) for every polynomial \(p\) of degree at most \(d\). This pairing is the primal moment–dual SOS interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The trace pairing between Gram and moment matrices equates moment-matrix positivity with nonnegativity of the truncated functional on polynomial squares.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_d(y)\succeq0\iff L_y(p^2)\ge0\) for every \(p\in\mathbb R[x]_d\).

knowledge_statements.title: Truncation-Level Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nesting and asymptotic exactness of moment relaxations under an Archimedean hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C_d\) be the order-\(d\) moment relaxation of a basic closed set \(K\). Whenever both levels are defined, truncating a feasible order-\(d+1\) sequence gives an order-\(d\) feasible sequence; hence
\[
\operatorname{conv}(K)\subseteq C_{d+1}\subseteq C_d.
\]
If the quadratic module generated by the defining polynomials is Archimedean, then \(K\) is compact and the hierarchy is asymptotically exact:
\[
\bigcap_{d\ge d_0}C_d=\operatorname{conv}(K).
\]
Finite-level equality is an additional property and is not guaranteed by Archimedeanity alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moment relaxations shrink monotonically toward the convex hull under an Archimedean condition, but exactness need not occur at any finite level.
assumptions_latex: \(C_d\) is the order-d moment relaxation of \(K\).
The defining quadratic module is Archimedean for the convergence conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(K)\subseteq C_{d+1}\subseteq C_d\) and \(\bigcap_{d\ge d_0}C_d=\operatorname{conv}(K)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Spectrahedral-versus-Shadow Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict separation between direct LMI descriptions and projections of LMI feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Every spectrahedron is a spectrahedral shadow, but the converse fails: there exist closed convex semialgebraic sets \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) for which
\[
C=\left\{x:\exists y,\ A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i+\sum_{j=1}^m y_jB_j\succeq0\right\}
\]
for suitable symmetric matrices, while no symmetric affine pencil \(L(x)\) satisfies \(C=\{x:L(x)\succeq0\}\). Thus eliminating lifting variables can destroy direct spectrahedral representability even though the projected set remains convex and semialgebraic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Spectrahedra form a strict subclass of spectrahedral shadows; projecting an LMI can yield a set admitting no direct LMI description.
assumptions_latex: Representations use finite-dimensional real symmetric affine pencils.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\text{spectrahedra}\}\subsetneq\{\text{spectrahedral shadows}\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Non-Spectrahedral-Shadow Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines failure of finite-dimensional semidefinite lifted representability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a non-spectrahedral-shadow set if no integers \(r,m\geq 0\) and symmetric matrices \(A_0,A_1,\ldots,A_n,B_1,\ldots,B_m\in\mathbb S^r\) satisfy
\[
C=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^m,\ A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i+\sum_{j=1}^m y_jB_j\succeq0\right\}.
\]
Thus nonrepresentability excludes every finite positive-semidefinite lift, not merely a representation without auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex set is not a spectrahedral shadow when no finite system of linear matrix inequalities with auxiliary variables projects exactly onto it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) admits no finite-dimensional positive-semidefinite lift.

notation.meaning: real symmetric matrices of order r

knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic-Boundary Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses semialgebraicity of spectrahedral shadows and their boundaries as a necessary condition for finite semidefinite lifts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every spectrahedral shadow \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is semialgebraic: a spectrahedron is described by the polynomial inequalities given by the principal minors of a symmetric affine pencil, and its projection is semialgebraic. Moreover, the topological boundary of a semialgebraic set is semialgebraic. Consequently, if a convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) has a nonsemialgebraic boundary \(\partial C\), then \(C\) is not a spectrahedral shadow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every spectrahedral shadow and its topological boundary are semialgebraic. Therefore, a convex set with a nonsemialgebraic boundary cannot have a finite semidefinite lift.
assumptions_latex: The topological boundary \(\partial C\) is not semialgebraic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is not a spectrahedral shadow.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the elementary ambient-dimension lower bound on positive-semidefinite lift size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) has affine dimension \(d\) and is the linear image of an affine slice of \(\mathbb S_+^r\). Since \(\mathbb S^r\) has dimension \(r(r+1)/2\), the affine dimension of that slice and of its linear image cannot exceed \(r(r+1)/2\). Therefore
\[
d\leq \frac{r(r+1)}2.
\]
Violation of this inequality rules out every positive-semidefinite lift of size \(r\), although it does not by itself rule out lifts of larger size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A size-r semidefinite lift cannot represent a set whose affine dimension exceeds r(r+1)/2; this is a size lower bound, not absolute nonrepresentability.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is the linear image of an affine slice of \(\mathbb S_+^r\).

children.title: Degree Obstructions

knowledge_statements.title: Degree Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to strictly feasible unlifted spectrahedra of prescribed matrix order, not arbitrary spectrahedral shadows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r\geq1\), let \(A(x)=A_0+\sum_{j=1}^n x_jA_j\) with \(A_0,\ldots,A_n\in\mathbb S^r\), and set \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:A(x)\succeq0\}\). Assume there exists \(x^0\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \(A(x^0)\succ0\). Then \(\det A(x)\) is a nonzero polynomial of degree at most \(r\), and \(\partial C\subseteq\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\det A(x)=0\}\). Hence, if the algebraic boundary of a candidate set has an irreducible hypersurface component of degree greater than \(r\), the set has no strictly feasible unlifted spectrahedral representation of order \(r\). This test alone does not exclude spectrahedral shadows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a strictly feasible order-r spectrahedron, the determinant is a nonzero polynomial of degree at most r containing the boundary in its zero set. A higher-degree irreducible boundary component therefore excludes such an unlifted representation, but not arbitrary lifted representations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial C\subseteq\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\det A(x)=0\}\) and \(\deg(\det A)\leq r\).

notation.meaning: symmetric affine matrix pencil of order r

knowledge_statements.title: Stability Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfers nonrepresentability from an affine section, including an exposed face, to its ambient convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Spectrahedral shadows are closed under intersection with affine subspaces. In particular, let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\). If \(C\) is a spectrahedral shadow and \(F=\{x\in C:a^{\mathsf T}x=\beta\}\) is an exposed face defined by a supporting equality, then \(F\) is also a spectrahedral shadow. Consequently, if such an exposed face \(F\) is not a spectrahedral shadow, then \(C\) is not a spectrahedral shadow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every exposed face of a spectrahedral shadow is again a spectrahedral shadow. Thus, a nonrepresentable exposed face obstructs representability of the entire set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex, \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\).
\(F=\{x\in C:a^{\mathsf T}x=\beta\}\) is an exposed face of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is not a spectrahedral shadow.

knowledge_statements.title: Obstruction Interaction Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates absolute obstructions from lower bounds on a prescribed lift size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proposed positive-semidefinite lift of order \(r\), all necessary conditions must hold simultaneously. Thus any violated closure, semialgebraicity, affine-dimension, or applicable boundary-degree condition rejects the proposed representation. Quantitative conditions such as \(\dim(\operatorname{aff}C)\leq r(r+1)/2\) generally provide only lower bounds on \(r\); absolute nonrepresentability follows only from an obstruction valid for every finite \(r\), or from a family of size-dependent bounds that diverges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Obstructions combine disjunctively: one violation rejects a lift. Size-dependent dimension or degree tests yield lower bounds unless they exclude every finite lift size.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a candidate for a positive-semidefinite lift.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A violated necessary condition excludes order \(r\); exclusion for all finite \(r\) establishes nonrepresentability.

notation.meaning: order of the proposed positive-semidefinite cone

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between fixed-size lower bounds and absolute nonrepresentability is mathematically plausible and the principle kind fits the interaction leaf, but the record supplies no citation for its combined taxonomy of obstructions.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Programs in Conic Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard equality-form linear program over the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The linear program
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\ c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax=b,\quad x\geq0
\]
is the conic program
\[
\min_x\ \langle c,x\rangle\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax=b,\quad x\in\mathbb R_+^n.
\]
Conversely, every finite-dimensional conic program over a nonnegative orthant is a linear program. Free variables and affine inequalities can be converted to this form using variable splitting and nonnegative slack variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear program is precisely a conic program over a nonnegative orthant; slacks and variable splitting convert general linear constraints to equality form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible cone is \(\mathbb R_+^n\), so the displayed problem is a conic program equivalent to the linear program.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equality-normalized homogeneous max-absolute formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous representation of the minimax absolute-deviation model on the affine slice whose last coordinate equals one; an explicit epigraph conversion to a standard LP is not included in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), define
\[
a_i=(\bar a_i^\top,-c_i)^\top\in\mathbb R^n,\qquad x=(y^\top,\tau)^\top\in\mathbb R^n,\qquad d=e_n,
\]
and
\[
f(x):=\max_{1\le i\le m}|\langle a_i,x\rangle|.
\]
The associated equality-normalized problem is
\[
\operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{f(x):\langle d,x\rangle=1\}.
\]
On its feasible slice, \(\tau=1\) and hence
\[
f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}|\langle\bar a_i,y\rangle-c_i|.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Augment each coefficient vector by its negated offset and augment y by a final coordinate tau. The maximum absolute inner product is homogeneous, and imposing tau equal to one recovers the original minimax absolute-deviation objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{f(x):\langle d,x\rangle=1\},\qquad \langle d,x\rangle=1\implies \tau=1\ \text{ and }\ f(x)=\max_i|\langle\bar a_i,y\rangle-c_i|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear programs and equality–nonnegativity standard form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear programs over real variables, represented using equality constraints and the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A linear program has a linear objective and constraints consisting of linear equalities and inequalities. Every such problem can be transformed into the standard form
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} c^T x\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax=b,\qquad x\ge 0,
\]
where \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\) are fixed. Each equality row may be multiplied by \(-1\), if necessary, so that \(b\ge 0\) componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear program has a linear objective and linear equality or inequality constraints. Every linear program can be converted to equality–nonnegativity standard form: minimize c-transpose x subject to Ax=b and x componentwise nonnegative. Equality rows may be sign-reversed so that b is componentwise nonnegative.
assumptions_latex: \text{The objective and all constraints of the original problem are linear.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The LP can be represented as }\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\text{, with }b\ge0\text{ obtainable by equality-row sign changes.}

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Linear Convex Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph reformulation for finite maxima of affine functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n,k,m\geq1\), let \(a_i\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(b_i\in\mathbb R\) for \(i=1,\ldots,k\), and define \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) by \[f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq k}\{a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i\}.\] Let \(F\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(g\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Fx\leq g\}\). Then minimizing \(f\) over \(P\) is equivalent to the linear program \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n,\ t\in\mathbb R} t\quad\text{subject to}\quad a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i\leq t\ \ (i=1,\ldots,k),\quad Fx\leq g.\] For each feasible \(x\), the smallest admissible \(t\) is \(f(x)\), so the formulations have the same optimal value and corresponding optimal \(x\)-vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a finite maximum of affine functions over a polyhedron becomes a linear program by introducing one real epigraph variable and one inequality per affine piece.
assumptions_latex: \(F\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(g\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Fx\leq g\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in P}f(x)=\inf\{t:x\in\mathbb R^n,\ t\in\mathbb R,\ a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i\leq t\ \forall i,\ Fx\leq g\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Extended-Formulation Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents a polyhedron as the projection of a higher-dimensional polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). A polyhedral extended formulation of \(P\) consists of integers \(p,q,s\geq0\), auxiliary variables \(y\in\mathbb R^q\), and data \(E\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\), \(F\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}\), \(g\in\mathbb R^p\), \(G\in\mathbb R^{s\times n}\), \(H\in\mathbb R^{s\times q}\), and \(h\in\mathbb R^s\) such that \[P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^q,\ Ex+Fy=g,\ Gx+Hy\leq h\}.\] For every \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), optimizing \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) over \(P\) is equivalent to optimizing the same objective over the displayed lifted constraints. Such an extension may use fewer inequalities than a direct description of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral extended formulation expresses a polyhedron as the projection of explicitly dimensioned linear equalities and inequalities in original and auxiliary variables. Linear optimization over the projection is equivalent to the lifted linear program.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) equals the projection of the displayed polyhedron.
\(E\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\), \(F\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}\), \(g\in\mathbb R^p\), \(G\in\mathbb R^{s\times n}\), \(H\in\mathbb R^{s\times q}\), and \(h\in\mathbb R^s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x=\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in\mathbb R^n,\ y\in\mathbb R^q,\ Ex+Fy=g,\ Gx+Hy\leq h\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Quadratic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rotated-second-order-cone epigraph for a positive-semidefinite quadratic objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(G\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\), and \(h\in\mathbb R^p\). Choose \(R\in\mathbb R^{q\times n}\) such that \(Q=R^{\mathsf T}R\). Then \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\ \frac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax=b,\quad Gx\leq h\] is equivalent to \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n,\ t\in\mathbb R}\ t+c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax=b,\quad Gx\leq h,\quad (t,1,Rx)\in\mathcal Q_{q+2}^{\mathrm r},\] where \(\mathcal Q_{q+2}^{\mathrm r}=\{(u,v,z)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^q:2uv\geq\|z\|_2^2,\ u\geq0,\ v\geq0\}\). The cone constraint is equivalent to \(t\geq\frac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex quadratic objective becomes linear after an epigraph lift into a rotated second-order cone using a factorization of its positive-semidefinite quadratic matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(G\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\), and \(h\in\mathbb R^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quadratic program is equivalent to the displayed rotated-second-order-cone program.

notation.meaning: matrix factor satisfying Q equals R-transpose R

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attainment in linearly constrained convex quadratic programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of an optimizer whenever the stated convex quadratic program has a finite optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be symmetric positive semidefinite, let \(c,a_1,\ldots,a_r\in\mathbb R^n\), and let \(b_1,\ldots,b_r\in\mathbb R\). If the optimal value of \(\min\{x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x:a_j^{\mathsf T}x\le b_j,\ j=1,\ldots,r\}\) is finite, then the minimum is attained by at least one feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linearly constrained convex quadratic program with a positive-semidefinite quadratic matrix attains its optimum whenever its optimal value is finite.
assumptions_latex: \inf\{x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x:a_j^{\mathsf T}x\le b_j,\ j=1,\ldots,r\}\in\mathbb R
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x^*:\ a_j^{\mathsf T}x^*\le b_j\ \forall j,\quad x^{*\mathsf T}Qx^*+c^{\mathsf T}x^*=\min_{a_j^{\mathsf T}x\le b_j}(x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x)

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Quadratically Constrained Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order-cone reformulation of convex quadratic inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(Q_i\in\mathbb S_+^n\), \(q_i\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(r_i\in\mathbb R\). Choose \(R_i\in\mathbb R^{p_i\times n}\) such that \(Q_i=R_i^{\mathsf T}R_i\). Define \(\mathcal Q_{p_i+2}^{\mathrm r}=\{(u,v,z)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{p_i}:2uv\geq\|z\|_2^2,\ u\geq0,\ v\geq0\}\). Then the convex quadratic inequality \[x^{\mathsf T}Q_i x+2q_i^{\mathsf T}x+r_i\leq0\] is equivalent to the existence of \(s_i\in\mathbb R\) such that \[s_i=-2q_i^{\mathsf T}x-r_i,\qquad (s_i,1/2,R_i x)\in\mathcal Q_{p_i+2}^{\mathrm r}.\] Indeed, the cone membership is exactly \(s_i\geq\|R_i x\|_2^2=x^{\mathsf T}Q_i x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex quadratic inequality is second-order-cone representable by factoring its positive-semidefinite quadratic matrix and using a correctly scaled rotated-cone constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quadratic inequality is equivalent to \(s_i=-2q_i^{\mathsf T}x-r_i\) and \((s_i,1/2,R_i x)\in\mathcal Q_{p_i+2}^{\mathrm r}\).

notation.meaning: rotated second-order cone with a p_i-dimensional vector coordinate
affine scalar used in the cone representation of constraint i

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lorentz cones and conic quadratic programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a conic quadratic program as a linear conic program over a finite product of Lorentz cones and gives its equivalent affine second-order-cone inequality form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\ge 2\), the Lorentz cone is \[\mathbf L^m=\left\{z=(z_1,\ldots,z_m)\in\mathbf R^m:z_m\ge\sqrt{z_1^2+\cdots+z_{m-1}^2}\right\}.\] Given \(k<\infty\), \(m_i\ge2\), and \(\mathbf K=\prod_{i=1}^k\mathbf L^{m_i}\), a conic quadratic program has the form \[\min_x\{c^Tx:Ax-b\ge_{\mathbf K}0\}.\] Writing each block as \(A_ix-b_i=(D_ix-d_i,\,p_i^Tx-q_i)\), the problem is equivalently \[\min_{x\in\mathbf R^n}\left\{c^Tx:\|D_ix-d_i\|_2\le p_i^Tx-q_i,\quad i=1,\ldots,k\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lorentz cone consists of vectors whose last coordinate is at least the Euclidean norm of the preceding coordinates. A conic quadratic program minimizes a linear objective subject to membership in a finite product of Lorentz cones; blockwise, each cone constraint is equivalent to bounding the norm of an affine map by an affine scalar.
assumptions_latex: x\in\mathbf R^n,\quad D_i\in\mathbf R^{(m_i-1)\times n},\quad d_i\in\mathbf R^{m_i-1},\quad p_i\in\mathbf R^n,\quad q_i\in\mathbf R
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A_ix-b_i\in\mathbf L^{m_i}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\|D_ix-d_i\|_2\le p_i^Tx-q_i\qquad(i=1,\ldots,k).

knowledge_statements.title: Norm Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order-cone formulation for affine Euclidean-norm objectives and constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathbb R^n\). For \(i=0,1,\ldots,k\), let \(A_i\in\mathbb R^{p_i\times n}\) and \(b_i\in\mathbb R^{p_i}\); for \(i=1,\ldots,k\), let \(c_i\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(d_i\in\mathbb R\). Define \(\mathcal Q_{p+1}=\{(u,z)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^p:u\geq\|z\|_2\}\). Then \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\ \|A_0x+b_0\|_2\quad\text{subject to}\quad \|A_i x+b_i\|_2\leq c_i^{\mathsf T}x+d_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,k)\] is equivalent to \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n,\ t\in\mathbb R}\ t\quad\text{subject to}\quad (t,A_0x+b_0)\in\mathcal Q_{p_0+1},\quad(c_i^{\mathsf T}x+d_i,A_i x+b_i)\in\mathcal Q_{p_i+1}\quad(i=1,\ldots,k).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine Euclidean-norm objectives and inequalities translate directly into Lorentz-cone memberships of the corresponding dimensions, yielding an equivalent second-order-cone program.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(A_i\in\mathbb R^{p_i\times n}\), and \(b_i\in\mathbb R^{p_i}\) for \(i=0,1,\ldots,k\).
The norm is the Euclidean norm \(\|\cdot\|_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The norm program and the displayed second-order-cone program have identical feasible \(x\)-vectors and the same optimal value.

notation.meaning: real epigraph variable for the objective norm

children.title: Conic Quadratic Programs
children.top_down_role: Programs expressed through Lorentz-cone or rotated-cone constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Quadratic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard finite-dimensional second-order-cone program with affine data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each nonnegative integer \(m\), let \(Q_{m+1}=\{(t,u)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^m:\lVert u\rVert_2\le t\}\). A conic quadratic program is an optimization problem of the form \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n} c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad (d_i^{\mathsf T}x+e_i,\,A_i x+b_i)\in Q_{m_i+1}\quad(i=1,\ldots,p),\qquad Fx=g.\] Its objective is linear, its equalities are affine, and each conic constraint requires an affine image of the decision vector to lie in a Lorentz cone. Products of Lorentz cones and nonnegative orthants may equivalently be collected into one product-cone constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic quadratic program minimizes a linear objective subject to affine equalities and second-order-cone constraints on affine expressions.
assumptions_latex: \(n,p\) are positive integers, \(r,m_1,\ldots,m_p\) are nonnegative integers, \(c,d_i\in\mathbb R^n\), \(e_i\in\mathbb R\), \(A_i\in\mathbb R^{m_i\times n}\), \(b_i\in\mathbb R^{m_i}\), \(F\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}\), and \(g\in\mathbb R^r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) is feasible exactly when \((d_i^{\mathsf T}x+e_i,A_i x+b_i)\in Q_{m_i+1}\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,p\) and \(Fx=g\).

notation.meaning: The Lorentz or second-order cone in dimension m+1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure under finitely many CQr constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of conic-quadratic reformulability under finite constraint augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If a problem admits a conic-quadratic-program reformulation and each \(X_i\), \(i=1,\ldots,k\), is CQr, then augmenting the problem by
\[
x\in X_i,\qquad i=1,\ldots,k,
\]
produces another problem admitting a conic-quadratic-program reformulation. In particular, this applies to every finite collection of scalar linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding finitely many conic-quadratic-representable set constraints to a conic-quadratic-reformulable problem preserves conic-quadratic reformulability. Finite collections of scalar linear inequalities are a special case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (P)\ \text{augmented by }x\in X_i\ (i=1,\ldots,k)\ \text{admits a conic-quadratic-program reformulation}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure under affine variable substitution and linear equalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine restriction of the design variables in a conic-quadratic-reformulable problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a problem in design variable \(x\) admits a conic-quadratic-program reformulation. If its design variables are restricted by an affine parametrization
\[
x=Ay+b
\]
in a new design vector \(y\), then the induced problem in \(y\) also admits a conic-quadratic-program reformulation. Consequently, imposing an arbitrary finite system of linear equality constraints preserves conic-quadratic reformulability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine substitution for the design variables preserves conic-quadratic reformulability. In particular, adding any finite system of linear equality constraints preserves that property.
assumptions_latex: x=Ay+b\ \text{is an affine parametrization in a new variable }y
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (P)\big|_{x=Ay+b}\ \text{admits a conic-quadratic-program reformulation};\quad\text{in particular, finite linear-equality augmentation preserves this property}.

children.title: Norm-to-Cone Reformulations
children.top_down_role: Structural conversion of norm expressions into second-order-cone form.

knowledge_statements.title: Norm-to-Cone Reformulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph reformulation of affine Euclidean-norm inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_{m+1}=\{(t,u)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^m:\lVert u\rVert_2\le t\}\). For every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\lVert Ax+b\rVert_2\le c^{\mathsf T}x+d\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (c^{\mathsf T}x+d,\,Ax+b)\in Q_{m+1}.\] Likewise, for every \((x,t)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\), \[t\ge\lVert Ax+b\rVert_2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(t,Ax+b)\in Q_{m+1}.\] Consequently, a problem with a linear objective, affine equalities, and finitely many affine Euclidean-norm inequalities has an exact second-order-cone formulation; the reformulation preserves its feasible set and objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine Euclidean-norm inequality is exactly a Lorentz-cone membership constraint; norm epigraphs therefore yield exact second-order-cone formulations.
assumptions_latex: \(m,n\) are nonnegative integers, \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(d\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), the norm inequality and the displayed Lorentz-cone constraint are equivalent.

notation.meaning: The Lorentz cone of pairs (t,u) satisfying the Euclidean norm bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Cone Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Low-dimensional boundary between linear and genuinely conic quadratic geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each nonnegative integer \(m\), let \(Q_{m+1}=\{(t,u)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^m:\lVert u\rVert_2\le t\}\). The regimes \(m=0\) and \(m=1\) are polyhedral: \(Q_1=\mathbb R_+\), while \[Q_2=\{(t,u)\in\mathbb R^2:t-u\ge0,\ t+u\ge0\}.\] Hence constraints using only these cones reduce to linear inequalities after an invertible linear change of coordinates. For \(m\ge2\), the section \(\{(1,u):u\in\mathbb R^m,\ \lVert u\rVert_2\le1\}\) is a Euclidean ball with infinitely many extreme points, so \(Q_{m+1}\) is nonpolyhedral. This is the dimensional boundary at which second-order-cone constraints cease to be merely linear constraints in disguise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lorentz cones are polyhedral only in dimensions one and two; from dimension three onward they are nonpolyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{m+1}\) is polyhedral if and only if \(m\le1\).

notation.meaning: The Lorentz cone with scalar coordinate t and vector coordinate u.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Semidefinite Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal linear semidefinite program in affine-LMI form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear semidefinite program is an optimization problem \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n} c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad F(x):=F_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iF_i\succeq0,\qquad Ax=b,\] where \(F_0,ldots,F_n\) are real symmetric matrices and \(F(x)\succeq0\) means \(z^{\mathsf T}F(x)z\ge0\) for every \(z\in\mathbb R^k\). Multiple linear matrix inequalities may be combined into one block-diagonal inequality. Equivalently, the program has a linear objective over the intersection of an affine subspace with the inverse image of the positive-semidefinite cone under an affine map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear semidefinite program minimizes a linear function subject to affine equalities and an affine symmetric matrix being positive semidefinite.
assumptions_latex: \(n,k\) are positive integers, \(r\) is a nonnegative integer, \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \(F_0,\ldots,F_n\in\mathbb S^k\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible region is \(\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ F(x)\in\mathbb S_+^k\}\).

notation.meaning: The cone of real symmetric positive-semidefinite k by k matrices.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Standard-Form Linear Semidefinite Program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a linear semidefinite program over the cone of real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices and its matrix inner product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(C,A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathcal S^n\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), a standard-form semidefinite program is
\[
\min_{X\in\mathcal S^n} C\bullet X\quad\text{subject to}\quad A_i\bullet X=b_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad X\succeq0,
\]
where \(U\bullet V=\sum_{j=1}^n\sum_{k=1}^n U_{jk}V_{jk}=\operatorname{Tr}(UV)\), and \(X\succeq0\) means that \(X\) is positive semidefinite. This generalizes standard-form linear programming by replacing componentwise nonnegativity with membership in the positive-semidefinite cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A standard-form semidefinite program minimizes a linear function of a real symmetric matrix subject to linear equality constraints and a positive-semidefinite constraint. It generalizes standard-form linear programming by replacing the nonnegative orthant with the positive-semidefinite cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{C\bullet X:A_i\bullet X=b_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ X\succeq0\}\text{ is a semidefinite program in standard form.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coefficient-matrix representation of a linear semidefinite program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real linear maps into the symmetric-matrix space and the resulting primal SDP form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A_1,\ldots,A_n\in\mathbf S^m\), the linear mapping \(\mathcal A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbf S^m\) specified by these matrices is \(\mathcal A x=\sum_{j=1}^n x_jA_j\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\). Hence, for \(B\in\mathbf S^m\) and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), the associated linear semidefinite program is \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{c^Tx:\sum_{j=1}^n x_jA_j-B\succeq0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear map from a real vector space into the symmetric matrices is specified by one symmetric coefficient matrix per coordinate. Substituting this expansion into an affine positive-semidefinite constraint yields the standard coefficient-matrix form of a linear semidefinite program.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in\mathbb R^n,\quad \mathcal A x=\sum_{j=1}^n x_jA_j,\qquad \min_x\left\{c^Tx:\sum_{j=1}^n x_jA_j-B\succeq0\right\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Projected-Spectrahedral Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization over a linear image of a spectrahedron using lifted variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A projected-spectrahedral program minimizes a linear function of \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) over a feasible set admitting a lift \[C=\left\{x:\exists y\in\mathbb R^r,\ F_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iF_i+\sum_{j=1}^r y_jG_j\succeq0,\ Ax+By=b\right\}.\] The variables \(y\) are auxiliary and are eliminated by projection. Thus the program \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in C\}\) is solved as a linear semidefinite program in \((x,y)\), although \(C\) need not itself have an LMI description using only \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projected-spectrahedral program optimizes over variables whose feasible set is the projection of an affine slice of a positive-semidefinite cone.
assumptions_latex: \(F_i,G_j\in\mathbb S^k\), and all affine data have compatible finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is the coordinate projection onto \(x\) of the displayed spectrahedron in \((x,y)\).

notation.meaning: Auxiliary lifting variables removed by projection.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Inequality Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex programs whose constraints are affine symmetric matrix inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix-inequality program in linear semidefinite form is \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad H_j(x):=H_{j0}+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iH_{ji}\preceq0\quad(j=1,\ldots,p),\qquad Ax=b,\] where every coefficient matrix \(H_{ji}\) is symmetric. The relation \(H_j(x)\preceq0\) is equivalent to \(z^{\mathsf T}H_j(x)z\le0\) for every \(z\in\mathbb R^{k_j}\). Stacking \(-H_j(x)\) as diagonal blocks converts all matrix inequalities into one positive-semidefinite constraint, so this family is exactly a linear semidefinite program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine inequalities between symmetric matrices define semidefinite programs and can be combined into one block-diagonal positive-semidefinite constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(n,p\) are positive integers, \(r\) is a nonnegative integer, \(k_1,\ldots,k_p\) are positive integers, \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \(H_{ji}\in\mathbb S^{k_j}\) for \(j=1,\ldots,p\) and \(i=0,\ldots,n\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constraints are equivalent to \(\operatorname{diag}(-H_1(x),\ldots,-H_p(x))\succeq0\) together with \(Ax=b\).

notation.meaning: The Löwner partial order on real symmetric matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex optimization with eigenvalue or singular-value constraints on affine matrix maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A spectral program is a convex optimization problem whose matrix constraints use convex functions of the eigenvalues of symmetric matrices or the singular values of rectangular matrices. A canonical finite-dimensional instance is \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n} f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad \lambda_{\max}(F_j(x))\le t_j\quad(j=1,\ldots,p),\qquad \lVert G_\ell(x)\rVert_2\le s_\ell\quad(\ell=1,\ldots,q),\] together with convex scalar constraints, where \(F_j:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb S^{k_j}\) and \(G_\ell:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^{a_\ell\times b_\ell}\) are affine maps and \(t_j,s_\ell\in\mathbb R\) are prescribed bounds. The displayed spectral constraints are convex and have exact linear-matrix-inequality representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Spectral programs impose convex bounds on eigenvalues or singular values of affine matrix expressions; standard maximum-eigenvalue and operator-norm bounds are LMI representable.
assumptions_latex: \(n\) is positive, \(p,q\) are nonnegative integers, and all matrix dimensions \(k_j,a_\ell,b_\ell\) are positive integers.
\(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and all additional scalar constraint functions are convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed feasible set is convex, and each displayed spectral constraint admits an exact semidefinite representation.

notation.meaning: Largest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix.
Matrix operator norm, equal to the largest singular value.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral-to-LMI Reformulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact LMI forms for maximum-eigenvalue and operator-norm bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(X\in\mathbb S^m\), \(M\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}\), and \(t\in\mathbb R\), the standard spectral bounds satisfy \[\lambda_{\max}(X)\le t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad tI_m-X\succeq0,\] and \[\lVert M\rVert_2\le t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \begin{pmatrix}tI_p&M\\M^{\mathsf T}&tI_q\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.\] The second positive-semidefinite condition necessarily enforces \(t\ge0\). Therefore, when \(X\) and \(M\) depend affinely on decision variables and \(t\) is an affine expression or a decision variable, these spectral inequalities are exact linear matrix inequalities and can be inserted directly into a semidefinite program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum-eigenvalue bounds and rectangular operator-norm bounds have exact positive-semidefinite block-matrix formulations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(t\in\mathbb R\), both displayed spectral inequalities are equivalent to their corresponding LMIs.

notation.meaning: The r by r identity matrix.
The largest singular value of M.

children.title: Nonsymmetric Matrix Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsymmetric Matrix Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of eigenvalue-order LMIs outside symmetric or Hermitian matrix spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Löwner inequality \(tI-M\succeq0\) is an eigenvalue-bound representation only when \(M\) is symmetric, or Hermitian in the complex setting. For the real nonsymmetric matrix \[R=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\] the eigenvalues are \(i\) and \(-i\), so no real quantity \(\lambda_{\max}(R)\) exists and \(tI-R\) is not an element of the symmetric matrix space on which \(\succeq\) is defined. Nonsymmetric matrices must instead be handled through symmetric constructions; for example, \(\lVert M\rVert_2\le t\) uses the block LMI containing both \(M\) and \(M^{\mathsf T}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Löwner-order eigenvalue bounds require symmetric matrices; nonsymmetric matrices need symmetric dilations or other reformulations, as the rotation matrix demonstrates.
assumptions_latex: The positive-semidefinite order is taken on real symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing a symmetric matrix by an arbitrary square matrix invalidates the direct equivalence \(\lambda_{\max}(M)\le t\Longleftrightarrow tI-M\succeq0\).

notation.meaning: A real skew-symmetric rotation matrix with nonreal eigenvalues.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure phenomenon and counterexample are mathematically standard and fit the leaf, but no source is supplied for the nonsymmetric boundary claim.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity condition for singular-value semidefinite lifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the rectangular-matrix lift and preserves the additional coordinatewise-monotonicity boundary absent from the symmetric-eigenvalue result.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:\mathbb{R}_+^k\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be permutation invariant and coordinatewise nondecreasing on its effective domain: \[0\le y\le x,\quad x\in\operatorname{dom}g\ \Longrightarrow\ g(y)\le g(x).\] Suppose \[t\ge g(x)\iff\exists u:\mathcal S(x,t,u)\succeq0,\] where \(\mathcal S\) is affine in \((x,t,u)\). For \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times l}\) with \(k\le l\), define \(f(X)=g(\sigma(X))\) and \(\Sigma_j(X)=\sum_{i=1}^j\sigma_i(X)\). Then \(f\) is SDr, and \(t\ge f(X)\) if and only if there exist \(x_1,\ldots,x_k,u\) such that \[\mathcal S(x,t,u)\succeq0,\qquad x_1\ge\cdots\ge x_k,\qquad \Sigma_j(X)\le\sum_{i=1}^j x_i\quad(j=1,\ldots,k).\] Coordinatewise monotonicity is an additional hypothesis for this singular-value construction; symmetry and SDr alone are the hypotheses in the corresponding symmetric-eigenvalue construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A permutation-invariant, coordinatewise nondecreasing function on the nonnegative orthant with an affine-LMI epigraph representation induces a semidefinite-representable function of a rectangular matrix's singular values. Its epigraph uses ordered auxiliary values and bounds on all leading singular-value sums. The monotonicity assumption is the additional boundary condition relative to the symmetric-eigenvalue construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(X)=g(\sigma(X))\text{ is SDr with the stated leading-singular-value-sum epigraph representation.}
