knowledge_statements.title: Exponential-Cone Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic programs over products of exponential cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the closed exponential cone by \[K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(u,v,w)\in\mathbb R^3:v>0,\ v\exp(u/v)\le w\}.\] An exponential-cone program is a problem of the form \[\min_x c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax=b,\qquad H_i x+h_i\in K_{\exp}\quad(i=1,\ldots,p),\qquad Gx+g\in\mathbb R_+^q.\] Auxiliary variables may be included in \(x\). The closure adds the boundary points \((u,0,w)\) satisfying \(u\le0\) and \(w\ge0\), making \(K_{\exp}\) a closed convex cone suitable for conic optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exponential-cone program has a linear objective and affine constraints into products of closed exponential cones and nonnegative orthants.
assumptions_latex: All program data are real and finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible set is the inverse image of a product of closed convex cones under an affine map.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closed exponential-cone definition and boundary description are precise, but this nontrivial cone definition has no cited source.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Entropy Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential-cone representation of scalar and separable relative-entropy epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(u,v,w):v>0,\ v\exp(u/v)\le w\}\). For \(x\ge0\) and \(y\ge0\), using the closed perspective convention, \[t\ge x\log(x/y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(-t,x,y)\in K_{\exp}.\] Hence the separable relative-entropy epigraph satisfies \[\tau\ge\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log(x_i/y_i)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists t\in\mathbb R^n:\ \sum_{i=1}^n t_i\le\tau,\quad(-t_i,x_i,y_i)\in K_{\exp}\ \text{for all }i.\] Therefore, linear optimization with affine constraints and such epigraphs is an exponential-cone program after introducing the variables \(t_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each scalar relative-entropy epigraph is one exponential-cone constraint; summing auxiliary epigraph variables represents separable relative entropy exactly.
assumptions_latex: The closed convention sets \(0\log(0/y)=0\) for \(y\ge0\) and assigns \(+\infty\) when \(x>0=y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed lifted exponential-cone system is exactly the epigraph of separable relative entropy.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar and separable relative-entropy representations are mathematically plausible and the representation kind matches the statement, but the closed-perspective boundary convention and equivalences require an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Programs in Conic Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logarithmic and exponential-cone reformulation of posynomial geometric programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider positive variables \(z_j>0\) and set \(y_j=\log z_j\). A posynomial inequality \(\sum_{k=1}^r c_k z^{a_k}\le1\), with \(c_k>0\), becomes \[\sum_{k=1}^r c_k\exp(a_k^{\mathsf T}y)\le1.\] It has the exact exponential-cone lift \[\exists s\in\mathbb R^r:\quad(a_k^{\mathsf T}y+\log c_k,1,s_k)\in K_{\exp}\quad(k=1,\ldots,r),\qquad\sum_{k=1}^r s_k\le1.\] A monomial equality \(c z^a=1\) becomes the affine equality \(a^{\mathsf T}y+\log c=0\). Applying these transformations to every constraint and to an objective epigraph yields an equivalent exponential-cone program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking logarithms converts monomials to affine expressions and represents each posynomial inequality by exponential-cone epigraph variables plus a linear sum constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The logarithmically transformed geometric program has an exact lifted formulation over products of \(K_{\exp}\).

notation.meaning: The generalized monomial product of positive coordinates with real exponents.
The componentwise logarithmic change of variables.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The logarithmic transformation and exponential-cone lift are standard and fit the representation leaf, but no source supports the formulas or the claimed objective-epigraph extension.

knowledge_statements.title: Power-Function Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex programs represented using three-dimensional power cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\alpha<1\), define \(K_\alpha=\{(u,v,w)\in\mathbb R^3:u\ge0,\ v\ge0,\ |w|\le u^\alpha v^{1-\alpha}\}\). A power-function program is power-cone representable when, after introducing auxiliary variables \(y\), its feasible set has the form \[\{x:\exists y,\ A x+B y=c,\ (u_j(x,y),v_j(x,y),w_j(x,y))\in K_{\alpha_j}\quad(j=1,\ldots,m)\},\] where every displayed component is affine. A linear objective over this set is therefore a conic program over \(K_{\alpha_1}\times\cdots\times K_{\alpha_m}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A power-function program has an affine lift whose nonlinear constraints are memberships in power cones, making linear optimization over it a product-cone program.
assumptions_latex: All cone arguments are affine functions of the decision and auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{d^\top x:x\text{ satisfies the lifted system}\}\) is a conic program over \(\prod_{j=1}^m K_{\alpha_j}\).

notation.meaning: Three-dimensional power cone with exponent alpha.
Auxiliary variables in the conic lift.

review_flags: Exact power-cone representation requires an authoritative source locator not supplied by the inventory hints.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically plausible and the representation content kind fits the leaf, but no source with a specific locator supports the power-cone definition or the claimed program representation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\le\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{a_i}\iff\exists s\in\mathbb R:\ t\le s\text{ and }(x,s)\in\mathcal K_a\).

notation.meaning: Weighted geometric-mean cone with an absolute-value scalar coordinate.
Positive weight vector summing to one.

review_flags: An authoritative source locator for generalized power-cone representations remains required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted geometric-mean hypographs represented through generalized power cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_i>0\) satisfy \(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=1\), and define \[\mathcal K_a=\left\{(x,s)\in\mathbb R_+^n\times\mathbb R:|s|\le\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{a_i}\right\}.\] The full weighted geometric-mean hypograph \[G_a=\left\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R_+^n\times\mathbb R:t\le\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{a_i}\right\}\] has the lifted representation \[G_a=\left\{(x,t):\exists s\in\mathbb R,\ t\le s,\ (x,s)\in\mathcal K_a\right\}.\] Thus each geometric-mean hypograph constraint can be represented by one generalized power-cone membership and one affine inequality. For \(n=2\), \((x_1,x_2,s)\in\mathcal K_{(a_1,a_2)}\) is exactly membership in the three-dimensional power cone \(K_{a_1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted geometric-mean hypograph is the projection of a generalized power-cone constraint together with an affine inequality; in two dimensions the cone is the ordinary three-dimensional power cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometric-Mean Programs
Mixed Power–Exponential Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Programs combining power-cone and exponential-cone representable atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the closed exponential cone by \[K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(u,v,w)\in\mathbb R^3:v>0,\ v\exp(u/v)\le w\}.\] A mixed power–exponential program is a linear optimization problem admitting auxiliary variables \(y\) and an affine system \(A x+B y=c\) such that specified affine triples belong either to power cones \(K_{\alpha_j}\) or to \(K_{\exp}\). Collecting these triples yields one conic constraint \[F x+G y+h\in\left(\prod_{j=1}^{p}K_{\alpha_j}\right)\times K_{\exp}^{q}.\] Thus power and exponential atoms may coexist without altering conic standard form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed power–exponential program uses an affine lift into a product of power and exponential cones.
assumptions_latex: Every cone argument and coupling equation is affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F x+G y+h\in(\prod_{j=1}^{p}K_{\alpha_j})\times K_{\exp}^{q}\) is a mixed-cone representation of the program.

knowledge_statements.title: Product-Cone Standard Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard conic form with a Cartesian product of closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{m_i}\) be closed convex cones and set \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_r\). A product-cone standard-form problem is \[\min_{z\in\mathbb R^n}\ c^\top z\quad\text{subject to}\quad A z=b,\qquad H z+h\in K.\] Writing \(H z+h=(s_1(z),\ldots,s_r(z))\), the single product-cone constraint is equivalent to the block constraints \(s_i(z)\in K_i\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,r\). The blocks may have different dimensions and need not be cones of the same family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Product-cone standard form combines affine equations and blockwise memberships in a Cartesian product of closed convex cones.
assumptions_latex: \(K_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{m_i}\) is a closed convex cone for each \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H z+h\in\prod_{i=1}^r K_i\iff s_i(z)\in K_i\text{ for all }i\).

notation.meaning: Cartesian product of the cone blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Heterogeneous-Cone Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixed-cone models whose blocks belong to different cone families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A heterogeneous-cone model is a product-cone program in which \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_r\) contains blocks from at least two distinct cone families, such as nonnegative orthants, second-order cones, positive-semidefinite cones, power cones, or exponential cones. Its feasible set is \[\mathcal F=\{x:\exists y,\ A x+B y=b,\ H_i x+G_i y+h_i\in K_i\ \text{for }i=1,\ldots,r\}.\] Heterogeneity concerns the cone families only; all blocks remain coordinated through the common affine variables and equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A heterogeneous-cone model is an affine lift using blocks from at least two cone families, coupled through shared variables or equations.
assumptions_latex: Each \(K_i\) is a closed convex cone.
At least two blocks belong to distinct cone families.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F\) is the projection of an affine slice of \(\prod_{i=1}^r K_i\).

notation.meaning: Projected feasible set of the heterogeneous model.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Decomposition Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between product-cone membership and separate cone-block constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_r\), and partition an affine map as \(L(z)=(L_1(z),\ldots,L_r(z))\) with \(L_i(z)\in\mathbb R^{m_i}\). The cone-decomposition interface is the exact equivalence \[L(z)\in K\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L_i(z)\in K_i\ \text{for every }i=1,\ldots,r.\] Conversely, independently modeled block constraints can be assembled into the single product-cone constraint by stacking their affine maps. This interface changes neither the feasible set nor the objective and introduces no additional consistency conditions beyond shared variables already present in the maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A product-cone constraint can be split into block memberships, and separate block memberships can be stacked back without changing feasibility.
assumptions_latex: The affine map \(L\) is partitioned conformably with the product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{z:L(z)\in K\}=\bigcap_{i=1}^r\{z:L_i(z)\in K_i\}\).

notation.meaning: Affine map feeding the i-th cone block.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Reformulation Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact replacement of a convex constraint by an affine conic lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. An exact cone-reformulation interface for \(C\) consists of a closed convex cone \(K\), auxiliary variables \(y\), and affine data \(A,B,b,F,G,h\) satisfying \[x\in C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists y:\ A x+B y=b,\quad F x+G y+h\in K.\] Replacing every occurrence of \(x\in C\) by this lifted system preserves the feasible set after projection onto \(x\). If the original objective depends only on \(x\), its feasible objective values and optimal value are also preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact cone-reformulation interface replaces a convex constraint by an affine conic lift whose projection is precisely the original set.
assumptions_latex: The displayed equivalence holds for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\{x:\exists y,\ A x+B y=b,\ F x+G y+h\in K\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each local constraint admits a representation \(F_i x_i+G_i y_i+h_i\in K_i\). Cross-cone coordination introduces a global variable \(x\) and affine consistency equations \(x_i=P_i x+q_i\). The coordinated formulation is \[F_i x_i+G_i y_i+h_i\in K_i,\qquad x_i=P_i x+q_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,r).\] Eliminating the local copies gives \(F_i(P_i x+q_i)+G_i y_i+h_i\in K_i\), so the coordinated system remains an affine slice of \(K_1\times\cdots\times K_r\) and enforces agreement of quantities shared across cone families.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex conic lifts fail for genuinely nonconvex cross-block coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set represented as \(C=\{x:\exists y,\ A x+B y=b,\ F x+G y+h\in K\}\) with \(K\) convex must itself be convex, because affine inverse images, affine slices, and linear projections preserve convexity. Consequently, independently conic-representable blocks cannot be combined through an arbitrary nonconvex relation while retaining a convex-conic lift. For example, \[C_{\times}=\{(x,y,z)\in[0,1]^3:z=xy\}\] is nonconvex: it contains \((0,0,0)\) and \((1,1,1)\) but not their midpoint \((1/2,1/2,1/2)\). Thus this exact bilinear coordination has no affine lift over any convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact affine convex-cone lifts preserve convexity; genuinely nonconvex couplings, such as a bilinear graph, cannot be represented this way.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Slack Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex–facet slack matrix of a full-dimensional polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\ldots,v_N\}=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:a_j^\top x\le b_j,\ j=1,\ldots,M\}\), where the inequalities give an irredundant facet description. The slack matrix of these vertex and facet descriptions is the nonnegative matrix \(S_P\in\mathbb R_+^{N\times M}\) defined by \[(S_P)_{ij}=b_j-a_j^\top v_i.\] An entry is zero exactly when vertex \(v_i\) lies on facet \(j\). Positive rescaling of a facet inequality rescales the corresponding column, so the numerical slack matrix depends on normalization while its zero pattern does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polytope’s slack matrix records every facet inequality’s nonnegative residual at every vertex.
assumptions_latex: The listed inequalities form an irredundant facet description.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((S_P)_{ij}\ge0\), and \((S_P)_{ij}=0\iff a_j^\top v_i=b_j\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator directly addresses polyhedral slack matrices.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a standard and precise vertex-facet slack-matrix definition, and definition is the correct content kind. No inspectable source locator is supplied, so it cannot pass source review.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Body Slack Operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Slack kernel pairing a convex body with its polar body.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be a closed convex body with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), and let \(C^\circ=\{y\in\mathbb R^d:\langle x,y\rangle\le1\text{ for every }x\in C\}\). The convex-body slack operator is the nonnegative kernel \[S_C:C\times C^\circ\to\mathbb R_+,\qquad S_C(x,y)=1-\langle x,y\rangle.\] Restricting its arguments to extreme points of \(C\) and \(C^\circ\) retains the boundary slack data used in lift-factorization criteria. Zero slack means that \(x\) lies on the supporting hyperplane exposed by \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The slack operator assigns each point–polar-point pair the residual of the corresponding normalized supporting inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_C(x,y)\ge0\), with \(S_C(x,y)=0\iff\langle x,y\rangle=1\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator directly supports convex-body slack operators.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The polar-body slack operator is stated consistently and definition fits the leaf, but the claim about restriction to extreme points and lift-factorization criteria especially requires a direct authoritative locator.

children.title: Generalized Slack Matrices for Nested Sets

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Slack Matrices for Nested Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Slack data for a nested pair of convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), where \(D\) is a closed convex body and \(0\in\operatorname{int}D\). With \(D^\circ=\{y:\langle z,y\rangle\le1\text{ for every }z\in D\}\), define the generalized slack kernel of the nested pair by \[S_{C,D}:C\times D^\circ\to\mathbb R_+,\qquad S_{C,D}(x,y)=1-\langle x,y\rangle.\] For finite sample sets \(X=\{x_i\}\subseteq C\) and \(Y=\{y_j\}\subseteq D^\circ\), the generalized slack matrix is \((S_{X,Y})_{ij}=1-\langle x_i,y_j\rangle\). Nonnegativity follows from \(C\subseteq D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nested convex sets, generalized slack records how points of the inner set satisfy normalized supporting inequalities valid for the outer set.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a closed convex body with \(0\in\operatorname{int}D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_{C,D}(x,y)\ge0\) for every \((x,y)\in C\times D^\circ\).

notation.meaning: Polar body of the outer set D.
Generalized slack kernel for the nested pair.
Finite generalized slack matrix sampled from the kernel.

review_flags: No supplied source locator directly addresses generalized slack matrices for nested convex sets.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed kernel is nonnegative under the stated nesting assumptions and definition fits the leaf. However, the generalized-slack terminology and its precise domain convention for nested sets require a specific authoritative source locator, which is absent.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains no affine line.
\(K_C=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}\{(x,1):x\in C\}\) is its closed homogenization cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_C\) is nonnegative and includes slack against both ordinary supporting inequalities and recession constraints.

notation.meaning: Homogenization cone of the possibly noncompact set
Dual cone of the homogenization cone

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: homogeneous conic slack is the standard extension of convex-body slack to noncompact closed convex sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses homogenization so recession directions are retained rather than discarded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u\in K_C\) and \(z\in K_C^*\), define the homogeneous slack operator by \[S_C(u,z)=\langle u,z\rangle.\] In particular, if \(z=(-a,b)\in K_C^*\), then \(a^Tx\le b\) for every \(x\in C\), and \[S_C((x,1),(-a,b))=b-a^Tx.\] Values on vectors \((d,0)\in K_C\) record recession-direction slack, namely \(S_C((d,0),(-a,b))=-a^Td\). Thus the operator remains defined when \(C\) is unbounded and simultaneously represents finite-point and recession data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homogenizing an unbounded closed convex set yields a nonnegative cone-duality slack operator that records both supporting-inequality slack and recession-direction slack.
knowledge_statements.title: Noncompact Slack Operators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The homogeneous-cone construction is mathematically coherent and fits the noncompact-slack container, but no inspectable source supports the stated treatment of recession-direction slack. Supply an authoritative section, theorem, or page locator for homogeneous slack operators of closed unbounded convex sets.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty polytope that is not a singleton.
\(S\) is any slack matrix of \(P\), with rows indexed by vertices and columns by facet inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}(P)=\operatorname{rank}_+(S)\).

notation.meaning: Minimum number of inequalities in an extended formulation of the polytope

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical polyhedral version, counting inequalities in linear extended formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a linear extended formulation of \(P\) having \(r\) inequalities if and only if its slack matrix admits a nonnegative factorization of size \(r\): there are vectors \(a_v,b_F\in\mathbb{R}_+^r\) such that \[S_{vF}=\langle a_v,b_F\rangle\] for every vertex \(v\) and facet \(F\). Consequently, after minimizing over \(r\), the linear extension complexity of \(P\) equals the nonnegative rank of any slack matrix of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polytope has an extended formulation with r inequalities exactly when its slack matrix factors through the nonnegative orthant of dimension r.
knowledge_statements.title: Yannakakis Factorization Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is the appropriate theorem family and is essentially the classical Yannakakis characterization, but it has no citation. The source must also substantiate the convention under which extension complexity counts inequalities and the exact versus at-most-r formulation.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a full-dimensional convex body with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\).
\(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone, and a proper \(K\)-lift intersects \(\operatorname{int}K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A proper \(K\)-lift implies a \(K\)-factorization of \(S_C\), and any such factorization implies a \(K\)-lift of \(C\).

notation.meaning: Polar body of the convex body
Slack operator of the convex body
Dual cone of the lifting cone

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard cone-factorization characterization of proper conic lifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex-body characterization with the usual properness qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(S_C:C\times C^\circ\to\mathbb{R}_+\) by \(S_C(x,y)=1-\langle x,y\rangle\). The operator has a \(K\)-factorization when maps \(A:C\to K\) and \(B:C^\circ\to K^*\) satisfy \[1-\langle x,y\rangle=\langle A(x),B(y)\rangle\] for all \(x\in C\) and \(y\in C^\circ\). If \(C\) has a proper \(K\)-lift, then such maps exist. Conversely, existence of these maps yields an affine subspace \(L\subseteq E\) and linear map \(\pi:E\to\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(C=\pi(K\cap L)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proper lifts through a closed cone produce cone-dual factorizations of the slack operator, while any such factorization constructs a lift through that cone.
knowledge_statements.title: General Cone-Factorization Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits the general cone-factorization container and states the standard two directions, but the precise closedness, properness, and finite-dimensional hypotheses require an authoritative theorem locator before the record is reliable.

assumptions_latex: \(S:I\times J\to\mathbb{R}_+\) is a nonnegative matrix or operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A size-\(r\) positive-semidefinite factorization is precisely a \(\mathbb{S}_+^r\)-factorization under the trace pairing.

notation.meaning: Cone of real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices of order r

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real finite-dimensional positive-semidefinite factors with the trace pairing.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 From Linear to Semidefinite Optimization p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A positive-semidefinite factorization of \(S\) of size \(r\) consists of matrices \(A_i,B_j\in\mathbb{S}_+^r\) satisfying \[S(i,j)=\langle A_i,B_j\rangle=\operatorname{Tr}(A_iB_j)\] for every \((i,j)\in I\times J\). The least feasible \(r\) is the positive-semidefinite rank of \(S\). Because \(\mathbb{S}_+^r\) is self-dual under the trace pairing, both factor families lie in the same cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A PSD factorization expresses every slack entry as the trace inner product of two positive-semidefinite matrices; the smallest matrix size is PSD rank.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Semidefinite Factorizations

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 From Linear to Semidefinite Optimization p. 3
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

A source locator addressing PSD factorizations and their minimum size is required.

children.title: Symmetric Factorizations
children.top_down_role: Factorizations constrained by symmetry invariance.

assumptions_latex: A group \(G\) acts on index sets \(I\) and \(J\), and \(S(gi,gj)=S(i,j)\).
\(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The factorization is symmetric when every data symmetry is realized by a pairing-preserving cone automorphism of its factors.

notation.meaning: Dual action induced by an invertible linear map

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: symmetry of a cone factorization is conventionally realized by cone automorphisms preserving the primal-dual pairing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry is imposed on a fixed cone factorization, not merely on the slack data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S(i,j)=\langle A_i,B_j\rangle\) with \(A_i\in K\) and \(B_j\in K^*\). The factorization is \(G\)-symmetric if, for every \(g\in G\), there exists \(T_g\in\operatorname{Aut}(K)\) such that \[A_{gi}=T_gA_i,\qquad B_{gj}=T_g^{-*}B_j\] for all \(i\in I\) and \(j\in J\). The inverse-adjoint action ensures \(\langle T_gA_i,T_g^{-*}B_j\rangle=\langle A_i,B_j\rangle\), so the factor transformation realizes the prescribed symmetry of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A slack factorization is symmetric when each group symmetry acts on its factors through a cone automorphism and the induced dual action.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Factorizations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally consistent and deliberately weaker than equivariance because the automorphisms are not required to form a representation. That terminology choice is not universal, so a specific source defining symmetric factorizations in this sense is required.

children.title: Equivariant Factorizations
children.top_down_role: Factorizations compatible with prescribed group actions.

assumptions_latex: A group \(G\) acts on \(I\) and \(J\), and \(S(gi,gj)=S(i,j)\).
\(\rho:G\to\operatorname{Aut}(K)\) is a group representation by linear cone automorphisms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equivariance means that both factor maps intertwine the index actions with \(\rho\) and its contragredient action.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: equivariance is the intertwining condition for factor maps under primal and contragredient representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses one coherent group representation rather than unrelated automorphisms for individual elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A \(K\)-factorization \(S(i,j)=\langle A(i),B(j)\rangle\) is \(G\)-equivariant with respect to \(\rho\) when \[A(gi)=\rho(g)A(i),\qquad B(gj)=\rho(g)^{-*}B(j)\] for every \(g\in G\), \(i\in I\), and \(j\in J\). Since \(\rho(gh)=\rho(g)\rho(h)\), these transformations respect group composition. The contragredient rule preserves the pairing and therefore implies \(S(gi,gj)=S(i,j)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An equivariant factorization uses a single group representation so the primal and dual factor maps consistently intertwine both index actions.
knowledge_statements.title: Equivariant Factorizations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The intertwining equations correctly express equivariance through one cone-automorphism representation and its contragredient action, but no source or locator supports this specialized definition.

children.title: Group-Action Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Structural compatibility between slack data, factors, and group actions.

assumptions_latex: A group \(G\) acts on the primal index set \(I\) and dual index set \(J\).
\(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone and \(\rho:G\to\operatorname{GL}(E)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compatibility holds exactly when the cone, dual cone, pairing, and slack data are preserved by the associated actions.

notation.meaning: Linear group action on the factor space
Contragredient action on the dual factor space

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: compatibility requires invariant cones and the canonical contragredient pairing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates compatibility of ambient actions from existence of an equivariant factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The actions are compatible with \(K\)-factorization when, for every \(g\in G\), \[\rho(g)K=K,\qquad \rho(g)^{-*}K^*=K^*,\qquad S(gi,gj)=S(i,j).\] The primal and dual actions must use the canonical pairing, so \[\langle\rho(g)u,\rho(g)^{-*}v\rangle=\langle u,v\rangle\] for all \(u\in K\) and \(v\in K^*\). These conditions make the equivariance equations well typed and preserve every reconstructed slack value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Group actions are compatible when they preserve the factor cone, its dual, the primal-dual pairing, and the slack data.
knowledge_statements.title: Group-Action Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compatibility conditions fit the leaf, but the assumptions only declare a map rho from G to GL(E), not a group representation. An authoritative source is needed to fix the exact definition and confirm that rho is required to be a homomorphism.

children.title: Symmetry-Breaking Gaps
children.top_down_role: Factorization-size changes caused by removing symmetry restrictions.

assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}_K(S)\) and \(\operatorname{rank}_K^G(S)\) minimize the same cone-family size without and with equivariance, respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta_G(S)=\operatorname{rank}_K^G(S)-\operatorname{rank}_K(S)\ge 0\), with equality exactly when an unrestricted optimum can be chosen equivariant.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: restricting a minimization to equivariant factorizations can only increase its optimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the boundary between unrestricted and symmetry-constrained factorization size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\Delta_G(S)=\operatorname{rank}_K^G(S)-\operatorname{rank}_K(S).\] Because every \(G\)-equivariant factorization is also an unrestricted factorization, \(\operatorname{rank}_K^G(S)\ge\operatorname{rank}_K(S)\), hence \(\Delta_G(S)\ge0\). The boundary \(\Delta_G(S)=0\) holds precisely when at least one minimum-size unrestricted factorization admits a compatible \(G\)-action. A positive gap certifies that imposing the data symmetry excludes every unrestricted optimum and forces larger factors or a larger cone in the chosen cone family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The symmetry-breaking gap is the extra factorization size forced by equivariance; it vanishes exactly when some unrestricted optimum respects the group action.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry-Breaking Gaps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The monotonicity idea fits a failure-boundary leaf, but rank_K is not well defined as a size invariant for a single fixed cone K unless an indexed cone family and its size parameter are specified. A source must establish the intended symmetric-rank convention and any strict-gap phenomenon.

assumptions_latex: \(S:I\times J\to\mathbb{R}_+\) is the slack data of a convex set.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone with dual \(K^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed primal-dual factors certify a \(K\)-factorization of the slack data and hence, under the cone-factorization theorem's hypotheses, a \(K\)-lift.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: cone-dual-cone factor pairs are directly checkable witnesses of slack factorization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A directly checkable witness once the slack data and cone memberships are specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cone-dual-cone factor-pair certificate consists of families \((u_i)_{i\in I}\subseteq K\) and \((v_j)_{j\in J}\subseteq K^*\) satisfying \[S(i,j)=\langle u_i,v_j\rangle\qquad(i\in I,\ j\in J).\] Verification requires checking membership in \(K\) and \(K^*\) and all displayed pairing equalities. These checks certify nonnegativity and a \(K\)-factorization. Whenever the applicable cone-factorization characterization holds for the underlying convex set, the same data certify existence of a \(K\)-lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal factors in a cone and dual factors in its dual certify a conic slack factorization when their pairings reproduce every slack value.
knowledge_statements.title: Cone–Dual-Cone Factor Pairs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Cone and dual-cone factors are correctly presented as a directly checkable factorization certificate. The further implication to lift existence depends on a cone-factorization theorem whose precise hypotheses and locator are absent.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone, \(L\subseteq E\) is affine, and \(\pi:E\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is linear.
\(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is the target closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two inclusions certify \(C=\pi(K\cap L)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: equality of a projected lift and its target is certified by mutual inclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-theoretic certificate for exactness of a proposed conic lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A projection-equivalence certificate for \(C=\pi(K\cap L)\) consists of the two conditions \[z\in K\cap L\Longrightarrow \pi(z)\in C\] and \[x\in C\Longrightarrow \text{there exists }z_x\in K\cap L\text{ such that }\pi(z_x)=x.\] Equivalently, these conditions certify the inclusions \(\pi(K\cap L)\subseteq C\) and \(C\subseteq\pi(K\cap L)\), respectively, and hence certify exact projection equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact projection is certified by checking that every lifted feasible point maps into the target and every target point has a lifted feasible preimage.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Equivalence Certificates

assumptions_latex: \(C=\pi(K\cap L)\) is a proposed conic lift in \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The intertwining and invariance identities certify that the lift realizes the prescribed action of \(G\) on \(C\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: invariance of the lifted feasible set plus an intertwining projection certifies symmetry compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate for a lift carrying a specified group action, beyond mere invariance of its projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A symmetry-compatible lift certificate consists of a group representation \(g\mapsto\widetilde g\in\operatorname{GL}(E)\) satisfying, for every \(g\in G\), \[\widetilde gK=K,\qquad \widetilde gL=L,\qquad \pi\circ\widetilde g=g_X\circ\pi.\] Together with \(C=\pi(K\cap L)\), these invariance and intertwining identities certify that the lift realizes the prescribed action of \(G\) on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetry-compatible lift is certified by lifted group transformations that preserve its cone and affine slice and intertwine projection with the original action.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry-Compatible Certificates

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}_+(M)\) is the smallest inner dimension of an entrywise nonnegative matrix factorization of \(M\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of nonnegative matrix rank
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite nonnegative matrices over the real numbers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The nonnegative rank of \(M\) is \[\operatorname{rank}_+(M)=\min\left\{r\in\mathbb{N}:M=UV,\ U\in\mathbb{R}_+^{m\times r},\ V\in\mathbb{R}_+^{r\times n}\right\}.\] Equivalently, it is the least \(r\) for which vectors \(a_i,b_j\in\mathbb{R}_+^r\) satisfy \(M_{ij}=\langle a_i,b_j\rangle\) for every row \(i\) and column \(j\). Under the convention \(\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), the zero matrix has nonnegative rank zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative rank is the smallest number of nonnegative components needed to factor a nonnegative matrix, equivalently the smallest dimension of nonnegative vector factors.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonnegative Rank

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is precise, includes equivalent matrix and vector forms, and handles the zero-matrix convention consistently. It fits the Nonnegative Rank leaf, but the record supplies no inspectable source locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Semidefinite Rank
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines PSD rank for a finite nonnegative matrix using trace-inner-product factorizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a matrix \(M\in\mathbb{R}_+^{p\times q}\), its positive-semidefinite rank is
\[
\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{psd}}(M):=\min\left\{r\in\mathbb{N}:\exists A_1,\ldots,A_p,B_1,\ldots,B_q\in\mathbb{S}_+^r,\ M_{ij}=\langle A_i,B_j\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(A_iB_j)\ \forall(i,j)\right\}.
\]
If no such factorization exists, the minimum is \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: PSD rank is the smallest matrix size permitting every entry of a nonnegative matrix to be expressed as a trace inner product of PSD factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{psd}}(M)\) equals the displayed minimum factor size.

notation.meaning: cone of real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices of order r

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the leaf and are mathematically standard, but no citation supports the PSD-rank formula or the convention for the zero matrix and natural-number indexing.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Family-Relative Rank
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines matrix factorization rank relative to a sized family of closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal{K}\) be a family of closed convex cones in finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, equipped with a size map \(\sigma:\mathcal{K}\to\mathbb{N}\). For \(M\in\mathbb{R}_+^{p\times q}\), define
\[
\operatorname{rank}_{\mathcal{K}}(M):=\inf\left\{\sigma(K):K\in\mathcal{K},\ \exists a_i\in K,\ b_j\in K^*,\ M_{ij}=\langle a_i,b_j\rangle\ \forall(i,j)\right\}.
\]
The value is \(+\infty\) when no cone in \(\mathcal{K}\) admits such a factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cone-family-relative rank is the least declared size of a cone through which the nonnegative matrix factors by primal–dual inner products.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{K}\) is a sized family of finite-dimensional closed convex cones
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathcal{K}}(M)\) is the displayed infimum.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but this generalized invariant depends essentially on the chosen cone family and size map; no source establishes this convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Slack Factorizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses normwise additive error for a prescribed finite slack matrix and cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a nonnegative slack matrix \(S\in\mathbb{R}_+^{p\times q}\), a closed convex cone \(K\), a matrix norm \(\|\cdot\|\), and \(\varepsilon\ge0\). An \(\varepsilon\)-approximate \(K\)-factorization of \(S\) consists of \(a_i\in K\) and \(b_j\in K^*\) such that, for \(\widehat S_{ij}:=\langle a_i,b_j\rangle\),
\[
\|S-\widehat S\|\le\varepsilon.
\]
For entrywise tolerance, the defining condition is instead \( |S_{ij}-\widehat S_{ij}|\le\varepsilon\) for every \((i,j)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate slack factorization replaces exact slack entries by primal–dual cone inner products whose residual obeys a specified normwise or entrywise tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a finite-dimensional closed convex cone
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) has an \(\varepsilon\)-approximate \(K\)-factorization exactly when the displayed residual condition holds.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the topic, but it combines normwise and entrywise variants while the scope specifies normwise error. A source is needed to select and normalize the approximation convention used by the lift–factorization correspondence.

knowledge_statements.title: Inner–Outer Approximation Pairs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a centered multiplicative inner–outer approximation pair for a convex body.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a convex body with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), and let \(\alpha\ge1\). Convex bodies \(C_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(C_{\mathrm{out}}\) form an \(\alpha\)-multiplicative inner–outer approximation pair for \(C\) when
\[
0\in\operatorname{int}C_{\mathrm{in}},\qquad C_{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq C\subseteq C_{\mathrm{out}}\subseteq \alpha C_{\mathrm{in}}.
\]
Here dilation is about the common origin; a different center must be translated to the origin before applying this definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inner–outer pair sandwiches a centered convex body, with the outer approximation contained in an alpha dilation of the inner approximation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((C_{\mathrm{in}},C_{\mathrm{out}})\) is an \(\alpha\)-pair precisely under the displayed inclusions.

notation.meaning: origin-centered dilation of C by alpha

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The centered sandwich definition is coherent and the content kind fits, but the particular inner–outer multiplicative convention has no supporting citation.

children.title: Polarity Transformations
children.top_down_role: Polarity operations applied to lifted approximation settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Polarity Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the fundamental inclusion, scaling, and bipolar transformations for centered convex bodies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a convex body \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), define \(C^\circ:=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\le1\ \forall x\in C\}\). If \(C,D\) are such bodies and \(\lambda>0\), then
\[
C\subseteq D\Longrightarrow D^\circ\subseteq C^\circ,\qquad (\lambda C)^\circ=\lambda^{-1}C^\circ,\qquad (C^\circ)^\circ=C.
\]
Thus polarity is an inclusion-reversing involution, while positive dilation is transformed into reciprocal dilation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity reverses containment, converts scaling by lambda into scaling by its reciprocal, and returns a closed centered convex body after two applications.
assumptions_latex: \(C,D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) are convex bodies containing the origin in their interiors
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^\circ\subseteq C^\circ\), \((\lambda C)^\circ=\lambda^{-1}C^\circ\), and \((C^\circ)^\circ=C\).

notation.meaning: polar body of C with threshold one

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property correctly states standard polarity transformations under the given full-dimensional assumptions, but no inspectable source locator is supplied.

children.title: Approximation Transfer
children.top_down_role: Transfer of approximation guarantees across dual geometric descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfers a centered multiplicative outer approximation through polarity with reciprocal scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C,P\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex bodies with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\cap\operatorname{int}P\), and let \(\alpha\ge1\). If
\[
C\subseteq P\subseteq \alpha C,
\]
then polarity gives
\[
\alpha^{-1}C^\circ\subseteq P^\circ\subseteq C^\circ.
\]
Equivalently, after rescaling, \(C^\circ\subseteq\alpha P^\circ\subseteq\alpha C^\circ\). Hence the same multiplicative approximation factor transfers to the polar bodies, with containment direction reversed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A centered alpha-factor outer approximation becomes an alpha-factor inner approximation after polarity, with reciprocal scaling and reversed inclusions.
assumptions_latex: \(C,P\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) are convex bodies with the origin in both interiors
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha^{-1}C^\circ\subseteq P^\circ\subseteq C^\circ\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the leaf, and the reciprocal scaling and reversed inclusions are consistent, but the claim lacks an inspectable source locator.

children.title: Inner–Outer Role Reversal
children.top_down_role: Exchange of inner and outer approximation roles under polarity.

knowledge_statements.title: Inner–Outer Role Reversal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expresses how polarity exchanges inner and outer members of a convex-body sandwich.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q,C,P\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex bodies containing the origin in their interiors. The sandwich
\[
Q\subseteq C\subseteq P
\]
is transformed by polarity into
\[
P^\circ\subseteq C^\circ\subseteq Q^\circ.
\]
Consequently, the polar of the outer approximation \(P\) is an inner approximation of \(C^\circ\), whereas the polar of the inner approximation \(Q\) is an outer approximation of \(C^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under polarity, the outer approximant becomes an inner approximant of the polar body, and the inner approximant becomes an outer one.
assumptions_latex: \(Q,C,P\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) are convex bodies containing the origin in their interiors
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^\circ\subseteq C^\circ\subseteq Q^\circ\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property correctly expresses inner–outer role reversal under polarity, but no source with a specific locator is provided.

children.title: Nonfull-Dimensional Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Transfer limitations caused by lower-dimensional or improperly positioned sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonfull-Dimensional Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows why ambient polarity of a lower-dimensional bounded set need not be a convex body.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Ambient-space polarity does not preserve boundedness for lower-dimensional convex sets. For
\[
C=[-1,1]\times\{0\}\subset\mathbb{R}^2,
\]
one has
\[
C^\circ=\{(y_1,y_2)\in\mathbb{R}^2:|y_1|\le1\},
\]
which is unbounded in the \(y_2\)-direction. Thus convex-body polarity and multiplicative transfer statements requiring \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\) fail in the ambient space. They may be recovered using relative polarity inside \(\operatorname{aff}C\), after choosing the origin in \(\operatorname{relint}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-dimensional bounded set can have an unbounded ambient polar; relative polarity in its affine hull is needed to recover convex-body behavior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^\circ=\{(y_1,y_2):|y_1|\le1\}\) is unbounded.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample and failure-boundary kind fit the leaf, but the recovery claim involving translation and relative polarity requires an authoritative source.

children.title: Extension Complexity
children.top_down_role: Size measures, construction mechanisms, lower-bound methods, and restrictions for lifted formulations.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Expressing Combinatorial Optimization Problems by Linear Programs

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Extension Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts inequalities in the smallest polyhedral extended formulation of a polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a polytope \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), its linear extension complexity is
\[
\operatorname{xc}_{\mathrm{LP}}(P):=\min\left\{m:\exists d,\ A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d},\ b\in\mathbb{R}^m,\ \pi:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^n\text{ linear},\ P=\pi(\{y:Ay\le b\})\right\}.
\]
Only inequalities are counted; affine equalities used to describe the extension are free and may equivalently be eliminated. Redundant inequalities may be removed before counting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear extension complexity is the fewest inequalities in any polyhedron whose linear image equals the given polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}_{\mathrm{LP}}(P)\) equals the displayed minimum inequality count.

notation.meaning: linear projection map from the extension space

source_refs.locator: 2 From Linear Programming to Conic Programming p. 43

source_witnesses.locator: 2 From Linear Programming to Conic Programming p. 43

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and inequality-count convention fit the leaf, but the cited general conic-programming chapter is not an exact locator for extension complexity. The quantified extension dimension d also lacks an explicit domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Extension Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measures the smallest single PSD cone admitting an affine-slice lift of a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a closed convex set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), its semidefinite extension complexity is
\[
\operatorname{xc}_{\mathrm{SDP}}(C):=\inf\left\{r\in\mathbb{N}:\exists\text{ affine }L\subseteq\mathbb{S}^r,\ \exists\text{ linear }\pi:\mathbb{S}^r\to\mathbb{R}^n,\ C=\pi(L\cap\mathbb{S}_+^r)\right\}.
\]
The value is \(+\infty\) if no such lift exists. Under this convention, size means PSD matrix order, not the scalar dimension \(r(r+1)/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semidefinite extension complexity is the smallest PSD matrix order whose affine slice projects exactly onto the convex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}_{\mathrm{SDP}}(C)\) is the displayed minimum PSD order, or \(+\infty\).

notation.meaning: affine subspace defining the cone slice

source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry
source_refs.locator: 2.1 From Linear to Semidefinite Optimization p. 3

source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry
source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 From Linear to Semidefinite Optimization p. 3

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The PSD-lift definition and matrix-order convention fit the leaf, but the cited introductory SDP section does not specifically support semidefinite extension complexity or its size convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order-Cone Extension Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses total Lorentz-block dimension as the explicit size convention for SOC lifts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal{Q}^q:=\{(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{q-1}:t\ge\|x\|_2\}\). For a closed convex set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), define
\[
\operatorname{xc}_{\mathrm{SOC}}(C):=\inf\left\{\sum_{k=1}^s q_k:\exists\text{ affine }L,\ \exists\text{ linear }\pi,\ C=\pi\left(L\cap\prod_{k=1}^s\mathcal{Q}^{q_k}\right)\right\}.
\]
The value is \(+\infty\) when no finite product lift exists. This convention counts total cone dimension; counting blocks instead gives a different invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SOC extension complexity is the least total Lorentz-cone dimension in a product-cone affine lift projecting onto the convex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}_{\mathrm{SOC}}(C)\) is the displayed infimum of total block dimension.

source_refs.locator: 2 From Linear Programming to Conic Programming p. 43

source_witnesses.locator: 2 From Linear Programming to Conic Programming p. 43

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits, but total Lorentz-block dimension is a convention-dependent invariant not supported by the cited general chapter. The ambient space of L and the domain and codomain of π are also not stated.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Family Extension Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines exact lift size relative to a family of cones carrying a prescribed size map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal{K}\) be a family of finite-dimensional closed convex cones with size map \(\sigma:\mathcal{K}\to\mathbb{N}\). For a closed convex set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), define
\[
\operatorname{xc}_{\mathcal{K}}(C):=\inf\left\{\sigma(K):K\in\mathcal{K},\ \exists\text{ affine }L\subseteq\operatorname{span}K,\ \exists\text{ linear }\pi,\ C=\pi(K\cap L)\right\}.
\]
The value is \(+\infty\) if no member of \(\mathcal{K}\) yields an exact lift. Comparisons require the family and size map to be fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone-family extension complexity is the least declared size of a family member whose affine slice projects exactly onto the convex set.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{K}\) is a sized family of finite-dimensional closed convex cones
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}_{\mathcal{K}}(C)\) is the displayed infimum, or \(+\infty\).

source_refs.locator: 2 From Linear Programming to Conic Programming p. 43

source_witnesses.locator: 2 From Linear Programming to Conic Programming p. 43

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generalized definition fits the leaf, but the cited chapter does not establish this cone-family invariant or its prescribed size map. The domain and codomain of π must also be explicit.

children.title: Decomposition-Based Extensions
children.top_down_role: Extended formulations assembled from decomposed combinatorial or geometric pieces.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition-Based Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact tree-decomposition lift using local-configuration marginals and separator consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=(V,E)\) be a tree with bags \(B_t\), satisfying the running-intersection property, and let \(C_t\subseteq D^{B_t}\) be the permitted local configurations. Introduce \(\lambda_{t,a}\geq0\) for \(a\in C_t\), impose \(\sum_{a\in C_t}\lambda_{t,a}=1\), and, for every \(tt'\in E\) and \(s\in D^{B_t\cap B_{t'}}\), impose \[\sum_{a\in C_t:a|_{B_t\cap B_{t'}}=s}\lambda_{t,a}=\sum_{a'\in C_{t'}:a'|_{B_t\cap B_{t'}}=s}\lambda_{t',a'}.\] The projection defined by the induced coordinate marginals is exactly the convex hull of global assignments whose restriction to every bag belongs to \(C_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a running-intersection tree, normalized local-configuration weights with matching separator marginals form an exact extended formulation for globally compatible assignments.
assumptions_latex: The bags \((B_t)_{t\in V}\) satisfy running intersection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local-consistency lift projects onto the convex hull of feasible global assignments.

notation.meaning: bag associated with tree node t
weight assigned to local configuration a

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically plausible and fits the leaf, but the exact local-to-global consistency claim has no cited source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Dynamic-Programming Extensions
children.top_down_role: Extended formulations derived from finite-state dynamic-programming structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic-Programming Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path-flow formulation for a finite acyclic dynamic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(N,A)\) be a finite acyclic state-transition digraph with source \(s\), sink \(t\), and transition labels \(\ell_a\in\mathbb{R}^d\). For each arc introduce \(f_a\geq0\), impose one unit of flow from \(s\) to \(t\), and impose flow conservation at every other node. With \(x=\sum_{a\in A}\ell_a f_a\), the projection of this flow polytope is \[\operatorname{conv}\left\{\sum_{a\in P}\ell_a:P\text{ is an }s\text{-}t\text{ path in }G\right\}.\] Thus a dynamic program whose feasible objects correspond to such paths yields an extended formulation with one nonnegative variable per transition and one conservation equation per state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unit-flow polytope of an acyclic dynamic-programming graph projects to the convex hull of the outputs represented by source-to-sink paths.
assumptions_latex: Feasible objects correspond exactly to \(s\)-to-\(t\) paths.
Each transition has an additive output label.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The path-output polytope has a flow-based extended formulation of size \(O(|N|+|A|)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The acyclic unit-flow representation and its stated size are standard and locally appropriate, but no source supports the projection identity or complexity claim.

children.title: State-Space Lift Architecture
children.top_down_role: Lift variables and constraints indexed by dynamic-programming states.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Space Lift Architecture
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract lifted architecture indexed by states and admissible transitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite state-space lift for \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) consists of a directed state graph \(G=(N,A)\), nonnegative transition variables \(f\in\mathbb{R}_+^A\), affine conservation constraints \(Bf=b\), and an affine output map \(x=L f+c\), such that \[P=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:\exists f\in\mathbb{R}_+^A,\ Bf=b,\ x=Lf+c\right\}.\] States encode interface information retained between subproblems; arcs encode admissible local updates. Its formulation size is measured by the number of scalar conic inequalities and equations after redundant conservation equations are removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state-space lift represents a convex set as the affine image of nonnegative transition flows satisfying state-conservation equations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed projection identity defines an exact state-space lift of \(P\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the architecture leaf, but “state-space lift” and the proposed size convention require an authoritative source and precise locator.

children.title: Interface-Width Regimes
children.top_down_role: Extension-size behavior controlled by decomposition interfaces or state width.

knowledge_statements.title: Interface-Width Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Size bound for bounded-width, finite-domain decomposition lifts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a feasible family admits a tree decomposition with \(|V(T)|=m\), bag size at most \(w+1\), and variable domain of cardinality \(q\). If each bag state records a complete assignment on that bag, then there are at most \(q^{w+1}\) states per bag and at most \(q^{w+1}\) separator-consistency equations per tree edge. The standard local-marginal lift therefore has \[O\!\left(mq^{w+1}\right)\] variables and constraints. Consequently, for fixed \(q\) and fixed interface width \(w\), the resulting extension has size polynomial, indeed linear, in the number of decomposition nodes; unbounded \(w\) permits exponential growth through the state count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decomposition with domain size q and interface width w gives a lift of size proportional to the number of bags times q to the w plus one.
assumptions_latex: The decomposition has \(m\) bags of size at most \(w+1\).
Every original variable has at most \(q\) values.
Bag states enumerate complete local assignments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The formulation size is \(O(mq^{w+1})\), and is polynomial for fixed \(q\) and \(w\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counting argument is plausible and the complexity-bound kind fits the leaf, but the bound and its precise formulation-size convention are uncited.

children.title: Disjunctive Extensions
children.top_down_role: Extended formulations built from disjunctive structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Disjunctive Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balas-type formulation for the convex hull of a finite polyhedral disjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty bounded polyhedra \(P_i=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:A_i x\leq b_i\}\), where \(i=1,\ldots,k\), introduce \(x_i\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and selectors \(\lambda_i\geq0\). Then \[\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^k P_i\right)=\left\{x:\begin{array}{l}x=\sum_{i=1}^k x_i,\quad \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1,\\ A_i x_i\leq\lambda_i b_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,k),\quad \lambda_i\geq0\end{array}\right\}.\] Boundedness ensures that a block with \(\lambda_i=0\) contributes no nonzero recession direction. The formulation uses the homogenized constraints of every disjunct and one simplex constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homogenizing each bounded polyhedral disjunct and mixing the blocks with simplex weights gives an exact formulation of the union’s convex hull.
assumptions_latex: The number \(k\) of disjuncts is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed lifted system projects onto \(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_{i=1}^kP_i)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-polyhedron disjunctive formulation is mathematically standard and fits the representation leaf, but no Balas-type source or theorem locator is supplied.

children.title: Union-Based Extensions
children.top_down_role: Extended formulations for convex hulls or representations of unions.

knowledge_statements.title: Union-Based Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition bound from extended formulations of finitely many bounded components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty polytopes, and suppose \(P_i\) has an extended formulation \(Q_i=\{(x,y_i):E_i x+F_i y_i\leq g_i\}\) with \(r_i\) inequalities. Homogenize a separate copy of each \(Q_i\), scale it by \(\lambda_i\geq0\), impose \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\), and sum the component outputs. The resulting system projects onto \(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iP_i)\) and has at most \[\sum_{i=1}^k r_i+k\] inequalities, apart from equations. Hence \(\operatorname{xc}(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iP_i))\leq\sum_i\operatorname{xc}(P_i)+k\) under this inequality-count convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extended formulations of finitely many polytopes can be homogenized and combined, yielding a union-hull formulation whose size is essentially the sum of component sizes.
assumptions_latex: Formulation size counts inequalities and ignores equations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iP_i))\leq\sum_i\operatorname{xc}(P_i)+k\).

notation.meaning: number of inequalities in the component formulation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem and additive inequality bound fit the union-extension leaf, but the homogenization result and the +k convention lack cited support.

children.title: Selector-Variable Architectures
children.top_down_role: Lift architectures that encode membership among alternative components.

knowledge_statements.title: Selector-Variable Architectures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selector formulation distinguishing an exact disjunction from its convex-hull relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For bounded polyhedra \(P_i=\{x:A_i x\leq b_i\}\), introduce block variables \(x_i\) and selectors \(\lambda_i\). The system \[x=\sum_i x_i,\qquad A_i x_i\leq\lambda_i b_i,\qquad \sum_i\lambda_i=1\] represents \(\bigcup_iP_i\) when \(\lambda\in\{0,1\}^k\), because exactly one component is active. Replacing integrality by \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^k\) gives an ideal convexification in the original space: its projection is \(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iP_i)\). Thus selector variables encode component choice, while the component blocks prevent constraints belonging to inactive alternatives from restricting \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary selectors model the union itself; relaxing them to simplex weights in the homogenized block formulation yields exactly the convex hull.
assumptions_latex: Each component \(P_i\) is nonempty and bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Binary selectors project to \(\bigcup_iP_i\), while continuous simplex selectors project to \(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iP_i)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary and continuous selector claims are plausible under boundedness and fit the architecture leaf, but neither exact projection claim has an inspectable citation.

children.title: Overlapping-Component Regimes
children.top_down_role: Representation behavior when union components share substantial structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Overlapping-Component Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of non-disjoint components on union-hull formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_1,\ldots,P_k\) be nonempty bounded polyhedra, without any disjointness assumption. The homogenized selector formulation remains exact for \(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iP_i)\). If a point \(x\) lies in several components, then it can have several valid lifts, including lifts using different unit selectors and convex mixtures of component representations. This nonuniqueness does not enlarge the projection: every lifted point is a convex combination of points drawn from the components, and every such convex combination admits a lift. Consequently, component overlap changes neither validity nor the additive formulation-size bound, although it may create redundant blocks and inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Overlapping components cause nonunique lifted representations but do not invalidate the homogenized union-hull formulation or worsen its standard additive size bound.
assumptions_latex: Each \(P_i\) is a nonempty bounded polyhedron.
The family of components is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Overlap affects lift uniqueness and redundancy, but the projection remains \(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iP_i)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The overlap property is consistent with the homogenized disjunctive formulation and fits the leaf, but its validity and additive-size assertion are unsupported by a citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry-Adapted Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivariant extended formulations preserving a prescribed finite group action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite group \(G\) act linearly on \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\). An extended formulation \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) with affine projection \(\pi:Q\to P\) is \(G\)-symmetric if there is an action \(g\mapsto\rho_g\) by affine automorphisms of \(Q\) such that \[\rho_g(Q)=Q\quad\text{and}\quad \pi(\rho_g(y))=g\,\pi(y)\] for every \(g\in G\) and \(y\in Q\). Its symmetric extension complexity is the minimum number of inequalities among all such equivariant formulations. This restricted minimum can exceed unrestricted extension complexity because a smaller lift may break the action of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetry-adapted extension carries a lifted group action preserving the feasible lift and commuting with projection to the original symmetric set.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is a finite-dimensional polyhedral extension of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equivariance of \(Q\), its lifted action, and \(\pi\) defines a \(G\)-symmetric extension.

notation.meaning: lifted affine action of group element g
projection from the lift to P

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is locally relevant, but admissible lifted group actions and symmetric extension complexity depend on convention; an authoritative definition with locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Factorization-Rank Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Yannakakis correspondence between linear extensions and nonnegative slack factorizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be a polytope with facet description \(Ax\leq b\), vertices \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\), and slack matrix \(S\) defined by \(S_{ij}=b_i-A_i v_j\). Under the convention that extension complexity counts inequalities and redundant rows and columns are removed, \[\operatorname{xc}(P)=\operatorname{rank}_+(S),\] where \(\operatorname{rank}_+(S)\) is the least \(r\) for which \(S=TU\) with \(T\in\mathbb{R}_+^{m\times r}\) and \(U\in\mathbb{R}_+^{r\times n}\). Therefore every lower bound on the nonnegative rank of a slack matrix is a lower bound on linear extension complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polytope’s linear extension complexity equals the nonnegative rank of its slack matrix, converting factorization-rank bounds into extension lower bounds.
assumptions_latex: Rows of \(S\) index facets and columns index vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}(P)=\operatorname{rank}_+(S)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The central equality is a theorem rather than a duality record and needs a Yannakakis theorem citation. Its dimensional or degenerate-polytope conventions should also be made explicit after sourcing.

children.title: Support Methods
children.top_down_role: Lower bounds derived from support patterns of slack data.

knowledge_statements.title: Support Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boolean-support lower bound for nonnegative rank and extension complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonnegative matrix \(S\), let \(M\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\) satisfy \(M_{ij}=1\) exactly when \(S_{ij}>0\). Let \(\operatorname{rc}(M)\) be the minimum number of combinatorial rectangles contained in the one-entries of \(M\) whose union covers every one-entry. Every nonnegative rank-one summand has rectangular support, so any nonnegative factorization of inner dimension \(r\) supplies a cover by at most \(r\) rectangles. Hence \[\operatorname{rank}_+(S)\geq\operatorname{rc}(M).\] If \(S\) is a slack matrix of \(P\), then \(\operatorname{xc}(P)\geq\operatorname{rc}(M)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Covering the positive support of a slack matrix by one-rectangles lower-bounds its nonnegative rank and therefore the polytope’s extension complexity.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is the Boolean support matrix of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}_+(S)\geq\operatorname{rc}(M)\), and for slack matrices \(\operatorname{xc}(P)\geq\operatorname{rc}(M)\).

notation.meaning: nonnegative matrix, typically a slack matrix

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The support-cover lower bound is mathematically standard and the complexity-bound kind fits, but the nonnegative-rank and extension-complexity implications are uncited.

children.title: Rectangle Methods
children.top_down_role: Lower bounds based on rectangle covers or partitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Rectangle Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rectangle-cover obstruction as a verifiable extension-complexity certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\). A one-rectangle is a product \(R=I\times J\) such that \(M_{ij}=1\) for every \((i,j)\in R\). To certify a lower bound \(k+1\) by the rectangle method, exhibit a set \(F\) of one-entries such that every one-rectangle contains at most one member of \(F\), with \(|F|=k+1\). Any rectangle cover of the one-support must then use at least \(k+1\) rectangles. For the support matrix of a polytope slack matrix, this certificate implies \[\operatorname{xc}(P)\geq\operatorname{rc}(M)\geq|F|=k+1.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set of positive entries no valid one-rectangle can cover twice certifies a rectangle-cover, nonnegative-rank, and extension-complexity lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is the Boolean support of a slack matrix of \(P\).
Every one-rectangle contains at most one element of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}(P)\geq|F|\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed certificate is specifically a fooling-set certificate—pairwise rectangle-incompatible entries—and therefore belongs to the immutable sibling “Fooling-Set Methods,” not the broader “Rectangle Methods” leaf. It is also uncited.

children.title: Fooling-Set Methods
children.top_down_role: Lower bounds based on mutually incompatible slack entries.

knowledge_statements.title: Fooling-Set Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-based certificate for the nonnegative rank of a finite nonnegative matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\mathbb{R}_+^{I\times J}\), where \(I\) and \(J\) are finite. A fooling set is a set \(F=\{(i_t,j_t):t=1,\ldots,k\}\) such that \(M_{i_tj_t}>0\) for every \(t\) and, for all distinct \(s,t\), at least one of \(M_{i_sj_t}\) and \(M_{i_tj_s}\) is zero. Then \[\operatorname{rank}_+(M)\ge |F|=k.\] If an applicable factorization theorem identifies an extension size with \(\operatorname{rank}_+(M)\), the same fooling set certifies an extension-size lower bound of \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fooling set of k positive entries, with a zero in every crossed pair, certifies nonnegative rank at least k and conditionally gives the corresponding extension-size lower bound.
assumptions_latex: The extension-size conclusion requires an applicable factorization theorem identifying extension size with \(\operatorname{rank}_+(M)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}_+(M)\ge |F|\).

notation.meaning: fooling set of positive entries of M

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard fooling-set lower bound for nonnegative rank

children.title: Combinatorial Method Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Relative strength and transfer among support, rectangle, and fooling-set arguments.

knowledge_statements.title: Combinatorial Method Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of fooling-set, rectangle-cover, and nonnegative-rank lower-bound parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite matrix \(M\in\mathbb{R}_+^{I\times J}\), let \(\operatorname{fs}(M)\) be its maximum fooling-set cardinality. Let \(\operatorname{supp}_+(M)=\{(i,j)\in I\times J:M_{ij}>0\}\), and let \(\operatorname{rc}(M)\) be the minimum number of combinatorial rectangles contained in \(\operatorname{supp}_+(M)\) whose union is \(\operatorname{supp}_+(M)\). Then \[\operatorname{fs}(M)\le \operatorname{rc}(M)\le \operatorname{rank}_+(M).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum fooling-set size is at most the positive-support rectangle-cover number, which is at most nonnegative rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{fs}(M)\le \operatorname{rc}(M)\le \operatorname{rank}_+(M)\).

notation.meaning: index set of positive entries of M

children.title: Deterministic Communication Methods
children.top_down_role: Extension-complexity bounds derived from deterministic communication models.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Communication Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative-rank lower bound for exact deterministic communication with constant terminal outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) and \(J\) be finite, and let \(M\in\mathbb{R}_+^{I\times J}\). Suppose an exact deterministic binary protocol receives \(i\in I\) and \(j\in J\), communicates at most \(c\in\mathbb{N}_0\) bits, and has a constant nonnegative output on each terminal transcript equal to \(M_{ij}\) for every input reaching that transcript. Then \[\operatorname{rank}_+(M)\le 2^c\quad\text{and}\quad c\ge\left\lceil\log_2\operatorname{rank}_+(M)\right\rceil.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated exact constant-terminal-output model, deterministic communication cost is at least the base-two logarithm of nonnegative rank.
assumptions_latex: The protocol is deterministic, binary, and exact.
Every terminal transcript has a constant nonnegative output.
\(c\in\mathbb{N}_0\) is the worst-case number of communicated bits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c\ge\left\lceil\log_2\operatorname{rank}_+(M)\right\rceil\).
review_flags: constant-terminal-output convention must be matched to the cited source

children.title: Randomized Communication Methods

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Communication Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Communication bound for finite nonnegative-output expectation protocols with factorizable terminal contributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) and \(J\) be finite and let \(M\in\mathbb{R}_+^{I\times J}\). Consider a private-coin protocol with a finite terminal-transcript set \(\mathcal{T}\), worst-case communication cost \(c\in\mathbb{N}_0\), and nonnegative output whose expectation on input \((i,j)\) is \(M_{ij}\). Assume that for every \(\tau\in\mathcal{T}\), the expected contribution of terminal transcript \(\tau\) has the form \(u_\tau(i)v_\tau(j)\), where \(u_\tau\in\mathbb{R}_+^I\) and \(v_\tau\in\mathbb{R}_+^J\). Then \[\operatorname{rank}_+(M)\le |\mathcal{T}|\le 2^c,\qquad c\ge\left\lceil\log_2\operatorname{rank}_+(M)\right\rceil.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite private-coin expectation protocol whose nonnegative terminal contributions factor by the two inputs yields nonnegative rank at most its number of terminal transcripts and hence at most two to its communication cost.
assumptions_latex: The protocol has finitely many terminal transcripts and communicates at most \(c\) bits.
The output is nonnegative and has expectation \(M_{ij}\) on every input \((i,j)\).
Each terminal transcript has a factorizable expected contribution \(u_\tau(i)v_\tau(j)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}_+(M)\le |\mathcal{T}|\le 2^c\).

notation.meaning: nonnegative input-side factors for transcript τ
